caution: Wild watercress gathered from streams shared with grazing livestock can carry liver flukes; it should only be picked from clean, cold, fast-moving water well away from pastureland.

name: Peppergrass
people: Southern rural households, including a documented Civil War-era pepper-substitute use
use: Leaves used as a pepper substitute and gathered as 'creasy greens' in early spring
method: Young leaves were gathered in early spring as “creasy greens” and cooked like other bitter wild greens, while the dried seeds were crushed and used as a sharp, peppery seasoning.
note: During the Civil War, with imported black pepper scarce and costly behind naval blockades, Southern households leaned on peppergrass and other home-grown stand-ins to season food — a small, specific way the war reached straight into the pantry.

name: Royal Jelly
use: A beekeeping product taken as a general health tonic
method: Harvested from the specially provisioned cells bees build to raise a queen, the thick white substance was eaten directly by the spoonful, or sold in small jars and capsules as a health-food supplement.
note: Royal jelly’s American popularity rode a mid-20th-century health-food wave alongside things like wheat germ and bee pollen, leaning on the genuinely striking biology of an ordinary larva transformed into a queen bee by royal jelly alone — even though that effect doesn’t carry over to humans who eat it.

name: Nutritional Yeast
use: Deactivated yeast flakes eaten as a vitamin and general-health supplement
method: Deactivated yeast, a byproduct of brewing and other fermentation, was dried into flakes or powder and sprinkled over food or stirred into drinks, prized for a savory, almost cheesy flavor as much as its vitamin content.
note: Nutritional yeast rode the same early-to-mid-20th-century American health-food wave as royal jelly, and it got a particular boost from vegetarian advocates, who valued it as a rare plant-based source of B vitamins, including B12.

name: Limewater
people: American households following pediatrician L. Emmett Holt's widely-followed infant-feeding guidance, late 19th/early 20th century
use: Mixed into infant formula to help settle a baby's digestion
method: A small amount of slaked lime was dissolved in water and left to settle and clear, and the clear liquid poured off the top was stirred into cow’s-milk infant formula in careful proportions to make it easier on a baby’s stomach.
note: L. Emmett Holt’s 1894 guide “The Care and Feeding of Children” became one of the most influential American parenting manuals of its era, and limewater-in-formula was standard enough advice to turn up across decades of pediatric guidance and home-nursing manuals that followed it.
caution: Limewater is an alkaline solution, and too much — or too concentrated a mix — can upset the careful balance infant formula needs; it was meant to be used in small, precisely measured amounts, not improvised.

name: Beef Tea (Bone Broth)
people: American households, following period cookery and invalid-care manuals
use: Broth made by simmering beef bones and meat, given to the sick and convalescent for strength
method: Lean beef and bones were simmered low and slow, sometimes for many hours (or, in the “raw beef tea” method meant to preserve more nutrients, barely simmered at all), then strained into a clear, savory broth given by the spoonful or cupful to invalids and convalescents.
note: Victorian-era doctors and nurses debated beef tea’s real nutritional value even at the time — despite its rich smell and taste, strained beef tea actually contains very little protein, which makes it more of a comforting, appetite-stirring ritual than the restorative food it was believed to be.

name: Peanut Oil Massage (Carver's Polio Treatment)
people: George Washington Carver, promoted to the American public, 1930s
use: Peanut oil massage promoted by Carver as a treatment for polio-related muscle weakness
method: Warm peanut oil was massaged into weakened or paralyzed limbs, sometimes paired with light exercise, following a regimen Carver developed and publicized through his Tuskegee Institute correspondence and public talks.
note: Carver was careful to describe the massage as easing circulation and comfort rather than a cure, but during the era’s polio panic the press and public ran further with the story than Carver’s own claims — patients and families traveled to Tuskegee by the hundreds hoping for relief.

name: Poison Ivy
people: Documented in old American medical records as an experimental irritant, and in homeopathic 'Rhus tox' preparations
use: Historically tested as an irritant/counter-irritant in old medical records and used in tiny homeopathic doses for rheumatic complaints
method: Physicians sometimes deliberately applied poison ivy extract to the skin as a counter-irritant, and homeopaths prepared “Rhus toxicodendron” by diluting a tincture of the plant so many times over that, by the final preparation, not a single molecule of the original plant typically remained.
note: That extreme dilution isn’t unique to poison ivy — it’s standard homeopathic practice, built on the founding idea that a substance grows more potent the more it’s diluted, which is also exactly why mainstream science considers homeopathic remedies pharmacologically inert.
caution: Causes severe allergic contact dermatitis (urushiol) in the great majority of people who touch it. This entry documents historical curiosity only — never handle, burn, or apply poison ivy in any form.

name: Kentucky Coffeetree Seeds
people: Pioneer households, used as a coffee substitute when real coffee was unavailable
use: Roasted seeds used as a pioneer-era coffee substitute
method: Seed pods were gathered in fall, and the hard seeds inside were roasted long and thoroughly — a non-negotiable step — before being ground and brewed like coffee grounds.
note: The tree’s Latin name, Gymnocladus dioicus, means “naked branch,” a nod to its stark, coarse winter silhouette, and pioneers reached for its seeds as a coffee substitute mainly out of necessity, since real coffee was an expensive, hard-to-get import on the frontier and again scarce during wartime shortages.
caution: The raw seeds and pods contain toxic compounds (cytisine-like alkaloids) and are unsafe unless thoroughly roasted; historically, improperly prepared seeds caused poisoning. Documented as history only, not a recommendation.

name: Dutchman's Breeches
people: Documented mainly as a livestock hazard on American farms
use: Known historically mainly as a poisonous plant causing 'staggers' in grazing livestock, not as a human remedy
note: The odd common name comes from the flower’s shape — it really does look uncannily like a tiny pair of pantaloons hung upside down to dry. Unlike many toxic plants that still turn up in the old medical record in tiny homeopathic doses, Dutchman’s breeches barely appears in human folk-remedy writing at all; its documented legacy is almost entirely as a plant farmers learned to watch for and keep grazing animals away from.
caution: Contains isoquinoline alkaloids that are toxic if ingested, historically causing tremors and 'staggers' in livestock. Not a safe home remedy in any form.

name: Baneberry
people: Recognized and avoided across many Eastern Woodlands communities and settler households
use: Historically known and avoided as a dangerously poisonous plant ('doll's eyes'), not used as a remedy
note: Its common nickname, “doll’s eyes,” comes from the white berries’ unsettling look — each one tipped with a dark leftover flower scar that really does resemble a small staring pupil, which made it a plant parents pointed out to children by name so they’d remember to leave it alone.
caution: All parts of the plant, especially the berries, are highly toxic and can cause cardiac symptoms if eaten. This is documented as a recognized poison only — never ingest any part of this plant.

name: Fly Agaric Mushroom
people: Documented in general American mycological/folk knowledge as a toxic and psychoactive mushroom
use: Historically recognized as a toxic, psychoactive mushroom rather than a remedy
note: Fly agaric gets its common name from an old, only partly reliable European practice of crumbling the cap into milk to stun or kill flies; its bright red-and-white cap is also the classic storybook “toadstool” image, which is part of why it’s so recognizable despite being genuinely dangerous.
caution: Contains toxic and psychoactive compounds (muscimol, ibotenic acid) that cause serious illness and can be fatal, especially if misidentified. Never eat this mushroom.

name: Destroying Angel Mushroom
people: Documented in American mycological history as one of the deadliest wild mushrooms
use: Not a remedy of any kind — historically significant only as a lethal poisonous mushroom, frequently fatally confused with edible species
note: Destroying angels are especially dangerous because the early symptoms — vomiting and cramping — fade after a day, creating a false sense of recovery before severe, often fatal liver and kidney damage sets in days later.
caution: One of the deadliest mushrooms in North America; ingestion causes fatal liver and kidney failure and there is no reliable folk antidote. Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification.

name: Moonseed
people: Recognized and avoided by foragers as a toxic wild-grape lookalike
use: Chiefly notable as a poisonous vine easily confused with true wild grapes, not as a remedy
note: The name comes from the shape of the seed inside each berry, which curves into a distinctive crescent — the one reliable way experienced foragers learned to tell it apart from true wild grape seeds, which are shaped more like a teardrop.
caution: The berries closely resemble wild grapes but contain toxic alkaloids; ingestion can cause serious poisoning. Never eat unless positively identified by an expert.

name: Death Camas
people: Western Indigenous nations, who worked hard to distinguish it from the edible camas root it closely resembles
use: Not a remedy — historically significant as a deadly poison that Indigenous root-gatherers had to carefully avoid while harvesting edible camas
note: Death camas and edible blue camas often share the very same meadows and look nearly identical until they flower — death camas blooms cream-white, true camas blooms blue — which is exactly why experienced root-diggers waited until after the bloom, when the two could no longer be confused.
caution: All parts of this plant are highly toxic and can be fatal if ingested; it closely resembles the edible camas lily and has caused fatal poisonings from misidentification. Never eat any part of this plant.

name: California Pipevine (Birthwort)
use: Root historically used medicinally by some California Indigenous communities, in the same family as the archive's Virginia Snakeroot
method: The root was dried and prepared as a decoction, in the same general tradition as other Aristolochia “snakeroot” medicines.
note: Aristolochia’s toxicity wasn’t pinned down scientifically until quite recently — aristolochic acid was only conclusively linked to kidney failure and cancer in the 1990s and 2000s, after poisoning outbreaks traced to Aristolochia in herbal weight-loss preparations, long after traditional use had begun.
caution: Aristolochia species contain aristolochic acid, now recognized as a potent kidney toxin and carcinogen. Documented as historical use only — this plant should not be used medicinally.

name: Pomegranate Root Bark
people: 19th-century American medicine, drawn from a long Old World tradition
use: Root bark decoction historically used as a tapeworm remedy
method: The bark was stripped from the root, dried, and boiled into a decoction, carefully dosed and often followed by a purgative to help expel the tapeworm afterward.
note: Pomegranate root bark’s use against tapeworms is ancient, described in Sanskrit and Greek medical texts long before it crossed the Atlantic, and it remained an official entry in the U.S. Pharmacopeia into the 20th century before safer synthetic dewormers replaced it.
caution: The alkaloid (pelletierine) that made root-bark tea effective against tapeworms is also toxic in excess and historically caused dangerous side effects at the doses needed to work. Documented as history only.

name: Cannabis (Hemp) Tincture
people: American pharmacies and patent-medicine makers, 19th century
use: A tincture made from the flowering tops, official in the U.S. Pharmacopeia and sold for pain, spasms, and sleeplessness
method: Flowering tops were dried and extracted in alcohol into a tincture, standardized as best the era’s methods allowed and dispensed by the dropperful for pain, muscle spasm, and insomnia.
note: Cannabis tincture was official in the U.S. Pharmacopeia from 1850 until 1942, sold openly under brand names by major pharmaceutical makers of the day like Parke-Davis and Eli Lilly — a mainstream medicine-cabinet item, not a fringe one, until shifting law and medical fashion pushed it out.
caution: Historical tincture dosing was highly unpredictable and cannabis is a controlled substance today; this entry documents 19th-century pharmacy history only, not a usable or legal remedy.

name: Artist's Conk
use: The smooth underside of this bracket fungus was etched with a fine point and used as a folk-art 'canvas'
method: The smooth white underside of a fresh bracket fungus was scratched or scored with a fine point — any pressure on that surface bruises it dark brown, which is what makes the etching visible — then the fungus was dried, permanently fixing the design.
note: That same bruising reaction is a handy field trick for foragers generally — several bracket fungi darken distinctively where they’re scratched, which experienced mushroom hunters use to help tell similar-looking species apart.

name: Dryad's Saddle
use: A wild mushroom eaten for its distinctive watermelon-rind flavor when young
method: Young caps — the older ones turn tough and woody — were sliced and sautéed, prized for a smell and taste foragers often compare to fresh watermelon rind or cucumber.
note: The name comes from old European folklore, picturing the fungus’s wide, saddle-shaped shelf as a fitting seat for a dryad, a tree spirit — an apt bit of whimsy for a mushroom that grows in tiers straight out of the trunks of dying or dead hardwoods.

name: Oyster Mushroom
use: A common wild mushroom gathered and eaten as food
method: Found growing in shelf-like, overlapping clusters on dead or dying hardwood trunks — beech, poplar, maple — especially after fall rains, and cut free at the base with a knife. Eaten fresh sautéed in butter, or threaded on string and hung to dry for winter, since oyster mushrooms dry unusually well.
note: Named for their shape and faint briny smell rather than any relation to the shellfish. They're also one of the safer mushrooms for a beginner to gather — the genus has very few dangerous lookalikes, which is part of why they stayed a reliable, trusted forager's mushroom across generations.

name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
use: A distinctive wild mushroom eaten as food
method: The whole toothy, cascading clump was cut from a wound or scar on a living or dead hardwood — oak and beech especially — in late summer or fall, then sliced and pan-fried, its meaty texture often compared to crab or lobster. It can also be torn into pieces and dried for later use.
note: The dangling spines rather than gills earned it a string of folk names — bearded tooth, pom-pom, satyr's beard, bear's head — long before 'lion's mane' became the common one.

name: Maitake (Hen of the Woods)
use: A prized wild mushroom gathered and eaten by Italian-American and Appalachian foragers
method: Cut in whole rosette clusters from the base of oak trees — often the very same tree, in the same spot, year after year, which is why foragers guard their 'hen spots' as closely held family secrets. Sliced and sautéed, added to soups, or dried and strung for winter use.
note: The English name describes the ruffled, overlapping fronds, which do resemble a hen's fluffed feathers; Italian-American foragers around New York and New Jersey often call it by its Italian name, and treat the location of a good hen tree as inheritance-worthy information.

name: Berkeley's Polypore
use: A minor wild mushroom gathered and eaten as food
method: Harvested young and tender from tiered, fan-shaped clusters at the base of oak and other hardwood trees — it toughens and turns bitter fast with age, so timing mattered. Sliced thin and fried, since older specimens are too tough to chew.
note: It's named for the English clergyman-mycologist Miles Joseph Berkeley, who catalogued huge numbers of fungi in the 1800s. The mushroom itself never picked up a widely used folk name of its own, which is part of why it stayed a minor, locally known edible rather than a widely marketed one.

name: Cauliflower Mushroom
use: A choice wild edible mushroom gathered and eaten as food
method: Found growing in a single dense, ruffled mass at the base of pine and other conifers, cut free whole. The folds trap dirt, pine needles, and insects, so it needed careful rinsing before slicing and sautéing, or drying for later use — its noodle-like texture holds up well either way.
note: The lobed, ruffled shape is what earns it both of its common names — cauliflower mushroom in most places, and 'noodle mushroom' in some regional accounts, for how the sliced strips look and cook.

name: Shaggy Mane Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom eaten as food while young; its inky, self-dissolving cap was also sometimes used as a curiosity ink
method: Picked young, while the cap is still tight and white, because the mushroom self-digests into black ink within hours — it had to be cooked the same day, usually sautéed. Older, already-inking caps were sometimes collected on purpose and simmered down to produce a genuine, usable writing ink.
note: That self-dissolving ('deliquescing') habit is where both the food-safety rule and the ink-making trick come from — it's the same process just caught at two different points. Some 19th-century naturalists really did write field notes with shaggy mane ink.

name: Morel Mushroom
use: A highly prized wild mushroom gathered every spring, especially across the Midwest
method: Hunted on foot each spring — often around dying elms, ash, or old apple trees, or the spring after a forest fire — and sliced lengthwise both to check for insects and to confirm the cap is genuinely hollow, the test for a true morel. Always cooked before eating, classically soaked in salted water, dredged in flour, and fried in butter.
note: Morel hunting became such a fixture of Midwestern spring life that Michigan still runs a National Morel Mushroom Festival, and dedicated hunters famously keep their best patches secret even from family.
caution: True morels must be cooked — eaten raw they cause real stomach upset — and they have a toxic lookalike, the false morel, which is solid or cotton-filled inside rather than hollow.

name: Lobster Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom prized as food for its color and texture
method: Gathered whole from the forest floor wherever the parasitic mold has taken over a host Russula or Lactarius mushroom, turning it a deep orange-red and unusually firm. Sliced and sautéed in butter, where its dense, almost seafood-like texture holds up far better than the soft mushroom it started as.
note: It isn't really one mushroom — it's a parasitic mold that infects certain gilled mushrooms and essentially takes them over, turning the host orange-red, firming its flesh, and erasing its gills. What foragers pick and eat is the infected mushroom, transformed by the mold into something entirely different.

name: Blewit Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom carried into American use by European-immigrant foraging tradition
method: Gathered from leaf litter in late fall — often one of the last mushrooms of the season, sometimes appearing after the first frost — and always cooked, since it causes stomach upset eaten raw. Sliced and sautéed, its lilac color fading to tan as it cooks.
note: The name is an old English dialect corruption of 'blue hat' or 'blue coat,' describing the violet cap and stem that fade once cooked — a naming habit European foragers simply carried across the Atlantic along with the mushroom-hunting itself.

name: King Bolete (Porcini)
use: A prized wild mushroom central to Italian-American foraging tradition
method: Cut at the base wherever it fruits under pine, oak, or spruce — its underground threads live in partnership with those very tree roots. Some was sliced fresh for the pan, but most was sliced thin and dried, strung up near a stove or in the sun, since drying concentrates porcini into an intensely flavorful seasoning that keeps for a year or more.
note: Italian immigrant families turned autumn mushroom hunting ('cercare funghi') into one of the most durable food traditions carried into America — dried porcini from a family's own hunting grounds were, and still are, treated as a prized pantry staple rather than a store-bought spice.

name: Matsutake Mushroom
use: A highly prized wild mushroom central to Japanese-American Pacific Northwest foraging culture
method: Found by scent as much as sight — its strong spicy-pine aroma gives away a patch under specific conifers, often in sandy soil. Pulled or carefully twisted free rather than cut, and pickers traditionally cover the disturbed ground back over with duff so the same patch keeps fruiting in later years.
note: Oregon's matsutake harvest grew into a real export economy serving Japan, where the mushroom carries far greater prestige and price than in general American cooking — a rare case of a foraging tradition becoming genuine international trade rather than staying a private household habit.

name: Saffron Milkcap Mushroom
use: A wild mushroom carried into American use by European-immigrant foraging tradition
method: Identified by the orange, saffron-colored 'milk' that oozes out when the gills are cut or broken — flesh and milk both bruise green with handling or age. Found under pines, sliced, and pan-fried; in some European-immigrant households it was also salted and packed in jars for winter, a method carried over from the old country.
note: The green bruising can look alarming to anyone unfamiliar with it, but it's completely normal for the species — European foragers who grew up with it used that exact color change to confirm they had the right mushroom, not to reject it.

name: Russula Mushrooms
use: A large, variable-quality genus of wild mushrooms gathered by foragers
method: Identified in the field partly by texture — Russula flesh snaps cleanly like chalk rather than tearing like most mushrooms — and partly by an old, widely used field test: a tiny nibble, chewed and spat out rather than swallowed. A mild or nutty taste meant the mushroom was probably safe to cook; a peppery, acrid bite meant leaving it alone.
note: Because the genus swings from genuinely delicious to inedible or mildly toxic species that often look alike, foragers leaned on that taste-and-spit test rather than on appearance alone — one of the few wild-mushroom identification tricks where flavor itself is treated as real evidence.
caution: Some Russula species are mildly toxic and cause stomach upset — the traditional taste test screens out the acrid ones, but it is not a foolproof safety method on its own.

name: Dulse (Pacific)
use: A red seaweed dried and eaten as food
method: Hand-picked from intertidal rocks at low tide, then spread on rocks or racks in the sun to dry — the traditional way to preserve any dulse, whether Atlantic or Pacific. Eaten dried as a chewy, salty snack, or torn into soups and chowders.
note: It's easy to lump all dulse together, but the Pacific and Atlantic seaweeds sold under that name are different species entirely, harvested independently on opposite coasts rather than through any shared migration of the tradition.

name: Laver
use: Widely dried and eaten as food by many Pacific coast peoples
method: Picked from intertidal rocks, rinsed, and dried in thin sheets or pressed cakes on rocks or woven mats in the sun — dried this way it kept for months and could be crumbled into soups or eaten on its own as a savory snack.
note: The same genus of seaweed became a staple food independently on at least three continents with no contact between the traditions — as laver in Wales, nori in Japan, and here among Pacific coast peoples — a case of very different cultures arriving at nearly the same food from the same plant.

name: Kombu-like Kelp
use: Eaten and used to wrap food for cooking
method: Harvested by cutting the blades from rocks at low tide, then used two ways: some was dried for later eating, and some was used fresh, wrapped around fish, shellfish, or roots as a moist wrapper for pit-cooking or steaming over hot stones.
note: Using kelp as a natural steaming wrapper is a practical trick — the wide, waterproof blade holds in moisture the way corn husks or large leaves do in other food traditions — and shows up independently in several Pacific coast cooking methods.

name: Eelgrass
people: Cape Cod and Long Island settler communities
use: Limited food use, and a later settler-era industrial use as dried insulation and upholstery stuffing
method: Raked up after storms washed it ashore in windrows, or cut directly from shallow beds, then dried. Dried eelgrass was baled and pressed into insulation board or loose-packed into wall cavities and furniture as a cheap, fire-resistant stuffing — an industry that ran along the Cape Cod and Long Island shore into the early 20th century.
note: That whole industry collapsed almost overnight in the early 1930s when a mysterious wasting disease wiped out most of the Atlantic coast's eelgrass beds — the same blight that also starved out the scallops and brant geese that depended on eelgrass meadows, making it as much an ecological turning point as an industrial one.

name: Kelp Iodine Industry
people: American industrial chemists, including a WWI-era California kelp-potash industry
use: Processed industrially for iodine and potash rather than used as a home remedy
method: Giant kelp was cut from beds off the Southern California coast using specially built harvesting vessels, then hauled to shoreside plants and processed by fermentation and chemical extraction into potash (for fertilizer and munitions) and iodine (used as a medical antiseptic).
note: The whole industry was a wartime improvisation: World War I cut off Germany's potash exports, so American companies built kelp-processing plants along the California coast almost overnight. Most shut back down within a few years once cheaper mineral potash sources returned after the war.

name: Sugar Kelp
use: Eaten as food
method: Cut from shallow subtidal rocks, then dried in the sun on lines or racks — the fronds develop a white, sugary bloom on their surface as they dry, which is where the name comes from. Eaten dried as a snack or simmered into soups and stews.
note: That white 'sugar' coating is mannitol, a natural sugar alcohol the kelp produces — it's genuinely sweet to the taste, not just a figure of speech, which is why so many languages that name this kelp call it some version of 'sweet' or 'sugar' kelp.

name: Winged Kelp (American Wakame)
use: Eaten as food, prepared like Japanese wakame
method: Cut from rocks in the low intertidal zone, then dried or salted the same way wakame is prepared in Japan — rehydrated by soaking before use. Softened this way, it went into miso soup and simple vinegared salads much as true wakame would.
note: It isn't the same species as Japanese wakame, just a close enough Pacific relative that Japanese-American households recognized it and adapted their own preparation to a plant growing right on their new coastline instead of importing the real thing.

name: Puffball for Sores (Yuki)
use: Puffball fungus used as a healing agent for sores; the same kind of puffball was also used as a rattle by a medicine man
method: Chestnut's record doesn't spell out the exact preparation, but puffball use for sores nearly always followed the same basic logic across many traditions: the ripe puffball's fine spore mass was dusted or pressed directly onto the wound, since the powder is naturally absorbent and was believed to help draw out moisture and stop minor bleeding.
note: This comes from V. K. Chestnut's 1902 USDA survey of Mendocino County plant use, one of the earliest serious ethnobotanical field studies done in California — the same source records puffballs being used as a medicine man's ceremonial rattle once dried, a completely separate, non-medicinal use of the same fungus.

name: Puffball Necklace for Respiratory Protection (Blackfoot)
use: Dried puffballs strung into necklaces or bandoliers and worn as a protective charm believed to ward off respiratory disease
method: Whole puffballs were gathered ripe and dried hard, then pierced and strung on cord into a necklace or slung bandolier-style across the chest — worn on the body rather than eaten, burned, or applied to the skin.
note: This was a protective charm, not a treatment — closer in spirit to wearing an amulet than taking a medicine. Puffballs release their spores as a visible puff of dark 'smoke' when disturbed, and that dramatic, smoke-like release may be part of why a respiratory-illness charm was built from this particular fungus. There is no established protective effect, so it shouldn't be read as prevention advice.

name: Puffball Spore Powder for Burns (Secwepemc)
use: Stored, dried puffball spore powder spread repeatedly over a severe burn, recalled in one family's oral history as home care used after hospital treatment
method: Ripe puffballs were dried and kept in storage until needed, then broken open to release the fine spore powder, which was sprinkled directly over the burned skin and reapplied repeatedly over the course of healing.
note: This comes from a single family's remembered oral history rather than a broad ethnographic record — a home-care practice used alongside, not instead of, hospital treatment, which is worth noting since it wasn't understood as a replacement for medical care even by the family that used it.
caution: Puffball spore powder is not sterile, and dusting any nonsterile material onto a serious burn carries a real risk of infection — this is preserved as documented family history, not a technique to try.

name: Puffball Wound Care (Inuit, Nunavik)
use: Puffball spores applied directly to wounds to speed healing, and puffball material shaped into bandages
method: Ripe puffballs were broken open for their fine, powdery spore mass, which was packed directly onto cuts and wounds to help stop bleeding and keep the wound dry. The tough outer skin of larger puffballs was also cut and shaped into a flexible covering, used the way a cloth bandage would be.
note: Using puffball spore powder as a wound dressing shows up independently across an enormous range of unrelated cultures — from northern Inuit communities to old European folk medicine, where puffballs were sometimes called 'devil's snuffbox' — because the fine powder is genuinely absorbent and mildly antiseptic, one of the rare folk remedies with a real, non-placebo mechanism behind it.
caution: Modern sterile wound dressings are safer and more reliable, but the underlying idea — a dry, absorbent powder to help a wound clot — is a genuine and even sound one, not just old superstition.

name: Serviceberry Eye & Ear Drops (Blackfoot)
use: Berry juice, or a decoction of dried berries, used as eardrops for ear trouble, and dripped into the eye (then covered with a piece of soft hide) for eye trouble
method: Fresh berries were crushed for their juice, or dried berries were simmered into a decoction; a few drops of either were put directly into a sore ear or a troubled eye, and for the eye, a small piece of soft-tanned hide was laid over it afterward like a makeshift patch.
note: The archive's main Saskatoon Serviceberry entry only covers what was eaten or drunk — this shows the same berry doing something entirely different: dosed drop by drop into the eye or ear, a scale of use closer to modern eye drops than to food or tea.

name: Serviceberry in Ceremony & Belief (Blackfoot & Cheyenne)
use: A blessed ceremonial berry soup served at events such as the opening of a Medicine Pipe or Beaver bundle (Blackfoot); a nursing mother drinking a serviceberry-and-chokecherry infusion in the belief its medicine would pass to her baby (Blackfoot); and smashed fruit added as an ingredient into other, unspecified medicinal mixtures (Cheyenne)
method: For the ceremonial soup, berries were cooked into a sweetened broth served to open events like the Medicine Pipe or Beaver bundle ceremonies. Separately, a nursing mother might drink an infusion of serviceberries steeped together with chokecherries, and Cheyenne healers sometimes worked smashed serviceberry fruit into other medicinal mixtures as one ingredient among several, rather than as a remedy on its own.
note: Medicine Pipe and Beaver bundles are among the most sacred ceremonial objects in Blackfoot religious life, opened only at specific times with specific protocols — serving berry soup at that opening put an everyday food into a genuinely sacred context, not a casual one.

name: Serviceberry Root Tea (Woodlands Cree)
use: Root decoction taken for teething sickness in children, and separately for chest pains and lung infections
method: Roots were dug, cleaned, and simmered into a decoction. A small amount was given to teething infants to ease their sickness, while a stronger dose of the same root tea was drunk by those with chest pain or lung infection.
note: This is a root-based tradition, distinct from the berry- and leaf-based Saskatoon serviceberry uses recorded for Blackfoot and Cheyenne elsewhere in the archive — a reminder that different nations often turned to entirely different parts of the very same plant.

name: American Beautyberry Root for Stomachache (Koasati)
use: Root decoction taken for stomachache
method: Roots were dug, cleaned, and boiled into a decoction, drunk to settle a stomachache.
note: Beautyberry's root, leaf, and bark were each put to separate uses across Southeastern nations — the archive's confirmed sweat-bath entry uses the root for rheumatism, fever, colic, and dysentery, so this plain stomachache use adds yet another distinct application of the same root.

name: Hickory Nuts as Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Caddo region and East Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Hickory nuts, including black hickory (Carya texana), eaten raw, boiled and leached, parched and stored, ground into meal, or pounded for oil added to stews
method: Nuts were gathered in fall and used several ways: eaten raw, boiled and leached to remove bitterness, parched and stored whole for later, ground into meal for cooking, or pounded shell-and-all and boiled so the rich oil could be skimmed off the water and added to stews.
note: The word 'hickory' itself comes from that last method — it's a shortening of 'pawcohiccora,' an Algonquian (Powhatan) word for the pounded, oil-rich nut-milk drink made this same way, which English colonists borrowed directly into the language.

name: Flowering Dogwood Bark for Sores & as a Blood Purifier (Cherokee & Rappahannock)
use: Bark poultice applied to sores and ulcers (Cherokee); root bark taken internally for diarrhea, as a tonic, and for 'blood purification' (Rappahannock)
method: Cherokee use ground or pounded the bark into a poultice pressed directly onto sores and ulcers. Rappahannock use instead stripped bark from the root, dried it, and boiled it into a decoction drunk for diarrhea and as a general tonic believed to 'purify the blood.'
note: 'Blood purifier' was one of the most common phrases in 19th-century folk and eclectic medicine on both sides of the Native-settler divide — it wasn't a specific diagnosis so much as a catch-all belief that a bitter tonic could clear out whatever was causing poor health, similar to how sassafras and sarsaparilla were marketed.

name: Persimmon-Wood Massage Stamper (Cherokee)
use: A stamper carved from persimmon wood used to massage patients for rheumatic pain — the wood itself as a physical therapeutic tool, not a preparation taken or applied to the body
method: A short club or stamper was carved from persimmon wood and used by hand to press and knead sore, rheumatic joints and muscles — the wood itself was the therapeutic tool, not something ingested or brewed.
note: Persimmon wood is exceptionally hard and dense — the same qualities that later made it the standard American wood for golf club heads, the original 'wood' in a set of golf clubs — which is likely exactly why it was chosen for a tool meant to press firmly into sore muscle without breaking.

name: Dried Persimmon Cakes (Cherokee)
use: Ripe fruit seeded, pounded, flattened into cakes, and sun-dried for winter food storage
method: Fully ripe persimmons were seeded and pounded into a pulp, then flattened by hand into cakes and laid out to dry in the sun, producing a dense, sweet, shelf-stable food for winter.
note: Unripe persimmons are notoriously, mouth-puckeringly astringent — the fruit has to fully ripen, almost to the point of looking spoiled, before it turns genuinely sweet, which is exactly the stage Cherokee cooks were waiting for before pounding it into cakes.
caution: Unripe persimmons are strongly astringent and unpleasant to eat — not dangerous, but worth knowing before trying one.

name: Tinder Fungus — Additional Traditional Uses
people: North American Indigenous peoples (specific nation not recorded in the source review)
use: Reported traditional use as a diuretic and laxative, to calm the nerves, and for rheumatism — beyond the moxibustion-for-rheumatism practice already documented for the Okanagan-Colville nation
method: No preparation was recorded in the source for these particular uses. Elsewhere, Fomes fomentarius was most often dried and shaped into a slow-smoldering punk — the material burned directly against the skin in moxibustion, the practice already documented for the Okanagan-Colville — so it's plausible, though not confirmed here, that these additional uses relied on a similar dried or charred preparation rather than a tea.
note: This same fungus has one of the longest documented medicinal-use records of any fungus on Earth — a piece was even found in the gear of Ötzi, the roughly 5,300-year-old mummy found in the Alps — which makes the thinness of this particular North American record more a gap in the surviving sources than a sign the practice wasn't real.

name: White Ash Cambium as Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Inner cambium layer cooked and eaten
method: The inner cambium layer just beneath the bark was peeled or scraped away and cooked, eaten as a starchy food in times of scarcity.
note: Cambium eating like this shows up as emergency or supplemental food across many different tree species and Indigenous food traditions in North America — a genuinely practical use of a tree that also strips and often kills the section of bark it's taken from, which is likely why it was done sparingly rather than as an everyday habit.

name: Yaupon Holly Black/White Drink Ceremony (Apalachee, Creek, Muskogee & Seminole)
use: Dried, roasted leaves brewed into a dark, caffeinated 'black drink' used for ceremonial purification before ball games and trials (Apalachee), and in the broader Southeastern 'white/black drink' purification ceremony (Creek, Muskogee & Seminole)
method: Leaves and young twigs were dried and roasted, sometimes until nearly scorched, then boiled into a strong, dark, foaming, caffeinated tea — brewed far stronger than an everyday drink. It was consumed in large quantities during ceremonies, often from special shell cups, as part of ritual purification before events like ball games or important councils.
note: The plant's scientific name, Ilex vomitoria, comes from early European observers who assumed the ceremonial vomiting that sometimes followed drinking it meant the plant itself was an emetic. Modern botanists doubt that — the leaves contain caffeine, not anything that reliably induces vomiting — so the vomiting was more likely a deliberate, ritualized act of purification than a drug reaction, and the plant has carried an inaccurate name ever since because of that old misunderstanding.

name: Black Walnut Leaf Remedies (Comanche & Delaware)
use: Leaves pulverized and applied for ringworm (Comanche); leaves used as a household flea repellent (Delaware)
method: Comanche use pulverized fresh or dried black walnut leaves into a powder or paste applied directly onto ringworm patches on the skin. Delaware households instead scattered or strewed the leaves themselves around bedding and floors, relying on their strong smell to drive off fleas rather than applying anything to the body.
note: Black walnut leaves really do contain juglone, a compound with genuine antifungal and insect-repelling properties — this is one of the folk remedies in the archive where the traditional use and the plant's actual chemistry point in the same direction, unlike many 'blood purifier' style tonics.

name: Black Walnut Nuts as Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Nuts eaten raw, and boiled to render oil
method: Nuts were cracked from their notoriously hard, thick shells and eaten raw, or boiled so the oil could be skimmed from the water and used in cooking.
note: Black walnuts have one of the hardest shells of any North American nut — hard enough that cracking them by hand was, and still is, genuinely difficult work, which is part of why the milder English (Persian) walnut eventually displaced it commercially even though the black walnut's flavor is stronger and many still prefer it.

name: Sweetgum Resin Salve for Skin Complaints (Cherokee)
use: Rosin mixed with sheep or cow tallow and applied topically for itches, cuts, sores, wounds, and cankers; plant material used as a poultice ('drawing plaster') for bruises and sores
method: Hardened sweetgum rosin, scraped or chipped from wounds in the bark, was melted down and mixed with rendered sheep or cow tallow into a soft salve, spread on itches, cuts, sores, and cankers. Separately, other plant material was pounded into a 'drawing plaster' poultice and bound over bruises and sores.
note: Sweetgum trees seal their own bark wounds with that same fragrant resin — people were essentially harvesting the tree's own first-aid response and repurposing it as a salve base, mixed with tallow the way petroleum jelly gets mixed into a modern ointment.

name: Red Mulberry Bark for Worms (Cherokee)
use: Bark preparation ingested historically to expel intestinal worms
method: The source doesn't preserve exact proportions or timing, but like most Cherokee bark medicines, it was almost certainly prepared as a boiled bark decoction taken by mouth, rather than eaten directly or applied to the skin.
note: Red mulberry bark's other archived Cherokee uses — urinary complaints, ringworm, constipation — are all things a bitter, purgative-leaning bark tea was commonly reached for, so expelling worms fits the same general pattern of use even though it's recorded as a separate complaint.

name: East Texas Pineywoods Forest Resources
people: Indigenous and settler communities of the East Texas Pineywoods (regional/ecological record, not nation-specific)
use: A catalog of the region's medicinally, materially, and edibly significant trees: sweetgum, sassafras, dogwood, black gum, yaupon, beautyberry, black cherry, oaks, hickories, elm, and holly, alongside the native longleaf, shortleaf, and loblolly pines that structure the forest
method: Not a single remedy but a regional summary — each species listed (sweetgum, sassafras, dogwood, and the rest) had its own separate preparation, many of which appear as their own individual entries elsewhere in this archive.
note: The Pineywoods is Texas's own slice of the wider Southern pine belt — longleaf, shortleaf, and loblolly pine forest that once ran nearly unbroken from East Texas to the Atlantic. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century logging cut almost all of the original old-growth longleaf stands, so the useful hardwoods this catalog lists — sweetgum, dogwood, hickory, oak — were often the trees still standing in the understory and along the forest edges after the big pines were gone.

name: White Pine Resin for Wounds & Infection (Cherokee & Ojibwe)
use: Resin used topically on wounds and inflammation (Cherokee), and on infected tissue including gangrene (Ojibwe)
method: Sticky resin was collected directly from wounds in the bark, sometimes warmed to soften it, and applied straight onto wounds and inflamed skin (Cherokee) or packed onto badly infected tissue, including gangrenous wounds, as a covering meant to draw out infection (Ojibwe).
note: Pine resin's use as a wound dressing is one of the more chemically plausible folk remedies in the archive — it's naturally antiseptic and forms a sticky, air-limiting seal over a wound, similar in principle to how pine tar and turpentine both later became standard ingredients in commercial wound dressings and salves.

name: Black Cherry Bark Medicine (Cherokee, Delaware, Iroquois & Lumbee)
use: Bark medicine used, with some variation by community, for cough, colds and flu, fever, worms, and diarrhea
method: The exact recipe wasn't preserved in the sources behind this record, but wild cherry bark medicine was almost universally made the same basic way across the many nations and settler communities who used it: the inner bark was stripped, dried, and steeped or simmered into a bitter, aromatic decoction taken by the spoonful or cupful.
note: Wild cherry bark's use for cough runs so deep in American medicine that it outlived folk practice entirely — it stayed a standardized ingredient in official U.S. pharmacy references and in commercial cough syrups well into the 20th century, a rare case of a Native and settler folk remedy graduating into mainstream pharmacy.
caution: Black cherry bark, leaves, and pits contain compounds that release cyanide when damaged or chewed — real medicine relied on careful, controlled preparation of the inner bark specifically, not casual use of the whole plant.

name: Chokecherry Bark for Pregnancy & Sore Throat (Great Plains Indigenous nations)
people: Great Plains Indigenous nations (multiple, not individually specified in the source)
use: Inner bark tea taken historically as a pregnancy tonic, and used as a gargle for sore throat
method: Inner bark was stripped, dried, and simmered into a tea — taken by the cup as a general pregnancy tonic, or brewed and used warm as a gargle rather than swallowed, for sore throat.
note: Chokecherry bark, like black cherry, contains cyanogenic compounds concentrated mainly in the bark, leaves, and pits — which makes the pregnancy-tonic use notable, since it's exactly the kind of use where dose and preparation would have mattered most, and almost certainly why it stayed inner-bark-only and modest in quantity rather than a strong daily brew.
caution: Chokecherry bark, leaves, and pits contain cyanogenic compounds; the ripe flesh of the fruit is safe, but bark preparations require real care with dose and part used.

name: Oak Leaves for Ceremonial Cleansing (Ramah Navajo)
use: Leaves used as an emetic for ceremonial cleansing, rather than as an everyday tonic
method: Leaves were boiled into a strong decoction meant to be drunk in enough quantity to induce vomiting, taken as part of a ceremonial cleansing rather than sipped as an everyday remedy.
note: Ceremonial emetics like this appear across many Southwestern and Plains traditions as a ritual reset — a deliberate, purposeful vomiting meant to cleanse a person before or after a ceremony, not a treatment for an upset stomach. It's a completely different use-logic than most of the archive's teas and tonics, even when the plant itself is a familiar one.

name: Acorns as Staple Food (Multiple Indigenous Groups)
people: Multiple Indigenous groups across Texas and North America (not nation-specific in the source)
use: Acorns shelled, ground, leached and rinsed to remove tannins, then cooked as meal, mush, or bread
method: Acorns were shelled and the nutmeats ground into a coarse meal, then leached repeatedly — spread in a sand basin and flushed with running water, or steeped through several changes of hot water — until the bitter, tannic taste was gone. The leached meal was then cooked into a mush or baked into bread.
note: That leaching step is the whole trick: raw acorns are so bitter with tannins they're nearly inedible, but the processing knowledge to make them a genuine staple food — not just emergency rations — was refined and passed down across an enormous number of separate Indigenous nations across North America, each with their own version of the same basic leaching logic.

name: Red Oak in Cherokee Material Culture & Food (Cherokee)
use: Wood used to keep a sacred eternal fire burning; inner bark fashioned into baskets; acorns sometimes used to make kenuche (a traditional hickory-nut dish)
method: Split red oak wood was chosen to feed the sacred fire because it burns slow and steady; strips of the flexible inner bark were peeled and woven into baskets; and acorns were sometimes shelled, leached of their bitterness, and pounded into kenuche, a traditional hickory-and-acorn dish.
note: The 'eternal fire' refers to a sacred fire historically kept continuously burning in Cherokee townhouses — tending it was a serious communal responsibility, not a household hearth, which is a very different kind of importance than the food and craft uses of the same tree.

name: Smooth Sumac Berries for Vomiting (Cherokee)
use: Red berries eaten historically as an emetic, to induce vomiting
method: Fresh red berries were eaten directly off the cluster, used deliberately to bring on vomiting rather than to settle the stomach.
note: This is almost the mirror image of the archive's confirmed Sumac Berry Syrup entry, where the same tart red berries are cooked down and used for the opposite purpose — settling diarrhea and digestive upset. Whether it soothed or purged seems to have depended on dose and preparation: a small amount of raw fruit versus a cooked, diluted syrup.

name: Smooth Sumac Root & Flower Remedies (Chippewa/Ojibwe)
use: A decoction of an abnormal growth or gall on the plant used for dysentery; root infusion taken for colds and separately used as an emetic; a compound flower decoction used as a mouthwash for a teething child
method: The gall (an abnormal growth on the plant, likely insect-induced) was boiled into a decoction for dysentery. Root was steeped as an infusion and taken for colds, or brewed stronger and taken deliberately as an emetic. Flowers were boiled together with other plants into a compound decoction, cooled, and used as a mouthwash rubbed on a teething baby's gums.
note: Using a plant gall — a growth caused by an insect laying eggs in the tissue, not a normal plant part — as medicine shows a level of close, opportunistic plant observation that goes beyond just knowing the ordinary parts of a plant; healers were reading the whole life of the plant, abnormalities included.

name: Smooth Sumac Root Uses (Meskwaki)
use: Root decoction taken as an appetite stimulant for invalids, and root bark used deliberately to raise a blister on the skin as a counterirritant treatment
method: For appetite, the root was boiled into a decoction and given in small doses to invalids or the weak. For the counterirritant treatment, root bark was prepared and applied directly against the skin, deliberately meant to raise a blister, on the old medical theory that drawing irritation to the surface could relieve deeper pain.
note: Counterirritation — deliberately blistering or irritating the skin to 'draw out' a deeper ailment — was a mainstream idea in both Indigenous and European-descended medicine well into the 1800s, related to the same logic behind the mustard plasters and blister plasters used in conventional doctors' offices of the era.
caution: Deliberately raising a blister on the skin with root bark as a counterirritant is a real historical folk practice, but it can cause burns, scarring, and infection. This is documented history, not a technique to try.

name: Smooth Sumac for Earache (Micmac)
use: Plant parts used for earache; the exact part and preparation were not recorded in the surviving source
method: No specific plant part or preparation survives in the source — just that some part of smooth sumac was used for earache. Elsewhere in Rhus glabra folk use, root, bark, leaf, and flower were all pressed into separate remedies, so any of those could plausibly be involved here, but nothing confirms which.
note: A named nation and a named ailment survived here, but the how didn't — a reminder that oral traditions collected secondhand by outside recorders often kept the what while losing the exact how, especially for small, easily overlooked entries like an earache remedy.

name: Black Willow Root Bark for Fever (Cherokee, Houma & Koasati)
use: Bitter root and bark decoction taken as a depurative and for intermittent and other fevers
method: Root bark was stripped, dried, and boiled into a bitter decoction, taken by the cup for fevers — including 'intermittent fever,' the old term for the recurring fever pattern typical of malaria — and more generally as a depurative, a tonic believed to cleanse the blood.
note: Willow bark of many species contains salicin, the same compound family behind aspirin, which is part of why willow bark fever remedies appear so independently and so often across unrelated cultures worldwide — one of the folk remedies where the traditional use and known pharmacology line up unusually well.

name: Sassafras Root for Diarrhea & as a Blood Builder (Cherokee)
use: Root tea brewed and taken for diarrhea, and root consumed as what old records call a 'blood builder'
method: Root bark was stripped, dried, and steeped into a tea for diarrhea, and taken more generally — sometimes just chewed or eaten directly — as what old records call a 'blood builder,' a general tonic believed to strengthen and restore the blood.
note: Sassafras tea was such a popular spring tonic across the wider American South, among Cherokee and settler households alike, that it became one of colonial America's earliest export crops back to Europe — though the safrole compound that gives it its distinctive smell is also why sassafras tea and root beer were both eventually reformulated to remove it.
caution: Safrole, the compound responsible for sassafras's characteristic smell and flavor, was banned by the FDA as a food additive in 1960 after being linked to liver damage and cancer in animal studies — a real reason modern sassafras tea and root beer are made without it.

name: Sphagnum Moss for Hygiene & Utility (Potawatomi & Ojibwe)
use: Moss used as an absorbent material for menstrual cycles and baby diapers (Potawatomi), and gathered and dried as general absorbent and mattress material (Ojibwe)
method: Moss was gathered from bogs, cleaned of debris, and dried, which made it far more absorbent. Potawatomi households used the dried moss as a menstrual pad and as diaper lining for babies; Ojibwe households dried and stored it in bulk as general absorbent packing and mattress stuffing.
note: Sphagnum moss can hold many times its own dry weight in liquid and has mild natural antiseptic properties, which is exactly why the same moss was later harvested by the ton for surgical wound dressings during World War I — the household hygiene use and the wartime medical use are really the same absorbency at different scales.

name: Northern White Cedar Steam & Tea (Mi'kmaq, Menominee, Ojibwe & Iroquois)
use: Leaves or inner bark taken as an infusion for cough (Mi'kmaq); leaves steamed and the vapor inhaled in a sweat-lodge context for colds, headache, fever, and rheumatism (Menominee, Ojibwe & Iroquois-related records)
method: Mi'kmaq use steeped leaves or inner bark into a drinkable infusion for cough. The Menominee, Ojibwe, and related Iroquois-documented practice instead poured water over cedar leaves laid on hot stones in a sweat lodge, and the patient breathed in the rising steam for colds, headache, fever, and rheumatism, rather than drinking anything.
note: Northern white cedar is often identified as the 'annedda' tree that Indigenous people showed to Jacques Cartier's scurvy-stricken crew in 1536 — an anti-scurvy remedy credited with saving the expedition, and a case where a household remedy plausibly rescued a European crew, though scholars still debate the exact species Cartier's hosts actually used.
caution: Cedar leaf preparations contain thujone, which is toxic in concentrated or excessive doses — traditional infusions were taken in modest, habitual amounts rather than as a concentrated extract.

name: Elm Inner Bark as Emergency Food (East Texas)
people: Indigenous communities of the Texas Post Oak Savannah (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Inner bark pulverized and cooked into cakes as emergency food
method: Inner bark was stripped, pounded into a fibrous pulp, and cooked into cakes, made and eaten specifically as an emergency food during periods of scarcity rather than as regular fare.
note: Elm inner bark is mucilaginous — slippery and gel-like when wet — the same property that made a related species, slippery elm, into one of the best-known soothing remedies in American herbal medicine; this Texas use leans on the food value of that same bark rather than its medicinal reputation.

name: Lowbush Blueberry in Ceremony (Iroquois)
use: Recorded in an indexed ethnobotanical source as having a ceremonial medicinal role, distinct from everyday food use
method: The specific ceremony and preparation weren't recoverable from the indexed summary behind this record, so no preparation can be responsibly reconstructed here.
note: Berries in general hold a real ceremonial place in Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) tradition — early-summer berry ripening is one of the seasonal markers celebrated in the Thanksgiving Address recited at community gatherings — so a specific ceremonial role for blueberries fits a genuine broader pattern, even though this particular source doesn't spell out which ceremony or how the berries were used in it.

name: Smooth Beardtongue
use: Leaves used for snakebite and muscle cramps
method: No specific preparation survives in the source, but Penstemon leaves used for snakebite elsewhere on the Plains were typically chewed fresh or pounded into a wet mash and applied directly to the bite as a poultice, rather than taken internally — plausibly the same approach here, though not confirmed for this specific record.
note: Plains snakebite poultices like this one were a genuine, widespread category of folk first aid, but modern medicine is clear that no topical plant poultice can neutralize venom — the real value of an entry like this is historical, not medical.
caution: No plant poultice, including this one, is an effective treatment for venomous snakebite — a real bite requires prompt medical care and antivenom.

name: Old World Licorice
use: Listed among "bitter roots and barks" in African American rootwork tradition
method: The source only lists it among 'bitter roots and barks' without detailing preparation. Rootwork roots along these lines were generally either chewed directly, brewed into a wash, or carried whole in a small flannel mojo bag — but nothing here confirms which applied to licorice specifically.
note: Rootwork traditions commonly grouped roots by the effect they were believed to have rather than by ordinary medicinal category, and licorice's natural sweetness put it among roots reached for to 'sweeten' a situation or a person's attitude — a different logic entirely from its separate, more mainstream use as a cough and stomach remedy, though this source doesn't spell out the exact ritual use in detail.
caution: Licorice root can raise blood pressure with regular heavy use — a genuine modern medical caution, regardless of how it's being used.

name: Kola Nut
use: Named as a stimulant root in rootwork tradition
method: Kola nuts were chewed directly — the bitter nut releases caffeine as it's chewed, giving an immediate stimulant effect, which is the same property that made it valued for energy and alertness rather than prepared as a tea or tincture.
note: Kola nut is one of the few rootwork ingredients with a direct, traceable line back to West Africa rather than a New World substitute — kola nut chewing and kola-nut hospitality customs there are ancient and well documented, carried across the Atlantic and surviving in some African American communities. It's also, more famously, the original source of the caffeine and flavor behind early cola sodas, including Coca-Cola, before synthetic caffeine and flavoring replaced the real nut.
caution: Kola nut is a genuine stimulant, high in caffeine — the same real caution that applies to any strong caffeine source, especially with heavy or repeated use.

name: Gum-Tree Leaves
people: Gullah/Geechee communities of the Southeast coast
use: Documented as part of Gullah/Geechee ethnobotanical medicinal-plant knowledge
method: No ailment or preparation is given in the source — just that gum-tree leaves appear in the Gullah/Geechee plant list. 'Gum tree' most likely refers to sweetgum or black gum, both common along the Southeastern coast, but nothing here confirms which, or how the leaves specifically (as opposed to the bark or resin) were used.
note: Gullah/Geechee ethnobotany is a genuinely distinct, well-studied body of plant knowledge — carried from West and Central Africa, adapted to Lowcountry species, and still actively practiced on the Sea Islands today — but the specific source behind this entry is only an indexed name list, not a description of practice, which is why so little detail survived here.

name: John the Conqueror Root (High John Root)
use: Culturally significant root in African American rootwork/hoodoo tradition
method: The whole, unprepared root was most often simply carried — kept in a pocket, a mojo bag, or sometimes dressed with oil or whiskey — rather than brewed into a tea or applied to the skin. Carrying the root itself, not extracting anything from it, was the point.
note: The root takes its name from High John de Conquer, a trickster-hero figure from enslaved African American folklore — someone who could outwit any master and never truly be conquered, whose spirit was believed to live on inside the root. Zora Neale Hurston wrote about this figure directly in the 1940s, describing him as a spirit of hope and secret resistance carried by enslaved people even when the man himself was only a story.

name: Black Snakeroot
use: Named in a Gullah/Geechee ethnobotanical plant list as a general medicinal root
method: Which plant this refers to isn't resolved, so no confident preparation can be given — 'a general medicinal root' is all the source specifies.
note: 'Black snakeroot' is one of the most confusingly overloaded names in American folk botany — depending on region and source, it's been applied to black cohosh, to several Sanicula species, and to other, unrelated plants entirely, usually because all of them were reached for as snakebite or general-purpose remedies and folk naming grouped them by function rather than by botany.

name: Late Boneset
use: General traditional medicinal use
method: No preparation is recorded specifically for this species — the screening study that flags it doesn't describe traditional practice, only that a traditional use was reported somewhere in the literature it reviewed.
note: Eupatorium as a genus was reached for feverish illness across a striking number of unrelated traditions, so it's plausible late boneset was used much like its close, well-documented relative common boneset — steeped into a bitter fever tea — but that's an educated inference from the wider genus, not something this particular source actually confirms.

name: Oak Bark
people: Historical North American medicine generally; specific community unstated
use: Astringent remedy for diarrhea, mouth sores, and bleeding
method: Bark was stripped, dried, and boiled into a strong, tannic decoction — swallowed by the spoonful for diarrhea, used as a gargle or mouth rinse for sores and bleeding gums, or applied on a cloth as a wash for minor bleeding wounds.
note: Oak bark's astringency comes from its very high tannin content, the same class of compound that makes strong black tea pucker the mouth — tannins bind and tighten tissue, which is genuinely why an oak bark gargle can help slow minor gum bleeding, one of the more pharmacologically sound mechanisms behind an old folk remedy.

name: Thyme
people: European immigrant households generally (no specific community named)
use: Household remedy for chesty cough and congestion
method: Fresh or dried thyme leaves were steeped into a strong tea, sometimes sweetened with honey, and drunk hot for a chesty cough. In some households the tea was simmered down further with sugar into a thicker cough syrup, kept on hand for the whole family.
note: Thyme's oil, thymol, has genuine antimicrobial and cough-suppressing properties — strong enough that thyme-based cough syrup is still sold as a standard over-the-counter remedy in Germany today, one of the more direct throughlines from old household folk medicine straight into a modern pharmacy shelf.

name: Coltsfoot
people: European immigrant households (unspecified); distinct from Alaska Native use of a related species
use: Traditional respiratory and cough remedy
method: Dried leaves and flowers were steeped into a tea, or in some households smoked in a pipe, both for cough and to ease breathing — smoking dried coltsfoot leaf was a genuinely documented old-world remedy for asthma-like wheezing and breathlessness, not just a modern habit applied to an old plant.
note: The Latin genus name Tussilago literally means 'cough dispeller' — it was such a reliable go-to cough remedy across Europe that its own scientific name is basically a job description, and pharmacies in some European countries once hung a painted coltsfoot flower on their sign as a kind of trade symbol.
caution: Coltsfoot contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can damage the liver, especially with prolonged use — a real concern serious enough that Germany restricted the sale of coltsfoot preparations over it, and it's one of the archive's more genuinely risky traditional remedies rather than a minor caution.

name: Butterbur
people: European "plague flower" herbal tradition, carried by immigrant households (no specific community confirmed)
use: Traditional headache and cough remedy
method: In European tradition the large rhizome was dried and steeped into a bitter tea for headache and cough; American immigrant households who kept up this Old World practice would most plausibly have done the same, though no source specifically documents it happening here.
note: The name comes from its enormous leaves — large enough that they really were once used to wrap butter for storage — while 'plague flower' points to a much darker history: it was reached for across plague-era Europe as a fever and headache remedy during outbreaks, at a time when almost nothing else on hand seemed to help.
caution: Wild butterbur contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that are toxic to the liver — modern commercial butterbur extracts are specially processed to remove them, but a preparation made from an untreated wild plant, historical or otherwise, carries a real poisoning risk.

name: Pacific Yew
use: Wood especially prized for bows and tools among Pacific Northwest nations; some additional medicinal use is also reported, though not well documented
method: The dense, strong, flexible wood was carved into bows — Pacific yew was one of the most prized bow woods among Pacific Northwest and Plateau nations, valued the way English yew was prized for longbows on the other side of the Atlantic — as well as into digging sticks, wedges, and paddles. Specific medicinal preparations aren't confirmed in the sources behind this record.
note: Pacific yew's fame today comes almost entirely from Taxol, the cancer drug first isolated from its bark in the 1960s-70s — a genuinely separate, much later chapter of this tree's story that has nothing to do with its real, much older reputation among Northwest nations as the best available bow wood, similar to how English yew became legendary for the same reason on the other side of the Atlantic.
caution: Pacific yew, like other yews, contains taxane compounds that are genuinely toxic if ingested — the wood's historical value was in its strength for tools and weapons, not as something eaten or brewed.

name: Kava
use: Ceremonial and medicinal use of 'awa (kava) root
method: The root was pounded or chewed to release its active compounds, then mixed with water and strained through fibrous plant material into a milky, mildly numbing drink — traditionally prepared and served as part of formal social and chiefly protocol, and also taken medicinally for troubles like insomnia, muscle tension, and urinary complaints.
note: In Hawaiian, it's called 'awa, and preparing and sharing it followed real social protocol — who prepared it, who served it, and in what order it was passed mattered as much as the drink itself, especially in contexts involving chiefs and formal gatherings. The numbing sensation it leaves on the lips and tongue is a genuine, immediate effect of the plant's kavalactones, not just a reported folk detail.
caution: Kava has been linked to rare but serious liver toxicity, particularly with concentrated commercial extracts and heavy regular use — traditional water-based preparation in moderate amounts is generally considered lower risk, but this is a real, documented modern medical concern.

name: Blanketflower
people: Plains Indigenous peoples generally (not confidently tied to a specific nation)
use: Skin-ailment remedy
method: No confirmed preparation survives for a specific nation, but Plains skin remedies from related composite-family flowers were typically made by crushing or mashing the plant fresh, or drying and powdering it, then applying it directly to the affected skin — plausible here too, though not confirmed for blanketflower specifically.
note: Blanketflower gets its English name from its concentric rings of red, orange, and yellow — resembling a woven blanket pattern — a common enough visual association that several unrelated plants with concentric-ringed flowers picked up similar 'blanket' names in different regions.

name: Wild Tomatillo
use: Stomach ailment and wound remedy
method: No specific preparation is recorded with enough confidence to reconstruct here.
note: 'Wild tomatillo' in Plains ethnobotany records most likely refers to a native groundcherry (Physalis species) — a relative of the cultivated tomatillo — rather than the Mexican culinary tomatillo itself, though the record behind this entry doesn't pin down the exact species or nation clearly enough to say more.

name: Partridge Pea
use: General medicinal use recalled among Cherokee tradition; specific ailment unspecified
note: Partridge pea’s seeds are such a prized food for bobwhite quail and other game birds that wildlife managers still plant it deliberately in game-food plots today — a reminder the plant had a life well beyond the sickroom. The specific Cherokee medicinal use recalled here couldn’t be pinned to a confirmed source, so it’s presented loosely rather than as settled fact.

name: Lovage (Nondo)
use: Cold remedy, similar to Osha root
method: The aromatic root was dug in fall, dried, and either chewed raw — a pinch carried in the cheek like a lozenge — or steeped into a strong tea for colds, cough, and sore throat. A piece of dried root was also commonly carried in a small pouch as a protective charm, worn rather than eaten.
note: Appalachian folk names for this plant — “nondo,” “sweet Osha,” “Indian parsley” — all point to the same root familiar in granny-woman herbal practice across the mountains, prized as a home-grown stand-in for the more famous (and more southwestern) Osha root.

name: Snowberry / Coralberry
use: Eyewash, soap, and skin wash
method: Crushed berries or leaves were worked with water into a foamy, soap-like lather — the plant's natural saponins make it suds up like a mild soap — and that lather was used to wash skin and hair, or diluted further and strained for use as an eyewash.
note: That same sudsing chemical (saponin) is exactly why the berries were never eaten: in many regions the waxy white fruit was nicknamed “snake berry” or “corpse berry,” a warning passed to children that a plant so useful for washing wasn’t meant for the mouth.
caution: The berries are mildly toxic if eaten in quantity, causing nausea, vomiting, or dizziness — a real reason behind the old “don't eat it” nicknames.

name: Wild Tarragon
use: Toothache remedy
method: Fresh leaves, or a bit of the root, were chewed to a pulp and packed directly against the aching tooth or gum. The plant's numbing, clove-like bite — the same quality that makes fresh tarragon tingle on the tongue — did the work of a topical anesthetic.
note: The species name dracunculus means “little dragon” in Latin, a name (echoed later in French “estragon”) usually traced to its coiled, serpentine root — the same twisting root that ends up chewed and packed against a sore tooth.

name: Catclaw Acacia
use: Astringent remedy for sore throat
method: Like other acacias, catclaw weeps a natural gum from wounds in its bark; the hardened gum was dissolved in water or simply chewed, valued as a soothing coating for a raw, scratchy throat, while the tannin-rich bark itself could be simmered into a decoction for a gargle.
note: Its hooked, thorn-covered branches earned it the nickname “wait-a-minute bush” in the Southwest — catch a sleeve on one and you stop exactly that long working it free.

name: Lousewort
use: Muscle relaxant
method: The leaves and flowering tops were gathered fresh and either chewed directly or steeped into a tea, taken for tense or aching muscles — a use later picked up by Western herbalists, who still cite lousewort (sometimes called “Indian warrior”) as a mild, genuinely relaxing muscle remedy.
note: The name “lousewort” is an old insult, not a description of its effects — European wort-plants with that name were blamed (wrongly, in most cases) for giving livestock lice, and the label simply crossed the Atlantic and got reattached to an unrelated American plant.

name: American Sycamore
use: Bark used for cough and dysentery
method: The inner bark was peeled, dried, and boiled down into a strong, astringent decoction, drunk for a nagging cough or for dysentery.
note: Sycamore is easy to identify even at a distance by its mottled, camouflage-like bark, which flakes away in patches as the tree grows — one of the few American trees where the bark itself, not just the leaf, was the reliable field marker for gathering the right one.

name: Redbud
use: Bark used for diarrhea and pain
method: The bark was stripped, dried, and boiled into a decoction taken for diarrhea and general pain.
note: The same shrub's straight young shoots, not its bark, are the famous part in California basketry — redbud rods are the classic source of the reddish-brown design elements woven into Pomo and other coiled baskets, a craft use as well documented as any medicinal one.

name: Thimbleberry
use: Leaf poultice for burns
method: The large, soft, fuzzy leaves were gathered fresh, crushed or chewed to release their juice, and laid directly over a burn as a cooling poultice, sometimes bound in place with a strip of cloth.
note: Those same oversized velvety leaves made thimbleberry a genuinely useful all-purpose wrapping material in the woods, well beyond medicine — among the largest, softest leaves of any common Pacific Northwest understory plant.

name: Virgin's Bower
use: Nerve and blood medicine
method: Fresh leaves were crushed and bruised, then rubbed directly onto the skin over an aching head or a sore, rheumatic joint. The plant's natural irritant compound raises a mild burning, sometimes blistering, reaction — a counter-irritant meant to draw the deeper pain to the surface.
note: That irritant compound (protoanemonin, found throughout the buttercup family Clematis belongs to) is exactly why this was a skin remedy and not one taken by mouth in any quantity — the same chemistry that makes it work also makes it something to handle with real care.
caution: Can cause skin blistering with prolonged contact, and is toxic if taken internally in any quantity — traditional use kept it strictly external and brief.

name: Smartweed
use: Rubbed on skin for pain
method: Fresh leaves and stems were crushed and rubbed directly onto sore, rheumatic joints and aching muscles — the plant's peppery, stinging sap was believed to draw the pain out, the same “urtication” principle behind rubbing skin with stinging nettle.
note: The name isn’t a metaphor — chew a leaf and it genuinely “smarts,” a sharp, peppery bite on the tongue that gives the whole plant family (and a close relative literally called “water pepper”) its common name.

name: Knotweed
people: European immigrant households (likely inherited Old World lore)
use: Astringent herb remedy
method: The whole trailing plant was gathered while flowering, dried, and steeped into a strongly astringent tea, drunk for diarrhea or used as a cooled wash for minor wounds and bleeding gums.
note: Common knotweed is a classic dooryard weed — it thrives in packed, trodden soil along paths and doorsteps — so households carrying this Old World remedy across the Atlantic usually found the plant itself had already made the same trip, growing right outside the door.

name: Gentian / Bottle Gentian
use: Bitter digestive tonic
method: The root was dug in fall, dried, and either chewed directly for its intense bitterness or steeped or tinctured in spirits as a bitters, taken in small doses before meals to stir a sluggish appetite and digestion.
note: Bottle (closed) gentian's flowers never actually open — they stay sealed shut at the tip, and only a strong bumblebee forcing its way in can pollinate them, a genuinely odd bit of natural history behind the plant's common name.

name: Frogfruit
people: Possibly Latin American/Caribbean-influenced tradition; U.S.-specific community unconfirmed
use: Traditional medicinal use (unspecified ailment)
note: A low, wiry, mat-forming native groundcover in the verbena family — still planted today as a drought-tolerant, pollinator-friendly lawn substitute in the Southwest — but a specific, confirmed U.S. medicinal-use story couldn't be pinned down beyond that general Latin American and Caribbean folk reputation.

name: American Germander
use: Diuretic; treatment for sores
method: The leafy flowering tops were dried and steeped into a tea, taken for its diuretic effect or cooled and used as a wash on sores.
