method: Dried hop cones were sewn into a small flat pillow and tucked under the sleeper's regular one at night; some households misted the hops lightly with whiskey first, since dry hops rustle and crackle while damp ones stay quiet and hold their scent longer.
note: For much of the 19th century that pillow was likely stuffed with hops from central New York State rather than the Pacific Northwest — Otsego and Madison Counties were the heart of American hop-growing until disease and Prohibition-era decline pushed the industry west.

name: Wintercress
people: Appalachian and Upland South settler households
use: A late-winter tonic green, eaten to shake off the sluggishness of a winter diet
method: The young leaves were gathered as soon as they showed — sometimes while snow still lay in sheltered hollows — boiled down with a piece of fatback, and eaten as the year's first "mess of greens," usually with cornbread.
note: Mountain households lumped wintercress in with its close cousins as "creasy greens," and the tradition of racing to find the first bitter greens of the year is still marked today by small-town festivals across the Appalachian South.

name: Shepherd's Purse
people: American Eclectic physicians and household herbal practitioners of European descent
use: Stopping heavy bleeding, especially after childbirth and with heavy menstrual periods
method: The whole flowering plant was dried and brewed into a strong tea, or reduced to a fluid extract; a midwife would give it by the spoonful to a woman bleeding too heavily after delivery, in the belief it helped the womb clamp back down.
note: It held a real, lasting place in American medicine for exactly this — 19th-century Eclectic reference works like King's American Dispensatory listed it specifically as a uterine hemostatic, and physicians kept reaching for it as an emergency styptic whenever supplies of other bleeding-control drugs ran short.
caution: As a uterine stimulant, it was a postpartum and emergency remedy, not something taken earlier in pregnancy.

name: Celery Seed
people: American households and patent-medicine makers, late 19th century
use: Rheumatism and "nerves"
method: The seeds were steeped into a bitter tea or simply chewed after a meal; by the 1880s the same seeds were being extracted into commercial tonics, most famously "Paine's Celery Compound," whose relentless advertising put celery's reputation as a nerve-and-joint remedy into medicine cabinets across the country.
note: Paine's Celery Compound outsold nearly every other patent medicine of its era despite a hefty dose of alcohol in every bottle alongside the celery extract — a reminder that a good deal of the "tonic" feeling people paid for wasn't coming from the vegetable on the label.

name: Black Radish & Honey
use: Cough and sore throat
method: A large black radish was hollowed out like a small cup, packed with honey or sugar, and left to sit overnight; the radish drew its own sharp juice up into the honey, and the syrup that collected was given to a coughing child by the spoonful.
note: The same hollowed-radish trick shows up independently across Eastern European Jewish, Slavic, and German kitchens — different households, continents apart, all arriving at the same simple trick of drawing juice out of a sharp root with sugar.

name: Pumpkin Seed
people: Haudenosaunee and other Eastern Woodlands nations, later adopted into American settler and Eclectic medicine
use: Expelling intestinal worms, especially tapeworm
method: Raw seeds were shelled and either chewed or crushed into a paste and eaten on an empty stomach, sometimes followed hours later by a strong purgative to finish clearing the worm.
note: This is one of the rare folk dewormers that held up under later scrutiny — pumpkin seed contains a compound called cucurbitin that actually paralyzes tapeworms, part of why it stayed listed as an official vermifuge in American medical dispensatories long after most other traditional worm remedies had been dropped.

name: Watermelon Seed Tea
people: African American communities of the rural South
use: Water retention and kidney or bladder complaints
method: Seeds saved from summer melons were dried, then boiled into a mild tea drunk to "flush the kidneys" — turning the one part of the fruit usually thrown away into an everyday household remedy.
note: It wasn't only folklore: watermelon seed and rind genuinely have a diuretic effect, and the tea turns up again and again in early-20th-century collections of Southern home remedies as an ordinary household staple rather than a rare or secret one.

name: Barley Water
people: American households of English and European descent
use: Feeding and cooling a fever, and soothing an upset stomach
method: Whole barley was simmered a long time in water until the liquid turned cloudy and faintly thick, then strained and lightly sweetened; it was given by the cupful to a feverish patient or to a weaning baby who couldn't yet manage solid food.
note: It came straight out of English sickroom tradition — nearly every 19th-century American housekeeping and domestic-medicine manual copied its barley water recipe from English sources, usually printed right alongside beef tea as the two standard drinks for an invalid.

name: Oil of Cloves
people: American households and country doctors, nationwide
use: Toothache and sore gums
method: A drop or two of clove oil was pressed onto a wad of cotton and packed directly against the aching tooth, or a whole clove was simply held between the teeth at the sore spot until the throbbing eased.
note: Long before dentists understood why, this actually worked — clove's main compound, eugenol, is a genuine mild local anesthetic, which is exactly why dentists still use eugenol-based pastes and cements today.
caution: Undiluted, clove oil can burn or irritate the gum tissue if used too heavily or too often.

name: Baking Soda
use: Heartburn and sour stomach, and relief for bee stings, insect bites, and itching skin
method: A teaspoon stirred into a glass of water was drunk to settle a sour stomach, while a thick paste of baking soda and a few drops of water was patted directly onto a fresh bee sting, mosquito bite, or patch of poison ivy and left to dry.
note: Once Church & Dwight began selling their Arm & Hammer brand nationally in the 1860s, the little orange box became a fixture in nearly every American kitchen — as much a piece of the home medicine chest as it was a baking ingredient.

name: Coal Oil (Kerosene)
use: Coughs and croup, head lice, and disinfecting cuts
method: A teaspoon of coal oil stirred into sugar or honey was swallowed to break up a bad cough or croupy chest; the same oil was worked straight into the scalp and hair to kill head lice, and dabbed onto a fresh cut or scrape as a rough-and-ready antiseptic.
note: This remedy rode the same wave as the kerosene lamp itself — once coal oil was cheap and sitting in every household for lighting, families simply reached for the same jug when someone got sick, decades before anyone reckoned with what swallowing petroleum could actually do to a person.
caution: Genuinely dangerous by modern medical standards — swallowed or inhaled kerosene can cause severe chemical pneumonia. Preserved here strictly as documented history, not as something to try.

name: Eucalyptus Oil
use: Chest congestion, coughs, and colds
method: A few drops of eucalyptus oil were rubbed onto the chest and throat at bedtime, or added to a bowl of hot water so the vapors could be breathed in to loosen a tight, congested chest.
note: California's eucalyptus boom of the later 1800s — groves planted across the state for a lumber industry that never quite panned out — left behind cheap, abundant eucalyptus oil that found its real use in the sickroom instead. A few decades later, a North Carolina pharmacist named Lunsford Richardson combined that same eucalyptus oil with menthol and camphor into a chest salve called Vicks VapoRub, which became a household name during the 1918 flu pandemic.
caution: Eucalyptus oil is toxic if swallowed; it was used only externally or by inhalation, never taken by mouth.

name: Calf's Foot Jelly
people: Southern and early American households, following period cookery-and-invalid-care manuals
use: Building strength in the sick, consumptives, and new mothers
method: Calves' feet were split and simmered for hours until the liquid turned rich and gelatinous, then strained, skimmed, sweetened, and flavored with wine, lemon, or spice, and chilled into a jelly that a weak or feverish patient could manage to eat when little else would stay down.
note: Recipes for it turn up again and again in early American cookbooks written with invalids specifically in mind, like Mary Randolph's 1824 'The Virginia House-Wife' — a reminder that, before Knox Gelatine arrived in 1890 and made powdered gelatin a pantry staple, getting this particular kind of nourishment into a sick person meant a household boiling down actual calves' feet for the better part of a day.

name: Arrowroot Starch
people: American households, following 19th-century invalid- and infant-feeding advice
use: Feeding infants being weaned, and settling the stomach of the sick or those with diarrhea
method: Arrowroot starch was stirred into cold water to make a smooth paste, then poured into boiling water or milk and cooked briefly into a thin, bland gruel or pudding, spooned to infants, invalids, and anyone whose stomach couldn't manage heavier food.
note: Imported mostly from the Caribbean island of St. Vincent, arrowroot was marketed hard in 19th-century America as the gentlest food a sick stomach could hold — it turns up over and over in the era's home health guides as practically the default food for a weaning baby or a bedridden patient, well before rice cereal took over that job.

name: Fleischmann's Yeast Cakes
people: American households, following Fleischmann's national advertising campaign
use: Constipation, skin blemishes and boils, and general "run-down" health
method: A small cake of fresh, uncooked compressed yeast was eaten plain off a spoon, or crumbled into a glass of water or milk and drunk, typically three times a day, following the dosing printed right in the company's own magazine advertisements.
note: The compressed yeast itself traces back to Hungarian-Jewish immigrant brothers Charles and Maximilian Fleischmann, who built their yeast business in Cincinnati starting in 1868. By the 1920s, the company's advertising had convinced huge numbers of ordinary Americans that eating a cake of baking yeast a day was the secret to clear skin and a healthy gut — one of the odder health crazes ever to come out of a bread ingredient.
caution: Eating raw yeast in the quantities the ads recommended could itself cause gas and stomach upset.

name: Tincture of Myrrh
use: Canker sores, sore or bleeding gums, and mouth ulcers
method: A few drops of tincture of myrrh — myrrh resin dissolved in alcohol — were dabbed straight onto a canker sore or tender spot on the gums with a fingertip or cotton swab, or diluted into water as a gargle for a sore mouth or throat.
note: Myrrh's reputation as a wound and mouth remedy goes back to antiquity, but it earned an official, unglamorous place in the American medicine cabinet too — Compound Tincture of Myrrh sat in the U.S. Pharmacopeia for generations and lived on drugstore shelves as an ordinary household item, right alongside the iodine and the witch hazel.

name: Chickweed Salve
people: English colonial and later American settler households
use: Itchy, irritated skin, eczema-like rashes, and drawing out splinters
method: Fresh chickweed was simmered slowly in lard or oil until the fat turned green, then strained and left to cool into a soft salve that was rubbed onto itchy skin and rashes, or spread thickly over a splinter to help draw it out.
note: Chickweed is a plant the colonists brought with them rather than found here — a Eurasian weed that stowed away in crop seed and ballast soil, spread across the continent within a generation or two of settlement, and got folded straight into household medicine as if it had always grown there.

name: Bull Kelp
people: Makah and other Pacific Northwest Coast peoples
use: Fishing line for halibut, and watertight containers for oil
method: The long, hollow, rubbery stipe was harvested and dried, then used whole or twisted into cordage strong enough to land a halibut far from shore — line that held up in salt water far better than plant-fiber rope. The bulbous float at its base was dried, sealed, and turned into a natural bottle for storing rendered fish or seal oil.
note: A single stipe can run over 30 feet from float to blade. Dried kelp fishing line was cheap, strong, and nearly invisible underwater, and it stayed in everyday use along the Washington coast well after manufactured cordage had become available elsewhere.

name: Rockweed
people: Tlingit and Haida communities of Southeast Alaska
use: Harvesting herring roe (spawn) as a stored winter food
method: Branches of rockweed were weighted down and submerged in coastal bays during the spring herring run. Once the spawning fish had coated the branches thickly in roe, the branches were hauled up and the eggs dried or salted, yielding a rich, portable food that kept through the winter and was widely shared and traded.
note: Rockweed was one of several traditional spawn-catching materials, used alongside hemlock boughs. Roe-on-branch harvests like this are still practiced in Southeast Alaska today, and have been at the center of real subsistence-fishing-rights disputes between Alaska Native communities and state fisheries managers.

name: Sweetgum Twig & Yellowroot Mouth Care
people: Southeastern Indigenous nations, later Southern frontier households
use: Canker sores, bleeding gums, cleaning teeth
method: The tip of a sweetgum twig was frayed into soft bristles and used to scrub the teeth, while yellowroot was chewed or brewed into a gargle for sore gums.
note: A reminder that dental hygiene has always mattered — this frayed-twig toothbrush predates the store-bought kind by centuries.

name: Fire Cider (Master Tonic)
use: Warding off winter colds
method: Raw garlic, onion, horseradish, hot peppers, and ginger were chopped and submerged in raw apple cider vinegar for four weeks, then strained and stirred with honey — a spoonful taken daily through cold season.
note: A homestead tonic that never really went out of style — versions of “fire cider” are still sold in health food stores today.

name: Pine Pitch & Tallow Chest Rub
use: Deep bronchial congestion
method: Clean, sticky pine sap was melted into lard or tallow with a pinch of cayenne, then rubbed onto the chest and back under a warm flannel cloth.
note: The same pine resin that waterproofed cabins and boats also went straight onto aching chests — a household that already trusted pine sap for one job easily trusted it for another.

name: Cascara Sagrada Bark
use: Severe constipation
method: Bark was harvested, then aged and dried for a full year before use, and finally simmered into a decoction.
note: Indigenous bark medicine that settlers adopted wholesale — its Spanish name literally means “sacred bark.”
caution: Fresh, unaged bark triggers violent cramping and vomiting; the year of aging wasn't optional, it was the whole point.

name: Uva Ursi (Bearberry) Leaf Tea
use: Burning urination, bladder complaints
method: Leaves were soaked in cold water overnight to make a milder infusion than a hot brew would give.
note: Also called kinnikinnick, and historically mixed into ceremonial smoking blends as well as taken as medicine.
caution: Traditionally limited to five to seven days of use, and avoided in pregnancy.

name: Black Drawing Salve
use: Splinters, glass, deep boils
method: Lard or tallow was melted with pine resin, beeswax, and powdered charcoal into a thick black salve, spread over the spot and bandaged.
note: Believed to physically “draw” foreign objects and infection up out of the skin — a fixture of the homestead medicine chest.

name: Bread & Milk Poultice
use: Splinters, hard boils
method: Stale bread was soaked in scalding hot milk until it formed a soft mush, applied as hot as could be tolerated, and left overnight under cloth.
note: One of the simplest remedies in any pioneer kitchen — no garden required, just what was already on the table.
caution: The food material itself isn't sterile and can't drain a genuinely deep abscess.

name: The Dry Hot Salt Bag
use: Muscle spasms, stiff necks
method: Coarse rock salt was heated in a dry cast-iron skillet, poured into a clean wool sock, tied shut, and pressed against the sore muscle.
note: A remedy that needed no plants at all — just the hearth and the pantry.

name: Browned Wheat Flour
use: Diaper chafing
method: Dry flour was stirred in a skillet over low heat until golden brown and nutty-smelling, cooled completely, then dusted onto chafed skin.
note: A Great Depression and pioneer-era nursery trick — roasting the flour dried it out and made it safe to put on a baby.

name: Peach Leaf Tea
people: Southern Appalachian granny women & Cherokee midwives
use: Morning sickness
method: A small pinch of green peach leaves was steeped very weakly in hot water and sipped cool.
note: Granny midwives like these carried enormous responsibility with almost no formal recognition — for generations they were the only birth attendants many rural families, of any background, ever saw.
caution: Understood even then to be kept very weak and in small amounts — peach leaves are cyanogenic, like their cherry-family cousins.

name: Wood Ash & Lard Paste
use: Corns, calluses, warts
method: Clean white wood ash was mixed with a dab of lard into a stiff paste, applied only to the dead center of the corn or wart, and bandaged overnight.
note: Wood ash mixed with moisture forms a mild natural lye — homestead chemistry, whether the family had a word for it or not.
caution: Kept strictly to dead tissue; on healthy skin it causes a real chemical burn.

name: White Oak Bark & Walnut Hull Footbath
use: Athlete's foot, trench foot
method: Shredded white oak bark or green black walnut hulls were boiled in a bucket of water for thirty minutes, cooled to warm, and feet soaked for twenty minutes.
note: Born of necessity for men working weeks at a stretch in waterlogged leather boots.
caution: Stains skin and toenails dark brown for weeks afterward.

name: Calendula Nursing Salve
use: Sore, cracked nursing nipples
method: Orange calendula petals were simmered slowly in clean lard or beeswax into a gentle salve.
note: Chosen specifically because it was considered gentle enough to use while nursing an infant.

name: Mullein & Garlic Ear Oil
use: Earaches
method: Yellow mullein flowers and crushed garlic were steeped in warm olive oil or lard for two weeks, then warmed and dropped into the ear with a cotton plug.
note: A remedy passed down through generations of mothers on both Amish and Appalachian homesteads.
caution: Never dropped into an ear that is draining, bleeding, or has a suspected ruptured eardrum.

name: Wild Ginger Root Tea
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Nausea, colic, gas
method: Fresh wild ginger root was sliced thin and steeped in hot water with honey.
note: Not the culinary ginger of the spice rack, but a true woodland native gathered for the same complaints.
caution: Modern chemistry found this plant can contain kidney-damaging compounds — a case where the old use and the new warning sit side by side.

name: Rattlesnake Master Root
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Ceremonial purification; historically carried as protection against snakebite
method: The root was chewed, carried, or prepared ceremonially.
note: Despite the name and the old reputation, the National Park Service is direct about this one: there's no evidence it does anything for an actual snakebite. Its value was ceremonial, not medical — and that's a story worth keeping too.

name: Saw Palmetto Berries
use: Urinary and reproductive complaints
method: Berries were chewed fresh or prepared as a decoction.
note: A Southeastern Indigenous medicine later marketed heavily to American men for prostate health — one of the few old remedies to become a modern supplement-aisle staple.

name: American Beautyberry Leaves
use: Repelling biting insects
method: Fresh leaves were crushed and rubbed directly on the skin, or piled under horses' harnesses.
note: A distinctly practical piece of folk knowledge — this shrub's purple berries are unmistakable in a fall Southern hedgerow, and foragers still pass along its bug-repelling reputation today.

name: Yaupon Holly Tea
use: Ceremonial stimulant, general wellness
method: Roasted leaves were steeped into a strong, dark tea, historically brewed in quantity for ceremonial gatherings.
note: The only plant native to North America that naturally contains caffeine — Southeastern nations were brewing it long before coffee ever crossed the Atlantic, and it still grows wild and abundant across much of the Southeast today.

name: Wild Yam Root
use: Women's complaints, cramping
method: The root was decocted into a bitter tea.
note: Decades later, chemists found a compound in wild yam that became a starting point for early hormonal medicine — an odd, unplanned bridge between a woodland root and the modern pharmacy.

name: Skunk Cabbage Root
use: Bladder, blood, headache, and chest complaints
method: The root was prepared as a decoction for internal complaints, or poulticed for the chest.
note: Recorded across an unusually wide range of complaints — head to chest to bladder — by peoples of the Pacific Northwest, a breadth that suggests it was trusted as a general-purpose remedy rather than a narrow specialist one.

name: Fireweed Tea
use: Digestive complaints; also used topically
method: Leaves were dried and steeped into tea; the plant was also prepared as a topical wash.
note: One of the first plants to bloom after a wildfire clears the ground — northern peoples made use of it right alongside the land's own recovery.

name: Joe-Pye Weed (Gravel Root)
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Urinary complaints and kidney “gravel”
method: The root was decocted into a strong tea.
note: Named for a real historical figure — Joe Pye, said to have been a New England healer who used this plant to treat colonial fevers, a rare case where the person behind a plant's English name is actually remembered.

name: Wild Licorice Root
use: Respiratory and digestive complaints
method: The root was chewed fresh or prepared as tea.
note: A different plant entirely from Old World licorice, gathered by Plains nations as both food and medicine — its sweetness made it as much a treat as a treatment.

name: Purple Prairie Clover
use: General chewing and tea medicine
method: Leaves and flowers were chewed fresh or steeped as tea.
note: One of the quieter Plains prairie remedies — well documented in the historical record, even where its exact old uses are less specific than some of its neighbors.

name: Calamus (Sweet Flag) Root
use: Colds, digestive complaints, toothache
method: The aromatic root was chewed directly or dried and prepared as tea.
note: One of the most frequently recorded medicine plants across the entire Great Lakes record — nearly 260 documented uses by one modern count.
caution: Certain populations of this plant carry real toxicity concerns, so it was never treated as a casual, everyday tea.

name: Red-Osier Dogwood Bark
use: Skin, digestive, and pain complaints
method: The reddish bark was scraped and prepared as a decoction; the stems were also used in mixed ceremonial smoking blends.
note: Easy to spot in winter by its bright red branches along stream banks — a plant many nations turned to for more than one purpose.

name: Goat Weed
use: Inflammatory complaints
method: Leaves and bark were boiled down into a strong decoction taken by the spoonful.
note: One of several Louisiana swamp remedies researchers went back and actually tested — a reminder that folk medicine outside the famous traditions rarely gets a second look.

name: Mustard Plaster
use: Chest congestion
method: Dry mustard powder was mixed into a paste and spread between two layers of cloth, then applied to the chest for a limited time.
note: A genuinely active remedy — the same compounds that make mustard sting the nose also drove blood to the skin's surface.
caution: Left on too long, a mustard plaster causes real chemical burns; it was always removed the moment the skin reddened.

name: “Carron Oil” Burn Remedy
people: Settler households, via Scottish ironworks tradition
use: Burns and scalds
method: Equal parts raw linseed oil and clear lime water were shaken together into a white cream and applied with clean cloth.
note: Named for the Carron ironworks in Scotland, where the recipe was devised for workers' burns, and carried across the Atlantic into settler households.
caution: Modern burn care is different — cool a fresh burn under cool running water first, not oil. See “Setting the Record Straight” below.

name: Virginia Snakeroot
use: Historically: fevers, and kept as a household antidote
method: The root was chewed or prepared as a decoction.
note: Carried a reputation stretching back through colonial households as an all-purpose antidote.
caution: Modern toxicology traced this plant's aristolochic acid to kidney failure and a form of urinary-tract cancer — one of the clearest cases here of old medicine whose real cost we only understood generations later.

name: Prairie Coneflower
use: Stomachache, headache, fever, and poison-ivy rash
method: The plant was prepared as tea for internal complaints, or applied topically for poison ivy.
note: A well-documented Plains and Four Corners remedy for an unusually wide range of everyday complaints.

name: Fringed Sagebrush
people: Apsáalooke (Crow), Cheyenne, Lakota & other Plains nations
use: Bleeding, infection, and ceremonial medicine
method: Leaves and stems were burned as a ceremonial smudge, or steeped into a wash for wounds and infection.
note: The same plant trusted to clean a wound was trusted to carry a prayer — practical medicine and ceremony were never really separate categories. The Lakota and Cheyenne named here were also the allied nations behind one of the most decisive Indigenous military victories in American history, at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876.

name: Big Sagebrush
use: Pain, infection, respiratory complaints
method: Leaves were prepared as an infusion or used in steam preparations.
note: One of the most recognizable plants of the American West — researchers have catalogued over 200 distinct compounds across the sagebrush family.

name: Lingonberry
use: General nourishment
method: Berries were eaten fresh or preserved for winter.
note: Rich, tart, and abundant across the far north — everyday food carrying real nutrition through dark winters short on fresh produce.

name: Rosinweed & Cutleaf Coneflower
use: Respiratory, digestive, and topical complaints
method: Both were simmered into decoctions for internal complaints, or the fresh plant crushed into a poultice for topical use.
note: Two obscure Cherokee-record plants that modern researchers deliberately went back to test, specifically because almost nobody had studied them before — exactly the kind of forgotten knowledge this archive is for.

name: Milkweed Sap
use: Warts and skin growths
method: The milky sap was dabbed directly onto the skin.
note: A plant most people today know only as monarch butterfly habitat — its old medicinal use has almost entirely faded from memory.
caution: Milkweed contains cardiac glycosides and is not safe for casual internal use.

name: Lobelia (Indian Tobacco)
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Respiratory complaints; historically used to induce vomiting
method: The leaves were dried and smoked, chewed, or brewed as tea.
note: Became genuinely famous in early-1800s American medicine through the Thomsonian healing movement, which built a whole popular health system partly around this one plant.
caution: Its active compound affects the same receptors as nicotine, and the line between a therapeutic dose and a toxic one is uncomfortably thin.

name: Wild Indigo Root
people: Indigenous nations & settlers of the Southeast
use: Infections, antiseptic wound care
method: The root was prepared as a wash or decoction for wounds and infections.
note: One of several Indigenous and settler antiseptic remedies used before anyone understood what a germ was.
caution: Potentially toxic if taken internally in quantity; its traditional use was mainly external.

name: Bloodroot
people: Native nations of the Eastern Woodlands, later Gullah & Southern folk medicine
use: Warts, skin growths, respiratory complaints
method: Dried rhizome ground and mixed into a caustic paste — the ancestor of modern “black salve” — or prepared as a wash for oral and respiratory complaints.
note: Its blood-red sap made it impossible to mistake for anything else, feeding a belief that anything this dramatic-looking had to be powerful medicine — a belief that turned out to be true, just not a safe one.
caution: Highly caustic — destroys healthy tissue along with abnormal tissue and can cause disfigurement. Black-salve products containing bloodroot should never be used on a suspected skin cancer.

name: Elderberry
people: Indigenous nations, Appalachian & African American communities
use: Colds, influenza, feverish illness
method: Ripe berries — always cooked, never raw — simmered into a syrup with honey, or dried flowers steeped as tea.
note: The same plant that soothed a cold could sicken the household if picked too early or eaten raw, so knowing exactly when and how long to cook it was the whole skill.
caution: Raw or unripe berries, leaves, stems, and bark contain cyanide-producing compounds and can cause severe vomiting and diarrhea.

name: Blue Cohosh Root
use: Inducing or strengthening labor
method: Dried root decocted and taken in small, spaced sips once labor was already active.
note: It was one of the few plants entrusted specifically to start labor rather than just ease its pain — a trust modern medicine now knows came at a real cardiac cost to the newborn.
caution: Linked to coronary vasoconstriction, fetal stroke, and neonatal heart failure; never safe before full-term active labor and not a home-delivery medicine by modern standards.

name: Cotton Root Bark
people: Enslaved African women & Southern plantation healers
use: Inducing labor and uterine bleeding
method: Dried root bark decocted and taken to bring on contractions.
note: Beyond ordinary household use, this root carries a harder history too — some enslaved women are documented using it toward reproductive control and resistance under slavery, not routine self-care, and that history is worth keeping rather than smoothing over.
caution: A potent oxytocic; unsupervised use carries serious bleeding and labor-safety risks.

name: Pinkroot (Indian Pink)
people: African American Gullah communities & the wider Southern tradition
use: Expelling intestinal worms
method: Root decocted and given in small, carefully limited doses.
note: It clearly worked — Spigelia contains real anthelmintic alkaloids — which is exactly why it was risky: the dose that expelled worms sat uncomfortably close to the dose that damaged the nervous system.
caution: Narrow margin between an effective and a toxic dose; overdose caused dangerous neurologic effects, which is why safer wormers eventually replaced it.

name: Lady's Slipper Root
people: African American Gullah communities & broader American folk medicine
use: Nervousness, sleeplessness (“nerves”)
method: Root dried and brewed into a calming decoction.
note: Nicknamed “American valerian” for how closely its reputation echoed the unrelated European root of the same name — two plants an ocean apart, trusted for the same complaint.
caution: A slow-growing native orchid; wild populations are ecologically sensitive, and modern foraging pressure is itself a conservation concern.

name: Solomon's Seal
use: Sprains and dislocated joints
method: Fresh root sliced and applied directly over the injured joint, or mashed into a poultice and bound with linen.
note: Unlike most poultice remedies here, it was used fresh rather than dried and stored, so a healer needed to know exactly where the plant grew and reach it fast after an injury.

name: Wood Sorrel
use: Warts and corns
method: Fresh leaves crushed into a wet, acidic paste and applied directly to the growth.
note: Its sour, lemony bite comes from oxalic acid — the same tartness that told a forager the leaf was safe to nibble on the trail also made it a plausible wart cure, taste and use lining up neatly.

name: Pleurisy Root (Butterfly Weed)
use: Pleurisy and painful chest inflammation
method: Root simmered into a decoction for about fifteen minutes.
note: Its bright orange summer blooms made it easy to spot and gather at exactly the season damp, changeable weather brought on the most lung complaints.
caution: Large doses can cause vomiting and heart palpitations.

name: Roasted Onion Ear Pack
use: Earache, plugged or infected ear
method: A whole onion baked in coals or a low oven until soft, halved, wrapped in warm cloth, and held cut-side against the outer ear.
note: A fallback for households that didn't keep mullein-and-garlic ear oil steeping — moist heat and the onion's own sulfur vapors did the work instead.
caution: Kept strictly outside the ear canal, never packed inside it.

name: Meadowsweet
use: Sour stomach and stomach cramps
method: Flowering tops steeped into a tea.
note: Meadowsweet contains its own natural salicylic acid — the same pain-relieving chemical family later purified from willow bark into aspirin, discovered independently by a household reaching for a completely different plant.

name: Flowering Dogwood Bark
people: Settlers, drawing on Indigenous plant knowledge
use: Fever, as a substitute before quinine was reliably available
method: Inner bark simmered into a decoction.
note: Naturalist Alexander von Humboldt specifically recorded American dogwood among the plants early colonists leaned on for fever — though it never came close to matching quinine's reliability.

name: Tulip Tree (Tulip Poplar) Bark
use: Fever, general tonic, rheumatic complaints
method: Bark decocted into a bitter tonic tea.
note: One of early America's own homegrown “fever bark” substitutes, reached for the same way cinchona bark was reached for overseas, long before anyone knew why either plant worked.

name: Indian Physic Root
use: Induced vomiting; used as a purgative and digestive remedy
method: Root decocted and taken to induce vomiting or a bowel movement.
note: Its nickname, “American ipecac,” says a lot about old medicine's whole philosophy — inducing vomiting to “get the sickness out” was once a first resort, an idea modern medicine has almost entirely abandoned.

name: Mallow & Marshmallow Root
use: Sore throat, hoarseness, skin irritation, digestive complaints
method: Root chopped and soaked in cold water overnight rather than boiled, to preserve its slippery mucilage.
note: Cold water instead of hot was a deliberate choice — boiling breaks down the very mucilage that made the root worth reaching for in the first place.

name: Elecampane Root
use: Chronic cough and lung catarrh
method: Root simmered into a tea or syrup.
note: Grown right by the cabin door on purpose, the way a household keeps a first-aid kit within arm's reach — proof some medicine gardens were laid out for convenience as much as tradition.

name: Fennel & Wild Carrot Seed
use: Gas, bloating, colic after heavy meals
method: A teaspoon of seeds chewed after a greasy meal, or crushed and steeped in hot water.
note: Simple enough to need no garden trip at all — just the spice shelf, reached for right after dinner instead of days into an illness.

name: Spicebush Twig Tea
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Colds, fever, digestive complaints
method: Aromatic twigs and berries steeped into a tea.
note: Settlers later dried and ground its berries as an allspice substitute — the same aromatic oils that made it trusted medicine also made it a handy kitchen spice once true allspice wasn't an option.

name: Wild Mint Tea
use: Digestive complaints, colds
method: Leaves steeped into a tea.
note: One of the most frequently recorded medicine plants in the entire Plains ethnobotanical record, documented well over 200 times across different nations — rivaled by only a handful of other plants like sagebrush and yarrow.

name: Castor Oil Foot Pack
use: Corns, calluses, ingrown toenails
method: Flannel cloth soaked in cold-pressed castor oil, wrapped around the foot overnight, and covered with a wool sock.
note: A gentler overnight alternative to the caustic wood-ash-and-lard paste other households used on the very same complaints — same goal, a much softer method.

name: Chaparral (Creosote Bush)
people: Southwestern Indigenous nations, later Hispanic communities (gobernadora)
use: Pain, wounds, inflammation, rheumatism
method: Leaves and twigs used topically and as a tea.
note: One of the most chemically potent plants in the entire desert Southwest — its antioxidant NDGA is exactly the kind of powerful chemistry that turned out to be the problem, not the promise.
caution: Internal use has caused documented cases of serious liver injury, including some progressing to liver failure and transplant; historical interest only.

name: Larkspur Seed Wash
people: European apothecary tradition, carried by early settlers
use: Head lice
method: Dried seeds steeped in hot vinegar or whiskey and used strictly as an external wash.
note: It worked by being genuinely toxic to insects — the same neurotoxic chemistry that killed lice could also be absorbed through a child's scratched scalp, likely why gentler options like wild onion eventually won out.
caution: Diterpenoid alkaloids are lethal neurotoxins if ingested or absorbed through broken skin; never used on children or an irritated scalp.

name: Pokeweed
use: Swollen glands, rheumatism, skin eruptions, breast inflammation, “blood cleansing”
method: Root and berries prepared in poultices and washes for swelling and skin complaints; young shoots were separately boiled through multiple water changes as food (“poke sallet”).
note: The same plant was both a beloved spring vegetable and a medicine-chest staple, which made it easy to underestimate — its toxicity has nothing to do with how carefully the greens were boiled.
caution: Every part contains toxic saponins; root and mature plant are especially dangerous, and improperly prepared leaves have caused fatal poisoning even in recent case reports.

name: Aloe (Sábila)
use: Minor burns, sunburn, chafing, irritated skin
method: Clear gel from the fresh inner leaf applied directly to the skin.
note: One of the few plants on this list with real modern trial support behind the old habit — topical gel has been shown to speed healing of minor burns, not just soothe them.
caution: The yellow latex beneath the rind is a different substance from the clear gel and can cause severe diarrhea if swallowed.

name: Red Clover
use: Menopausal hot flashes, general women's tonic
method: Dried blossoms steeped as a tonic tea.
note: Contains plant compounds close enough to estrogen (isoflavones) that modern trials still measure a real, if modest, effect on hot flashes — proof some old women's remedies weren't just comfort tea.
caution: People with hormone-sensitive conditions should be cautious with concentrated extracts.

name: Cobwebs for Bleeding
people: African American communities, and broader Southern folk medicine
use: Stopping bleeding from small cuts
method: A cobweb was gathered from a corner or rafter, sometimes lightly singed over a flame, and pressed directly over a cut as a wound covering.
note: Spider silk really does have a mild clotting effect, and the belief crossed the Atlantic with English and other European folk traditions long before it took root in the American South — but a “clean” cobweb pulled from a dusty cabin rafter was never actually clean, making this one of the clearest cases where the old belief and the old method worked against each other.
caution: Cobwebs gathered from a house are not sterile and risk introducing infection into an open wound.

name: Clay (Kaolin) Poultice
people: Indigenous nations, and Southern settler & African American households
use: Skin complaints, digestive upset, and wound care; ceremonial body paint
method: Clay was mixed with water into a paste and applied directly to skin irritation or a wound; in some households a small amount was eaten for an upset stomach, while separately, clay was ground into ceremonial body paint.
note: Clay's use ran in two very different directions at once — a practical, adsorbent first-aid material on one hand, and a ceremonial body paint carrying real spiritual weight on the other — “medicine” and “meaning” were never fully separate categories in most of these traditions.
caution: Wild clay can carry lead, arsenic, or pathogens depending on the source soil, and eating clay regularly can cause constipation or interfere with medications.

name: Charcoal for Poisoning & Upset Stomach
use: Suspected poisoning, and digestive upset
method: Charred wood was ground into a fine powder and stirred into water as a rough suspension, swallowed when something poisonous was thought to have been eaten.
note: The basic idea turned out to be genuinely sound — activated charcoal, a specially processed version of the same material, is still real emergency medicine for certain poisonings today — though ordinary hearth charcoal was never as absorbent or as safe to swallow as the medical-grade product that idea eventually grew into.
caution: Charcoal isn't a universal antidote, and swallowing it wrong risks it going into the lungs instead of the stomach; ordinary charcoal is not the same product as medical activated charcoal.

name: Apple Cider Vinegar Tonic
use: Digestive complaints, sore throat, skin irritation, and general tonic use
method: Vinegar was diluted with water and drunk by the spoonful, gargled for a sore throat, or dabbed onto skin.
note: Almost every American farmhouse already had a barrel of it on hand from putting up apples each fall, which may explain why vinegar got reached for so often — it was already there, at a time when a special trip to buy a remedy wasn't always possible.
caution: Undiluted, its acid can damage tooth enamel, skin, and the lining of the throat over repeated use.

name: Onion Poultice & Syrup
use: Wounds, chest complaints, cough, and food-medicine
method: Raw onion was sliced or crushed into a poultice for wounds and chest congestion, or simmered slowly with sugar or honey into a cough syrup.
note: Onion's sting comes from sulfur compounds releasing the instant a cell wall is broken — the same chemistry behind both the tears at the cutting board and whatever mild antimicrobial effect the poultice actually had, cause and remedy sitting inside the exact same reaction.
caution: Raw onion applied to skin is not sterile and can irritate; it wasn't a substitute for real wound care.

name: Horseradish Root
use: Sinus and respiratory complaints, and digestive complaints
method: The root was grated fresh and eaten directly or stirred into food, or made into a poultice for the chest.
note: Fresh-grated horseradish clears a stuffy head almost on contact — the same volatile compounds that make eyes water at the cutting board also open the sinuses, an effect strong enough that no one needed convincing it was “working.”
caution: Can irritate skin, the stomach lining, and mucous membranes if used too strong or too often.

name: Oatmeal Skin Soak
use: Soothing itchy or irritated skin, and food-medicine
method: Oats were tied into a cloth bag and swirled through a warm bath, or cooked into a plain porridge eaten as a gentle food during illness.
note: This is one of the rare home remedies that walked straight into a modern pharmacy aisle unchanged — colloidal oatmeal is still an FDA-recognized skin-protectant ingredient today, the same plain oat bath a grandmother once ran, just finely milled and put in a box.
caution: Oat products can carry gluten cross-contamination, which matters for anyone with celiac disease or a wheat sensitivity.

name: Potato Poultice
use: Inflammation, boils, and minor burns
method: A raw potato was grated or sliced thin and laid directly over the sore or swollen spot, often called on to “draw” out the trouble.
note: Potato poultices belonged to a whole folk category of “drawing” remedies — the belief that the right substance held against skin could physically pull infection, pain, or swelling up and out — a theory of healing that shows up again and again under different plants and different names.
caution: Green-tinged potatoes contain natural toxins, and a raw potato pressed onto broken skin isn't sterile.

name: Cabbage Leaf Wrap
use: Breast engorgement and swelling
method: Whole cabbage leaves were chilled, lightly crushed to release their moisture, and tucked directly against the skin, held in place by clothing.
note: Several modern studies have specifically tested chilled cabbage leaves against breastfeeding-related engorgement and found real relief — whether from the cold, compounds in the leaf, or simply both — a rare old home remedy that got the exact clinical trial matched to its exact original use.

name: Molasses Tonic
use: An iron and energy tonic, mild constipation relief, and “blood-building”
method: A spoonful of molasses was taken plain, stirred into warm water, or mixed into food, often as a daily springtime habit.
note: Molasses genuinely does carry meaningful iron for a plain sweetener, which is exactly the kind of real nutrition that let it slot naturally into the same old “blood-building” tonic logic used for other bitter roots and tonics of the era.
caution: It's a real sugar load, not an actual treatment for diagnosed anemia.

name: Hot Toddy
use: Colds, cough, sleeplessness, pain, and “sweating out” a fever
method: Whiskey was mixed with hot water, honey, and sometimes lemon or spices, and drunk warm at bedtime.
note: It never cured anything viral, but it wasn't entirely useless either — a hot toddy is a genuinely effective sedative and a real vasodilator, which is exactly why it felt like it worked even though it was treating the discomfort, not the illness underneath it.
caution: Alcohol carries its own toxicity, interaction, and dependence risks, and it was never a safe remedy for a child.

name: Camphor Chest Rub
use: Chest congestion, aches, and as an insect repellent
method: Camphor crystals were dissolved into oil or lard and rubbed onto the chest, or kept in closets and drawers as a moth repellent.
note: Camphorated oil sat on so many nursery shelves that it became one of the 20th century's quieter child-poisoning stories — mistaken for other equally strong-smelling but far safer products often enough that the U.S. eventually restricted how concentrated a camphor product could legally be sold.
caution: Swallowed camphor can cause seizures and death, especially in small children — one of the more genuinely dangerous items in this cabinet despite how ordinary it once was.

name: Rue
people: Mexican-American & Tejano households, and other Hispanic immigrant communities
use: Menstrual complaints, digestive complaints, and spiritual cleansing
method: A few leaves were steeped into a very weak tea, or the fresh plant was used in a limpia, a ritual cleansing sweep of the body believed to remove bad energy or the “evil eye.”
note: Rue's reputation as spiritual protection ran every bit as deep as its reputation as medicine — sprigs were kept by the door or carried against mal de ojo — and curanderismo has never treated a plant's physical and spiritual power as two separate things worth arguing about.
caution: Rue is a documented abortifacient and can damage the liver and kidneys and cause severe skin reactions in sunlight — one of the more dangerous plants in the whole archive, historical interest only.

name: Tansy
use: Intestinal worms, menstrual complaints, digestive complaints, and insect repellent
method: The bitter flowering tops were steeped into a strong tea or tincture, or the dried plant scattered among linens and floors to repel insects.
note: Tansy's insect-repelling reputation was practical enough that dried bunches were once tucked into coffins and burial shrouds specifically to keep flies away — a use that says something blunt and honest about what people actually needed a strong-smelling plant to do.
caution: Its thujone content is neurotoxic in strong doses and dangerous in pregnancy; the line between a folk dose and a harmful one was never a safe one to guess at.

name: Blue Vervain Tea
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands, and settlers
use: Fever, nervousness, digestive complaints, and women's complaints
method: The flowering plant was dried and steeped into a bitter tea.
note: Its tall spikes of small purple flowers open in a slow, ring-by-ring order up the stem over weeks rather than all at once — the kind of distinctive, easy-to-track growth habit that made a plant simple to identify correctly and gather at exactly the right stage, season after season.
caution: Traditionally avoided during pregnancy, and its dosing was never precisely standardized.

name: Cramp Bark
use: Menstrual cramps and muscle spasms
method: Bark was simmered into a decoction or preserved as a tincture in spirits, taken in small doses at the first sign of cramping.
note: Its no-nonsense common name is also its whole sales pitch — 19th-century Eclectic physicians, a homegrown American medical movement that leaned hard on plant remedies over mineral ones, made it one of their standard antispasmodic tinctures.

name: Hepatica Leaf
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands, and settlers
use: Liver complaints and cough
method: The leaves were dried and steeped into an infusion.
note: Hepatica's three-lobed leaf looks enough like a liver that European settlers' “doctrine of signatures” — the old belief that a plant's shape was nature's label for what it cured — locked onto it immediately; the plant's own genus name literally means “of the liver” in Latin.

name: Eastern Skunk Cabbage Root
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands, later Eclectic physicians
use: Asthma, cough, and rheumatism
method: The root was dried, powdered, and taken in small doses, or the fresh leaves poulticed onto sore joints.
note: Its name comes from the genuinely powerful skunk-like smell released the moment a leaf is bruised or crushed, and old plant logic treated a smell that strong as proof of real medicinal power — the same reasoning that made yellowroot's bitterness and bloodroot's red sap feel like evidence rather than side effects.
caution: The fresh plant contains calcium oxalate crystals that can irritate skin and mouth tissue severely; historical interest only.

name: Wild Senna
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands, and settlers
use: As a laxative and purgative
method: Leaves and pods were dried and steeped into a strong, bitter infusion.
note: It's a genuine wild American cousin of the imported senna that enslaved and free African American healers relied on for the very same purpose — two related but different plants, continents apart in origin, independently trusted by different American communities for exactly the same complaint.
caution: Can cause real cramping and electrolyte loss with overuse, and dose and species varied a good deal in practice.

name: Virginia Iris Root
use: Inflammation and metabolic complaints
method: The rhizome was simmered into a decoction or steeped as an extract, taken by the spoonful.
note: Its showy blue-purple flowers made it easy to spot along the same swampy Gulf Coast ground that gave up goatweed and groundsel bush, but the part actually used sat hidden underwater — the tough rhizome, dug rather than picked.
caution: Iris rhizomes can be irritating or toxic internally; safety at a home-remedy dose was never well established.

name: Ramps (Spring Wild Onion)
people: Eastern Indigenous nations, and Appalachian settler households
use: Food, a spring tonic, and respiratory complaints
method: The pungent bulbs and leaves were dug fresh each spring and eaten raw, cooked into food, or simmered into a broth taken as a tonic.
note: Ramps were the very first green thing up after a mountain winter, which made them the literal, edible proof that the “spring cleaning” a body supposedly needed had actually arrived — less a tested medicine than a calendar you could eat.
caution: Wild ramp patches take years to recover from overharvesting, so a plant this beloved is now also a real conservation concern in parts of Appalachia.

name: Saskatoon Serviceberry
use: Digestive complaints, mild laxative use, coughs, colds and fever, and children's appetite
method: Berries eaten fresh or as juice, or smashed fruit; roots, stems, and sticks were separately decocted for other uses.
note: One Blackfoot record even holds that its medicinal value could pass to a nursing infant through its mother's milk — treating the berry's benefit as something that traveled through the body, not just something eaten directly.
caution: Some historical records include eye or ear applications — those specific uses shouldn't be copied without medical guidance.

name: Spotted Water Hemlock
use: External pain relief, rheumatism, and skin complaints
method: Applied externally in documented Paiute records; the exact historical preparation is intentionally left out here, the same way the original source withheld it — this plant is far too dangerous to describe as a how-to.
note: The same Paiute records that name it as a topical remedy also explicitly identify it as a poison — proof that recognizing a plant's danger and finding a narrow, external use for it were never contradictory ideas in traditional plant knowledge.
caution: One of the most acutely toxic plants in North America — potentially fatal if ingested, and easily confused with edible relatives like wild carrot or parsnip. This entry is historical record only; no preparation detail is included, and none should be attempted.

name: False Unicorn Root
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands & 19th-century Eclectic physicians
use: Women's reproductive complaints
method: The bitter root was dug, dried, and prepared as a decoction, or preserved as a tincture in spirits.
note: Its own name carries a mix-up baked right in — it was called “false” specifically to distinguish it from a similar-looking, unrelated plant sold as “true unicorn root” for the very same complaints, and 19th-century herb traders regularly confused or substituted one for the other. Digging up the root kills the whole plant, and roughly nine in ten roots sold today are still dug from the wild rather than farmed.
caution: Traditionally avoided in pregnancy, and now considered at risk in the wild from decades of root-digging demand.

name: White Pine Needle Tea
use: Coughs, congestion, and general respiratory complaints
method: Fresh needles were steeped into a vitamin-C-rich tea, the inner bark simmered into a decoction, and the sticky resin warmed and spread directly over sores and wounds.
note: The tree's five-needle clusters became a living symbol before they were ever a medicine chest: the Haudenosaunee Peacemaker chose the white pine as the Great Tree of Peace, its five needles bundled at the base standing for the five founding nations of the Confederacy. A tree already trusted to hold a political union together was an easy one to trust with a sore chest, too.
caution: Concentrated resin or oil preparations can irritate skin and airways.

name: Balsam Fir Pitch
use: Coughs, chest colds, and cuts
method: The clear, sticky resin was scraped straight from blisters on the bark and applied to wounds, or warmed into steam and tea alongside the needles for chest complaints.
note: This pitch stays remarkably clear and colorless as it hardens — exactly why chemists later prized the same resin, sold commercially as “Canada balsam,” as a near-perfect glue for mounting lenses and microscope slides. A substance trusted to seal a wound turned out to be trusted to hold a scientist's eyepiece together too.
caution: Concentrated resin can irritate skin and eyes.

name: Eastern Red Cedar
people: Indigenous nations of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Respiratory complaints, skin conditions, and ceremonial purification
method: Leaves and berries were steeped into a tea or a wash, or burned as a purifying smoke.
note: The same sharp, aromatic oils behind all three uses gave the wood a second life once its medicinal reputation faded — the cedar chests and closet linings still sold today for keeping moths away are drawing on a scent Eastern nations were already trusting the body with first.
caution: Concentrated internal use can be toxic; not a plant for casual dosing.

name: Raspberry Leaf Tea
people: Indigenous midwives & American granny-women across many traditions
use: Pregnancy support and women's health
method: The leaves — never the fruit — were dried and steeped into a mild everyday tea.
note: Unlike almost anything else in this archive, this one never really went out of fashion: raspberry leaf tea is still sold in ordinary grocery stores today as a pregnancy tea, one of the few old remedies whose reputation survived completely intact into the present.
caution: Pregnancy use should never be assumed automatically safe or effective without a midwife's or doctor's guidance.

name: Blueberry
people: Algonquian-speaking nations of the Northeast, including the Mi'kmaq & Passamaquoddy
use: Everyday nourishment and general health
method: Berries were eaten fresh off the bush, dried in the sun for winter, or pounded together with dried meat and fat into pemmican.
note: Look closely at the blossom end of a blueberry and a tiny five-pointed star is pressed into the skin — the scar left by the flower. Some Northeastern nations told of the Great Spirit sending down these “star berries” to feed hungry children during famine, a story still told to visiting schoolchildren today.

name: California White Sage
people: Chumash & other Southern California Indigenous nations
use: Respiratory and skin complaints, and ceremonial purification
method: Silvery leaves were bundled and burned as a purifying smoke, steeped into a tea, or simmered into a wash for the skin.
note: This is a genuinely different plant from the “prairie sage” already in this archive — a true sage, not a sagebrush, native only to the coastal hills of Southern California. That narrow range is now the problem: demand from the commercial smudge-stick trade has stripped wild plants from traditional gathering sites so completely that some Chumash harvesters have found their own family's longtime picking grounds picked bare by strangers.
caution: Concentrated or essential-oil preparations can be neurotoxic.

name: Mesquite
people: Southwestern Indigenous nations, including the Tohono O'odham, Pima (Akimel O'odham), Apache & Cahuilla
use: Everyday food and digestive support, sore eyes, wounds, and sore throat
method: Dried pods were pounded into a sweet flour for cakes and drinks; separately, the clear gum weeping from cracks in the bark was dissolved in water as a wash for wounds and sore eyes, or chewed straight like a stick of gum for a sore throat and an unsettled stomach. Screwbean mesquite, a close desert relative, had its root bark prepared separately as its own wound treatment.
note: Mesquite flour's natural sugars let it keep for years without spoiling, turning a desert tree into reliable stored food through droughts that could otherwise mean real famine. That same bark gum is the tree sealing its own wounds shut, which may be exactly why people trusted it to do the same job on skin and eyes — the Pima called the whole tree the “tree of life,” one plant supplying food, medicine, fuel, and building material to a household with little else to spare.

name: Yucca Root
use: Skin irritation, joint pain, and inflammation
method: The root was pounded and worked in water until it foamed, then used as a wash for skin and scalp, or separately cooked as food.
note: The same saponins that made yucca root foam up into soap without a drop of fat also made it the plant reached for on sore, inflamed skin — a household that already trusted it to clean hair and hides had every reason to trust it on the body too.
caution: Concentrated internal use is not well studied.

name: American Holly Leaf Tea
use: Fevers
method: Leaves were boiled into a bitter decoction; berries were sometimes chewed in small amounts for stomach complaints.
note: The same bright red berries that made this tree unmistakable enough to become a Christmas symbol — taken for centuries as a stand-in for drops of blood — are the part of the plant most likely to make someone sick if eaten carelessly. By the 1800s, cutting American holly for wreaths and greenery had grown into a full commercial harvest, stripping branches from wild Southeastern trees every winter.
caution: Berries and concentrated preparations can cause illness; species-specific safety data is limited.

name: Jewelweed Wash
people: Indigenous nations of the East & Appalachian settler folk
use: Poison ivy rash and skin irritation
method: Fresh stems and leaves were crushed on the spot and rubbed directly on the skin, or boiled down into a wash kept on hand for the rest of the season.
note: It grows in the same damp ground as poison ivy, often close enough to reach for one plant right after brushing against the other. A controlled trial later found it no more effective at stopping the rash than plain water — washing promptly with soap and water is what actually helps.
caution: Not a substitute for soap-and-water washing or medical care for a severe reaction.

name: Red Alder Bark Wash
people: Pacific Northwest Indigenous nations, including the Saanich & Cowichan Coast Salish
use: Skin irritation, wounds, and digestive complaints
method: The inner bark was scraped away and simmered into a decoction, used as a wash for the skin or taken for stomach complaints.
note: That same scraped inner bark also produced a deep red-orange dye strong enough to color fishing nets a shade fish couldn't easily see coming — turning a medicine-cabinet plant into fishing gear as well. Unlike most entries in this archive pulled from century-old field notes, this use is also confirmed directly by Coast Salish knowledge-holders in recent published research — proof it isn't only history, but a practice some families still carry today.
caution: Tannin-heavy preparations may irritate the stomach if taken too strong.

name: Largeleaf Avens & One-Flowered Wintergreen
use: General medicinal use
method: Both plants were prepared simply, as a decoction or infusion.
note: Neither plant was showy enough to leave much of a written trail — no dramatic color or strong smell to make an old-time ethnographer stop and take notes the way brighter, stronger-smelling plants did. It took a modern lab systematically screening dozens of lesser-known Pacific Northwest plants for antifungal activity to find that both of these easily overlooked plants were doing something real all along.

name: Balsamroot
people: Nez Perce & other Interior Northwest nations
use: Food-medicine, and respiratory and skin complaints
method: The long taproot was dug before the plant flowered each spring, then roasted or boiled; the same root was separately simmered into a decoction for the chest.
note: Timing the dig to before flowering wasn't superstition — the root's protein content, as high as 30 percent, peaks in exactly that early window, so digging late meant digging a root that had already spent its stored strength on the coming bloom.

name: Cottonwood Bud Salve
people: Northern & Pacific Northwest Indigenous nations, including the Gwich'in and the Sekw'el'was (Cayoose Creek) community, later adopted by settlers
use: Pain, wounds, colds and congestion, cough, tuberculosis, rheumatism and arthritis, cuts, and burns
method: Sticky spring buds were gathered just as they swelled with resin, boiled into a tea for colds, chewed and applied to insect bites, or infused slowly in warm lard or oil and strained into a salve for wounds and joint pain; bruised leaves were separately used as an antiseptic wash.
note: European settlers gave it a Biblical name it never really earned — “Balm of Gilead” properly belongs to a Middle Eastern balsam tree entirely unrelated to this one, but the buds' sweet, resinous smell reminded transplanted colonists of it closely enough that the name stuck to this very different American tree instead.
caution: Can cause topical allergic reactions in some people, especially those sensitive to salicylates.

name: Alaska Wormwood
use: Infection, skin wounds, arthritis, and fever
method: Leaves were dried and powdered into a salve for burns and infections, soaked in water and rubbed on the body or used as a poultice, or boiled into a tea and wash for sore eyes and blood poisoning.
note: Its other common name, “stinkweed,” says everything about how it was actually used day to day — crushed leaves smelled strong enough to cover the smell of fish, useful in its own right before anyone reached for it as medicine. This isn't knowledge frozen in old records, either: it was still relied on and actively taught by the late Della Keats, a respected Iñupiaq healer from Kotzebue honored for exactly this kind of plant knowledge.
caution: Strong volatile oils mean this was never treated as an everyday tea — taken with purpose, not casually.

name: Garlic
people: Amish, Pennsylvania German & immigrant households across America
use: Colds, infections, and general heart health
method: Raw cloves were eaten whole or chopped into food, infused into oil and vinegar, or cooked down into a syrup with honey for coughs.
note: During the 1918 influenza pandemic, families across the country — Pennsylvania German and Appalachian households among them — sewed cloves of garlic into small bags and hung them around children's necks alongside asafoetida root, on the belief that the smell alone could keep germs away. Whether or not it worked, garlic's reputation for fighting off illness was strong enough that people wore it like an amulet.
caution: Raw garlic applied directly to skin can cause a real chemical burn, and it can raise bleeding risk in people on blood thinners.

name: Peppermint Tea
use: Digestive cramps and colds
method: Leaves were steeped fresh or dried into a simple tea after meals.
note: This isn't the native mint already in this archive — peppermint is an Old World hybrid that became such a serious American cash crop that Ashfield, Massachusetts hosted the country's first commercial peppermint farm in 1812, and by the Civil War, Michigan's mint fields rivaled New York's as the nation's biggest source of peppermint oil.
caution: Can worsen acid reflux in some people; concentrated oil should be used cautiously.

name: Chamomile Tea
people: German, Central European & other immigrant households
use: Upset stomach, sleeplessness, and skin irritation
method: Dried flowers were steeped into a mild tea, or brewed strong and cooled as a skin wash.
note: German-speaking households held onto this one so completely that many kept calling it by its German name, kamille, long after other Old World habits had faded into plain English — usually the very first thing reached for when a baby wouldn't settle.
caution: Can trigger a real allergic reaction in people sensitive to ragweed and related plants.

name: Lavender
people: American households of European descent, and Shaker communities
use: Anxiety, sleeplessness, and fragrance
method: Flowers were steeped as tea, infused into oil, or dried and tucked into sachets for linens and clothing.
note: The Shakers, a distinctly American religious community, were the first group in the country to sell lavender as a commercial product — by 1850 their New Lebanon, New York settlement alone was producing about 100,000 pounds of dried medicinal herbs a year, mailed out from a catalog listing over 350 different plants.
caution: Can cause drowsiness or skin irritation from concentrated oil.

name: Valerian Root
use: Sleeplessness and nervous complaints
method: The root was dried and steeped into a tea, or preserved as a tincture in spirits for a stronger, more portable dose.
note: Valerian smells genuinely unpleasant, sharp and sweaty from a compound called isovaleric acid, and old herbalists took that pungency as proof of real strength rather than a reason for doubt. It was official medicine rather than folklore, listed in the United States Pharmacopoeia from 1820 to 1936 and issued to Civil War soldiers as a nerve remedy for the war's own kind of exhaustion.
caution: Causes real sedation and can interact with other calming medications.

name: Broom Snakeweed
use: Colds, cough, dizziness, wounds, snake and insect bites, and respiratory complaints
method: Preparation varied by nation: the Lakota brewed a decoction, the Navajo rubbed plant ash on the body and applied the chewed plant topically, the Blackfoot boiled the roots for a steam treatment, and the Zuni made an infusion from the blossoms or whole plant.
note: Four separate nations, spread across two very different regions, independently arrived at their own way of using the same scrubby roadside shrub — proof that useful plant knowledge didn't need one people to teach another for it to be discovered.
caution: Known to cause toxicity in grazing livestock; safe internal human dosing was never established.

name: Antelope Sage Buckwheat
use: Tuberculosis, bladder trouble, and rheumatism and lameness
method: Root and top growth were decocted into a tea, or the whole plant simmered into a hot compress and wash for aching joints.
note: Not every remedy in the old record held up under its own tradition's scrutiny — the Havasupai's own tea preparation was flagged as doubtful even by the ethnographer who first recorded it, a reminder that these old records preserve some genuine uncertainty right alongside the confident ones.
caution: Correct species identification matters, and safety data is limited.

name: Mormon Tea (Jointfir)
people: Shoshoni, Havasupai, Paiute, Navajo & Ute Mountain Ute
use: Coughs and colds, rheumatism, and stomach and kidney complaints
method: The green stems were steeped into a tea — Navajo households specifically boiled the tops for cough, while Ute Mountain Ute households favored the darkest green stems for their brew.
note: Its genus name, Ephedra, is the same one behind the potent Asian stimulant herb once sold in weight-loss supplements — but American desert ephedra is chemically its own thing, mild enough that Mormon settlers adopted it as an everyday coffee substitute once they learned it from Indigenous neighbors.
caution: Ephedra species vary significantly in chemistry from one to the next and shouldn't be assumed interchangeable; some carry real cardiovascular risk.

name: Nevada Jointfir
use: Gonorrhea, and burns
method: Stems were steeped into a tea combined with a second plant for internal use, while a concentrated decoction was mixed with badger oil into a salve for burns.
note: Pairing this plant with a co-ingredient rather than using it alone was deliberate — old formula medicine often worked as a recipe of several plants together, not a single cure-all, the same logic behind a modern prescription that combines more than one active ingredient.
caution: The exact co-ingredient in the original formula isn't confirmed enough to reconstruct responsibly, and Ephedra species carry real cardiovascular caution.

name: Four-Wing Saltbush
use: Insect bites, itching and rash, wound care, hair cleansing, cough, toothache, and stomach complaints
method: Flowers were made into a poultice, leaves were lathered with water into a genuine soap-like wash for skin and hair, and root preparations were separately taken for stomach and tooth complaints.
note: The same desert shrub that stung the skin with its own salty, mineral-heavy leaves also turned out to be the plant that washed that same skin clean — a household that already trusted it as soap had every reason to trust it as medicine too.
caution: High in natural salts and saponins; the old emetic and enema uses carried real risk and aren't something to recreate.

name: Mountain Mahogany
use: Stomach upset from overeating venison, postpartum recovery, and cough
method: Navajo households prepared extracts from the leaves; the Kawaiisu boiled the root and drank the liquid for cough.
note: Navajo hunters specifically chewed leaves already browsed by deer, believing it carried some of the deer's own hunting luck into the next hunt — medicine and superstition sharing the same leaf, reached for before the hunt as much as after a stomachache.
caution: Tannin-rich and astringent; no established safe dose.

name: Scarlet Globemallow
use: Bleeding, and illnesses believed caused by witchcraft
method: The plant was steeped into an infusion.
note: Explicitly reserved for sicknesses believed to come from witchcraft, this plant sat at the exact intersection of medicine and belief — not every illness in the old worldview had an ordinary cause, and not every remedy was chosen for a purely physical reason.
caution: Limited modern toxicology; no dosing guidance exists.

name: Prince's Plume
use: Glandular swelling, throat pain, earache and toothache, and as a general tonic
method: Paiute healers made a poultice from the plant; Shoshoni households applied root material directly to the gums for tooth pain.
note: This plant's bright yellow spikes are a real, visible warning sign in the desert — its color means it's actively pulling selenium out of the soil in concentrations that can be genuinely toxic, the same trait that once helped prospectors use it to spot mineral-rich ground.
caution: A selenium accumulator; internal use carries real toxicity risk and isn't something to attempt.

name: Rocky Mountain Beeplant
use: Deodorant use, insect bites, inflammation, intestinal complaints, and fever
method: A cold infusion of the leaves was placed in shoes or held against the body for its scent; seed tea was prepared for ceremonial use, and an infusion of the whole plant was taken for fever.
note: Its seed tea carried a specific ceremonial name — “good blood” medicine — treating the plant as something that renewed the body from the inside, not just a fix for one isolated symptom.
caution: Exact internal preparations varied by community and were never standardized.

name: Threadleaf Groundsel
use: Infected sores, kidney complaints, and postpartum "lockjaw"
method: The plant was steeped in water into an infusion, used both as a disinfectant wash on sores and, in some records, taken internally.
note: Recorded specifically as a postpartum remedy for a dangerous complication that genuinely could follow childbirth in that era — proof this wasn't a casual, everyday tea but medicine reached for in a real emergency.
caution: Senecio species contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids with real liver-toxicity risk; the internal use recorded here is historical documentation only, not a safe practice.

name: Wild Four O'Clock
use: Gynecological complaints, rheumatism, swelling, mouth disorders, and wound care
method: The root was made into washes and infusions for external use.
note: Beyond ordinary medicine, a Hopi medicine man could chew the raw root specifically to bring on a vision — one plant serving both as a wound antiseptic for the body and, in the right hands, a door into a completely different kind of knowing.
caution: The root can be pharmacologically active; safe dosing was never established.

name: Soaptree Yucca
use: Insect bites, constipation, sore throat, and cleansing
method: Pounded root was worked into an actual lathering soap and shampoo; root or leaf was made into a poultice for insect bites; the fruit was recorded as a laxative, and a piece of the trunk was chewed for sore throat.
note: Yucca root soap carried real ceremonial weight beyond hygiene — it's documented as part of a fertility rite, one more case of a plant doing double duty as both a practical household good and something with genuine spiritual meaning.
caution: Saponin-rich; safe only as an external soap, not something to eat in quantity.

name: Desert Broom
use: Cough and stomachache
method: The plant was steeped into a simple tea.
note: A clean, single-community record for an otherwise unassuming desert shrub — sometimes the old record keeps things exactly as simple as they actually were, one plant reached for the same plain way every time.
caution: Baccharis chemistry varies by species; internal safety isn't well established.

name: Black Currant Root
use: Kidney trouble
method: The root was prepared as a decoction.
note: The fruit of this same plant was also eaten as ordinary food, so a household reaching for the root as medicine and the berries as dinner never had to think of them as two different plants doing two different jobs.
caution: The fruit is generally food-safe, but the root's internal safety at a medicinal dose is less well characterized.

name: Purple Sage
people: Kawaiisu, Paiute, Shoshoni, Washoe, Okanagan-Colville & Hopi
use: Colds and congestion, headache, stomachache, fever, influenza, and pneumonia
method: Leaves and stems were made into infusions and decoctions, a leaf poultice applied to the chest, or the plant smoked or used in a steam bath.
note: The Kawaiisu also burned this sage specifically to keep spirits and ghosts away from a home, the same plant trusted for a feverish chest also trusted to guard a doorway — medicine and protection sharing one shrub across six different nations.
caution: Aromatic oils can irritate, and safe use during pregnancy or at internal doses was never established.

name: Mule's Ears
use: Inducing vomiting, and swellings
method: The resinous root was ground and soaked in water, or pulped fresh into a poultice for swollen areas.
note: Its resin-heavy root also turned up as one ingredient in old compound formulas recorded for syphilis and measles — serious diseases that called for a mixed remedy rather than any single plant working alone.
caution: The historical emetic use carried real risk and isn't safe to reconstruct without dosing knowledge that no longer survives.

name: Cliffrose
use: Eye irritation, wound cleansing, and skin irritation
method: Inner bark was prepared as an eyewash; the astringent leaves were used to clean wounds, and the Hopi separately used the bark as an emetic.
note: The same tannin-rich astringency that made this plant sting a little when used as an eyewash is exactly what made it useful for cleaning a wound — old medicine often didn't separate “this stings” from “this works.”
caution: The historical emetic use isn't recommended, and its tannins can irritate.

name: Antelope Bitterbrush
use: As a cathartic and emetic, skin problems, and colds, pneumonia, and general tonic use
method: Aerial parts and leaves were steeped into an infusion, or made into a poultice for skin complaints.
note: A close relative of cliffrose, sharing much of the same bitter, tannin-heavy chemistry — two different desert shrubs that different nations independently reached for along strikingly similar lines.
caution: Historical cathartic and emetic use carried real risk and isn't something to reconstruct.
