name: Spruce Pitch & Bark for Wounds and Internal Complaints (Gwich'in, Koyukon, Ten'a & Upper Tanana)
people: Chalkyitsik Kutchin (Gwich'in), Koyukon, Lower Yukon Ten'a, and Upper Tanana
use: Cuts and infected wounds, kidney trouble, dry skin and sores, bleeding cuts, internal troubles, burns, sore throat, and stomach pain
method: Clear pitch was applied directly to cuts, wounds, and infections (Gwich'in), and to bleeding cuts (Ninilchik village) and burns (Lower Yukon Ten'a). Boiled spruce tea treated kidney trouble and dry skin (Koyukon). Pitch was also taken for internal troubles and pressed onto cuts to keep out dirt (Upper Tanana), while bark treated sore throat and needles treated stomach pain (Lower Yukon Ten'a).
note: Four separate Athabascan nations, recorded independently, all reaching for the same tree's pitch, bark, and needles for a strikingly similar set of everyday complaints — further evidence of how central spruce was across interior and northern Alaska.
caution: Nonsterile pitch is not a substitute for real wound care by modern standards, and internal use for kidney trouble or general "internal troubles" treats conditions that need real medical evaluation, not home tea.

name: Pacific Madrone Bark & Leaves
people: Pacific Northwest tribes (specific nation not named in the source)
use: Bark decoction for sores and for colds and sore throat; leaf preparation for cramps and stomachache
method: The tannin-rich bark was stripped, dried, and boiled into a decoction — drunk for colds and sore throat, or used as a wash for sores — while the leaves were similarly steeped into a tea for cramps and stomachache.
note: Madrone is easy to spot even from a distance: it's one of the few Pacific Northwest trees that sheds its outer bark in curling strips each year, revealing smooth, often reddish new bark underneath.

name: Shore Pine — Pitch, Buds & Inner Bark (Pacific Northwest Coast)
people: Coastal Native communities of the Pacific Northwest (specific nation not named in the source)
use: Pitch for open sores, buds for sore throat, and inner bark as emergency food
method: Pitch was collected directly from wounds in the bark, sometimes warmed to soften it, and applied straight onto open sores as a sticky, protective dressing. Young buds were chewed or steeped for a sore throat. In lean seasons the soft inner bark (the cambium layer) was scraped out and eaten fresh or dried — a genuine emergency food used across many pine-using communities.
note: Shore pine is the coastal, often wind-stunted variety of the same lodgepole pine already documented elsewhere in this archive under nine named nations — same species, distinct coastal form and coastal-specific uses.

name: Western Swordfern (Rhizome & Leaves)
people: Northwest coastal peoples (specific nation not named in the source)
use: Rhizome for diarrhea and for sores and pain; young leaves for sore throat and tonsillitis; stems historically used around labor and childbirth
method: The thick rhizome was dug, then roasted or steamed and mashed into a paste — taken for diarrhea, or applied to sores and areas of pain. Young unfurled fronds were chewed raw or steeped for a sore throat and tonsillitis. Stems were prepared as part of practices around labor and childbirth, though the exact preparation for that particular use wasn't recorded.
note: Correct identification mattered here as much as the recipe — several ferns growing in the same understory look alike at a glance, and not all are safe to use the same way; bracken fern, for comparison, contains compounds now known to be carcinogenic, unlike swordfern, which was considered a safe, reliable choice when correctly identified.
caution: Fern identification matters: some similar-looking ferns (notably bracken fern) contain compounds now known to be harmful, which swordfern does not.

name: Oceanspray Leaf Tea (Pima) & Bark-and-Leaf Poultice
people: Pima (Akimel O'odham), and other Native communities within the plant's range (nation not specified for the burn/sore use)
use: Leaves steeped as a tea or tonic (Pima); dried bark and leaves powdered and used on burns and sores (regional)
method: Leaves were steeped in hot water as a tea or tonic, documented among the Pima (Akimel O'odham); elsewhere within the plant's range, the dried bark and leaves were ground into a powder and dusted directly onto burns and sores.
note: This archive already holds an Ocean Spray entry about the same plant's famously hard wood — dense enough to be called “ironwood” and used for digging sticks and arrow shafts — this is the separate medicinal side of the same shrub.

name: Western Larch — Multi-Use Medicine
people: Native American communities of the inland Pacific Northwest (specific nations not separated in the source)
use: Cuts and bruises, tuberculosis, colds and cough, sore throat, arthritis, skin sores, and as a blood purifier
method: The inner bark and pitch were boiled into decoctions and drunk for coughs, colds, sore throat, arthritis, and as a general tonic (“blood purifier”) taken over a longer course for tuberculosis; pitch was also applied directly to cuts, bruises, and skin sores.
note: Western larch produces a sweetish, crystallized natural gum in its sap — sometimes called larch sugar — that was chewed like a natural chewing gum, prized enough that it was gathered and even sold commercially in small quantities in the 19th century.

name: Sitka Spruce Pitch & Shoots (Pacific NW & Alaska Coast)
people: Coastal Native communities of the Pacific Northwest and Alaska (specific nation not named in the source)
use: Pitch used medicinally (specific indication not recorded); young shoots and inner bark used for tea and as emergency food
method: Pitch was gathered from the trunk and either chewed directly, like a natural chewing gum, or warmed and applied to wounds and sores as a sticky, protective dressing. Young spring shoots and the soft inner bark were peeled and eaten fresh or dried for later use, and steeped into a tea prized as a fresh source of vitamin C after a long winter.
note: A different spruce species than the interior boreal spruce already documented elsewhere in this archive — this one grows right along the coast, and its pitch and shoots were used almost interchangeably with those of other coastal conifers.

name: Balsam Poplar Buds & Bark (Yukon-Kuskokwim Region)
people: Alaska Native communities of the Yukon-Kuskokwim region (specific nation not separated in the source)
use: Leaf buds for migraine headache; bark for thrush in small children
method: The resinous leaf buds — widely known by the common name “balm of Gilead” buds — were gathered in spring and either crushed and applied directly to the temples and forehead for a migraine, or infused into oil to make a salve. Bark preparations for infant thrush were used regionally, though the exact recipe wasn't recorded.
note: This archive already holds a Cottonwood Bud Salve entry from Gwich'in and Sekw'el'was practice — this is a separate regional record with two additional uses. Balsam poplar is a close relative of willow, and its resinous buds carry the same salicylate compounds behind willow bark's pain-relieving reputation.
caution: The source is explicit that no infant-thrush recipe survives to reconstruct, and salicylate sensitivity is a real consideration for the migraine use, given the buds' chemical relationship to willow bark and aspirin.

name: Paper Birch Sap Tonic (Alaska Boreal)
people: Alaska Native communities of the boreal region (specific nation not separated in the source)
use: Sap tapped and drunk as a spring tonic beverage
method: In early spring, as the sap began to rise, a cut or tap was made in the trunk and the clear, faintly sweet sap collected in a container tied beneath it. It was drunk fresh as a tonic, believed to clear out the sluggishness of winter, or boiled down — much like maple sap, though it takes considerably more birch sap to yield the same amount of syrup — into a concentrated syrup.
note: That lower sugar content is part of why birch syrup remains a rare, prized Alaska specialty today rather than an everyday product the way maple syrup is in New England — the same tree, tapped the same way, just a thinner sap.

name: Bracket Fungus — Additional Uses Beyond Iqmik (Alaska)
people: Alaska Native communities, including Yupik (specific nation not separated for the ash/tobacco use)
use: Fruiting body prepared for constipation and stomach trouble (Yupik); ashes from a related bracket fungus used as a tobacco or snuff additive (regional)
method: The softer inner fruiting body was prepared as a decoction, or eaten in small amounts, for constipation and stomach trouble. Separately, a related bracket fungus was burned down to a fine ash, which was mixed into chewing tobacco or snuff.
note: That ash isn't just filler — it's an alkaline activator, the same basic chemistry that lets betel-nut and lime, or tobacco and wood ash, release more nicotine from the leaf than chewing tobacco alone would. It's the identical principle behind the iqmik ash already documented elsewhere in this archive, just from a related fungus species.

name: Willow Bark — Alaska Regional Uses
people: Alaska Native communities (specific nation and species not separated in the source)
use: Toothache, stomachache, diarrhea, dysentery, and dandruff
method: The inner bark was stripped, dried, and boiled into a decoction — drunk for stomachache, diarrhea, and dysentery, or held in the mouth for a toothache. For dandruff, a strong bark decoction was used as a hair rinse.
note: Willow bark contains salicin, the same compound family later purified into aspirin — meaning generations of households across Alaska already had a working, if unrefined, version of the world's most common painkiller growing along nearly every stream bank.

name: Porcelain Berry
use: General local folk use (the exact ailment isn't recorded in the source)
note: The berries ripen through a startling run of colors on the same cluster — speckled blue, purple, lilac, even turquoise — which is exactly why 19th-century gardeners prized it as an ornamental in the first place, well before it naturalized and became the aggressive vine it's known as today.

name: Goatweed
use: Inflammation, using the leaves specifically
method: Historic Creole use is documented in the source corpus; the exact traditional recipe wasn't preserved, though a modern screening study confirms it was the leaves that were later tested.
note: This obscure roadside weed turned out to be one of the strongest anti-inflammatory hits in a modern Louisiana plant screen — proof that some of the most promising leads hiding in old plant lists aren't the ones anyone expects.
caution: Croton species can be irritating or toxic and this has never been tested in humans; preserved here as history, not a recipe to try.

name: Sensitive Briar
people: Native nations of the Southeast and south-central US (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Medicinal use documented in North American ethnobotanical sources; the exact condition isn't recorded
note: True to its name, the leaflets fold shut within seconds of being touched — the same touch-sensitive trick used by its better-known relative, the “sensitive plant” (Mimosa pudica) — a real, easily observed piece of natural history even where the specific medicinal use wasn't preserved.

name: Dewberry
people: Native nations across the eastern US (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Medicinal use documented in North American ethnobotanical sources; the exact condition isn't recorded
method: The root bark was dug, dried, and boiled into a strong, astringent decoction, drunk for diarrhea and dysentery — the same well-documented use found across countless Rubus (blackberry and relatives) species in both Indigenous and settler American folk medicine.
note: Dewberry is essentially a trailing, ground-hugging form of blackberry, and its roots share the same tannin-rich astringency that made blackberry-root tea one of the most common home remedies for the “flux” (the old word for dysentery) in households across the eastern United States.

name: Bald Cypress
people: Native nations of the Southeast (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Medicinal use documented in North American ethnobotanical sources; the exact condition isn't recorded
note: Bald cypress is one of the very few conifers that drops its needles every fall (hence “bald”) and grows the odd, knobby root “knees” that rise up out of swamp water — a tree striking enough that historical accounts often dwell on its strange growth habit as much as any medicinal use, which wasn't preserved in this record.

name: Juneberry
people: Native nations of the Northeast (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Medicinal use documented in North American ethnobotanical sources; the exact condition isn't recorded
note: Juneberries are among the very first wild fruits to ripen after a long eastern winter, often as early as May depending on latitude — the common name is really a regional generalization, not a strict calendar promise. A relative of the Saskatoon serviceberry already in this archive, but this eastern species' own specific medicinal use wasn't preserved in the source record.

name: Century Plant (Agave parryi)
people: Southwestern Indigenous nations (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Medicinal use documented in North American ethnobotanical sources; the exact condition isn't recorded
note: “Century plant” is a poetic exaggeration — these agaves flower only once, sending up a tall stalk, then die, but it typically takes more like 10 to 25 years, not a hundred. A smaller, cold-hardy agave of the desert Southwest, distinct from the soaptree yucca already in this archive; the specific medicinal use wasn't preserved in the source.

name: Reishi-Like Varnish Conk
people: North American Indigenous and bioprospecting records (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Research candidate as a medicinal/bioactive bracket fungus; the exact traditional use isn't recorded
note: An eastern North American relative of the Asian reishi mushroom. The source flags it as a research candidate rather than a documented remedy with specifics.

name: Earthstar
people: North American Indigenous and bioprospecting records (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Research candidate as a medicinal/bioactive fungus, in the same family as puffballs already documented in this archive for wound care
note: Earthstars get their name from how they open: the tough outer layer splits into star-shaped rays as the fungus matures, peeling back to reveal the round spore sac at the center. The source flags this species as a research candidate rather than a documented traditional remedy with specifics.

name: Surfgrass
people: Pacific Coast Indigenous nations (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Food-medicine and coastal ethnobotanical use documented; the specific therapeutic use isn't recorded
note: Surfgrass is a genuine rarity: one of the very few true flowering plants that lives its whole life fully submerged in the open ocean — most of what people call “seaweed” is algae, not a flowering plant at all. The record confirms food-medicine use along the Pacific coast without specifying the therapeutic detail.

name: Fish Oil (General Household Use)
people: American households — Indigenous, settler, and immigrant alike (specific community not recorded in the source)
use: Used as a dressing, salve base, poultice component, smoke, wash, powder, or food supplement, depending on the material and source community
method: In the Pacific Northwest and Alaska, oily fish — often eulachon (“candlefish”), among the fattiest fish in the world — were rendered down, traditionally by letting them ripen briefly and then boiling them in water until the oil rose to the top and could be skimmed off. The resulting oil was used as a dressing on wounds and skin, a base for salves, and a food. In American households more broadly, plain cod liver oil was kept on the shelf and given by the spoonful, especially to children, as a general tonic.
note: Eulachon oil was valuable enough among Pacific Northwest coastal peoples that dedicated inland trade routes — still called “grease trails” today — carried it far from the coast, while, completely separately, a spoonful of plain cod liver oil became one of the most widely remembered “old-fashioned medicine” experiences of mainstream American childhood.

name: Obedient Plant
people: North American Indigenous and herbal traditions (specific nation not recorded in the source)
use: Medicinal use documented or strongly represented in North American ethnobotanical and herbal traditions; the exact condition isn't recorded
note: The common name comes from an odd, reliable trick: push one of its flowers sideways on the stalk and it stays put in its new position instead of springing back — a real, easily demonstrated piece of natural history, even where the specific medicinal use wasn't preserved in the source.

name: Downy Hawthorn
people: American Eclectic physicians and herbalists, 19th century
use: A tonic for a weak or fluttering heart
method: Ripe haws and flowering tops were steeped into a tea, or preserved as a tincture in alcohol — the tincture was the form doctors actually kept on hand and dosed, since it held its strength far longer than the dried plant.
note: Hawthorn barely appears in American herbal medicine before 1896. An Irish country doctor named Green had extraordinary results treating heart patients with a secret remedy; he refused to name it and took it to his grave in 1894, until his daughter finally revealed it was simply hawthorn. American Eclectic physicians picked it up almost immediately after and made it a standard heart tonic — one that faded from practice again by the 1930s.
caution: Hawthorn has real, measurable effects on heart rhythm and blood pressure — herbalists today still caution against combining it with heart medication without a doctor's knowledge.

name: Nannyberry
use: A diuretic tea, and to ease vomiting during long illness
method: The Pillager Ojibwe stripped inner bark from low on the trunk and steeped it as a diuretic tea. The Chippewa made an infusion or poultice of the leaves as a urinary remedy, and the Iroquois simmered the root into a decoction to ease vomiting in patients with the lingering, wasting illness then called consumption.
note: Nannyberry's sweet, raisin-like fruit was probably valued at least as much as its bark — eaten fresh, dried, or cooked down, it was a reliable food source in its own right, not just a medicine cabinet staple.

name: Greenleaf Manzanita
people: Native peoples of California's Sierra Nevada and Klamath ranges
use: Poultice for cuts and burns, and a wash for poison oak
method: Leaves and bark were infused into a liquid used as a poultice on cuts and burns, and the same infusion served as a wash for poison oak rash. Leaves were also chewed or brewed into a strong tea for bronchitis and other chest complaints.
note: The berries were eaten out of hand, pressed into a tart cider, or dried for storage. “Manzanita” is Spanish for “little apple,” a name early Spanish colonists gave the shrub for its small, apple-shaped fruit.

name: Bilberry
people: Algonquin and Cree peoples of the Great Lakes and boreal borderlands
use: Eased labor and infant colic
method: Dried leaves were steeped into a tea. The same tea, drunk cold, was used to help bring on labor, to settle colic in nursing infants, and to support women recovering after a miscarriage.
note: This is a North American blueberry relative, not the true European bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) its common name usually points to. Ojibwe families also gathered the berries in quantity, eating them fresh and sun-drying or canning the surplus for winter.

name: Quailbush
use: Smoked or inhaled for head colds and nasal congestion
method: The Cahuilla dried the leaves to smoke, or chewed them fresh, for head colds; crushed flowers, stems, and leaves were steamed and the vapor inhaled for a stuffed-up nose. The Pima ground the root into a powder and applied it as a poultice for sores, while both groups relied on the seeds, ground into flour or meal, as a food staple.
note: Crushed leaves and roots doubled as a rough soap for washing clothes and other items — one shrub covering cold remedy, food, and laundry all at once.

name: Carrion Flower
use: Rheumatism, skin sores, burns, and muscle cramps
method: Root was prepared as an analgesic decoction for rheumatism and back pain. Leaves were pounded into a poultice for burns and boils, and dried, powdered leaves were dusted directly onto burns as a dressing. The berries were used for hoarseness.
note: The small greenish flowers genuinely smell like rotting meat — an odor that draws in carrion flies as pollinators instead of bees, which is where the plant gets its rather unglamorous name.

name: Narrowleaf Cattail
people: Native peoples across nearly every region cattail grows
use: Burn dressing, wound poultice, and padding for infant care
method: The clear gel scraped from between young leaves was applied directly to burns and scalds. Pounded root was made into a poultice for wounds, sores, and stings, and the soft down from the mature seed heads was used to line cradleboards and dress wounds.
note: Cattail may be the single most widely used plant in North America — nearly every part became food, medicine, or material, from the starchy root pounded into flour to the pollen used in cooking and the stalks woven into mats. It's hard to find a region where it wasn't relied on in some way.

name: Sweetflag
people: Ojibwe and other Great Lakes nations
use: Sore throat, toothache, cough, and as a stimulant
method: The aromatic root was chewed fresh for sore throats and toothaches, or dried and carried for chewing on long journeys to fight fatigue. A decoction was also drunk for coughs and stomach complaints.
note: The Ojibwe called it wiike and treated it as close to a cure-all — carried in medicine bundles, chewed before speaking in council for a clear head and strong voice, and traded between nations for its wide reputation.
caution: Sweetflag is generally regarded as safe in the small amounts historically chewed, but the related Old World calamus is not, and the two are easy to confuse — large or frequent doses of either are best avoided.

name: Wild Petunia
people: Native peoples of the eastern prairies and woodlands (no specific nation or use documented)
use: No confirmed historical remedy use
note: Despite the name, this isn't related to the garden petunia — it's in the acanthus family. I found no credible, specific record of it being used medicinally by any named nation, and didn't want to invent one. The wider Ruellia genus shows up in folk medicine elsewhere in the world, but that history doesn't belong to this particular American wildflower on the evidence I have.

name: Snapdragon Vine
people: Native peoples of the Arizona–Sonora borderlands (no specific nation or use documented)
use: No confirmed historical remedy use
note: A delicate desert vine, also called “roving sailor,” native to rocky canyons and washes in Arizona and Sonora. I found no credible record of a specific medicinal use — it's included here honestly as unresearched rather than confirmed.

name: Willowherb
people: Native peoples of the West (no specific nation or use documented)
use: No confirmed historical remedy use
note: A common, weedy relative of fireweed that colonizes disturbed ground. Fireweed itself (Epilobium angustifolium) has a real, separate food and medicine history among various nations, but I don't have solid evidence tying this particular species to its own remedy tradition, and didn't want to simply borrow its more famous cousin's story.

name: Mistflower
use: Fevers, colds, and stomach ailments
method: Leaves and flowers were steeped into an infusion and drunk for fever and stomach complaints. The Houma of Louisiana used it specifically for fevers, and the Cherokee used it, often alongside other plants, for cold and flu symptoms.
note: It was formerly classified in the genus Eupatorium, alongside boneset — a genus European botanists named after Mithridates Eupator, an ancient king famous for his knowledge of medicinal plants and antidotes, long before any European had seen this particular American wildflower.

name: Maximilian Sunflower
use: Primarily a food plant, not a documented remedy
method: The sweet, artichoke-like tubers were dug up, roasted, or added to soups, and the seeds were eaten parched or pressed for their oil.
note: Named for Prince Maximilian of Wied, a German naturalist who documented Plains life and plants in the early 1830s. Its own record here is culinary rather than medicinal — I didn't find a specific, well-documented remedy tradition tied to this species, even though other sunflowers were put to medicinal use elsewhere.

name: Burnet
use: Wounds, internal bleeding, and chest and menstrual complaints
method: Root was chewed fresh or prepared as a decoction to stop lung hemorrhaging, menstrual bleeding, and chest pain. The resin was chewed like gum, and the sap was chewed to freshen the breath and ease colds and fever.
note: Sanguisorba comes from Latin for “blood absorber,” a name earned by its use for bleeding. The Ho-Chunk drank a preparation of it to purify themselves before a buffalo hunt, and the Iroquois used it in preparations meant to protect children from illness believed to be caused by the recently dead — a reminder that a plant's medicine and its spiritual purpose were rarely separate things.

name: Illinois Bundleflower
people: Native nations of the tallgrass prairie (specific nation not confidently documented)
use: Itchy skin, and a folk treatment for eye infection
method: A tea brewed from the leaves was applied to itchy skin. In a striking, very specific treatment, five seeds were placed in the eye overnight and washed out the next morning to treat trachoma, a chronic eye infection.
note: The dried, rattling seed pods doubled as a rattle to entertain and soothe babies. It's also a nitrogen-fixing prairie legume, which is why today it's grown mainly for pasture and soil health rather than remembered for its old medicinal use.
caution: Trachoma is a serious bacterial eye infection — this is a historical folk treatment, not a substitute for real medical care.

name: Tick Trefoil
use: Coughs and lung ailments
method: The root was steeped into a tea and drunk for coughs and lung trouble; other Great Lakes nations used preparations of the plant more generally as a digestive tonic.
note: The seed pods are covered in tiny hooked hairs that cling to clothing and fur, splitting apart into single-seeded segments — a hitchhiking trick some tribes reportedly put to practical use as a rough, natural fastener, or for working thorns and splinters out of the skin.

name: Lupine
people: Great Lakes and Eastern Woodland nations, including the Ojibwe
use: Nausea and internal bleeding; seeds as a lean-season food
method: Leaves were brewed into a tea and drunk cold for nausea and internal hemorrhaging. The seeds, bitter and toxic raw, were soaked repeatedly in water over several days to leach out their alkaloids before being roasted and eaten — worth the labor as a reliable source of protein in early spring, when little else was ready to harvest.
note: Lupine fixes nitrogen in poor, sandy soil and is often the first real color back on the land after winter, which may be part of why a plant that took so much work to detoxify was still considered worth the trouble.
caution: The raw seeds and foliage contain genuinely toxic alkaloids — the reason for the repeated soaking — and lupine remains a recognized poisoning risk for grazing livestock today.

name: Starflower
use: General sickness, consumption, and eye ailments
method: The Montagnais steeped the whole plant for general sickness and what was then called consumption. The Paiute used the plant's juice as an eye treatment, while the Ojibwe included the root in a scent mixture for hunting rather than medicine.
note: It wasn't a major medicine for most nations who knew it — starflower turns up here and there in the record rather than as a widespread standby, and that's worth saying plainly instead of dressing it up as more than it was.

name: Palmer Amaranth
people: Pima (Akimel O'odham), Tohono O'odham, Navajo, Cocopah, Mohave, and Quechan (Yuma)
use: Primarily a food plant across the Sonoran Desert, not a documented remedy
method: Leaves were boiled as greens, dried and stored for winter, or cooked and rolled into balls for keeping. Seeds were parched and ground into meal, or the parched seed was chewed for its natural sugars.
note: Today it's mostly known as an aggressive, herbicide-resistant farm weed, which makes it easy to forget it was once a genuine dietary staple across several Sonoran Desert nations. I didn't find a distinct remedy tradition to go with that food tradition, so I'm not inventing one.

name: Miner's Candle
people: Native peoples of the Southwest (no specific nation or use documented)
use: No confirmed historical remedy use
note: A hairy, spike-flowered desert plant in the borage family. The record here is genuinely thin — even close relatives in the same genus are noted in the literature as having no reported medicinal use or folklore attached to them, so I'm not going to manufacture one.

name: Goji Relative
people: Native peoples of the Southwest desert (no specific nation or use documented)
use: Primarily a food plant, not a documented remedy
method: The small orange-red berries were eaten fresh off the shrub, or dried like raisins for later use.
note: It's a genuine wild relative of the goji berry sold in health-food stores today — both are in the nightshade genus Lycium — but I didn't find solid evidence of a specific remedy use for this species in America, only food use, so that's what's recorded here.

name: Borage
people: English and other European colonists, and their American descendants
use: Fevers, colds, low spirits, and to bring in milk for nursing mothers
method: Leaves and the star-shaped blue flowers were steeped into a tea for fevers and cold symptoms, or infused into wine or cider — a use going back to Roman times — for a low or anxious mood.
note: Colonists carried borage seed across the Atlantic on some of the earliest voyages; the naturalist John Lawson recorded it growing in Carolina gardens by 1709. Its old nickname, “herb of courage,” likely comes from a folk mangling of the Latin cor, heart — Gerard's 16th-century herbal even gives it a little rhyme: “I, borage, bring always courage.”

name: Marjoram
people: English and other European colonists, and their American descendants
use: Coughs, colds, and headache
method: Dried leaves were steeped into a tea for coughs and colds, or combined with other garden herbs like sage and lavender into a headache remedy. Made stronger, the same tea went into old cough-syrup recipes.
note: It was a standard fixture of the colonial physic garden, grown right alongside food herbs rather than set apart as something special — in most colonial households, the line between the kitchen garden and the medicine cabinet barely existed.

name: Winter Savory
people: Pennsylvania German (“Pennsylvania Dutch”) households, and other European settler communities generally
use: Bee and wasp stings, and settling the stomach after a bean dinner
method: A fresh leaf, crushed and rubbed directly on a sting, was a quick field remedy. Cooked into a pot of beans, the herb was also credited with settling the digestive trouble beans are famous for causing.
note: German-speaking farm households still call it Bohnenkraut — literally “bean herb” — and it's genuinely still cooked into bean dishes today for that same old, practical reason, not just for tradition's sake.

name: Coriander
people: English and other European colonists, and their American descendants
use: Gas and stomach cramping
method: Dried seeds were chewed whole or steeped into a tea to ease bloating and cramping after meals. Apothecaries also relied on coriander's strong, pleasant flavor to mask the taste of more bitter medicines dosed alongside it.
note: It's one of the oldest cultivated spices in the world, with a documented history running back thousands of years before it ever reached an American kitchen garden.

name: Cumin
people: Spanish colonists, and later Mexican and Mexican-American households
use: Mostly a flavoring spice; a general digestive folk use, not a distinct American remedy
method: Seeds were toasted and ground into cooking, in the same carminative role — settling gas and mild digestive upset — cumin has played in cuisines worldwide for thousands of years.
note: Cumin's American story runs through Spanish colonization rather than English kitchen gardens — it arrived with Spanish settlers and became, and remains, a defining flavor of Southwestern and Mexican-American cooking. I don't have solid evidence of a distinct home-remedy tradition specific to America beyond that general old-world digestive reputation, so I'm not overstating it.

name: Chervil
people: European settlers generally, especially those following English and French herbal tradition
use: A minor “spring tonic” herb, more by inference than solid documentation
method: Fresh leaves were eaten in salads or brewed into a mild tea each spring, in the same tradition as dandelion greens and other early tonic herbs meant to rouse the appetite and digestion after a winter of preserved food.
note: Chervil's reputation as a spring cleansing tonic is well documented in medieval and later European herbals, and it was certainly grown in American kitchen gardens by colonists and later French and German immigrants. But I don't have a specific citation putting it to use as a remedy, rather than just a cooking herb, in American households — so treat the tonic use as a reasonable inference from its Old World reputation, not a confirmed American practice.

name: Leek
people: English, Scottish, and other European settlers
use: Broth for the sick and convalescent
method: Leeks were simmered into a plain broth or soup given to the sick and recovering as an easily digested, restorative food — the same logic behind the old Scottish dish cock-a-leekie soup.
note: Leek's medicinal reputation has always been the quiet, food-adjacent kind, nothing like the vivid tradition around onion (poulticed straight onto a congested chest) or garlic. It shows up mostly as a gentle food for the sick rather than a dedicated home remedy in its own right, which is worth saying honestly rather than dressing it up to match its more famous relatives.

name: Chives
use: Believed to aid digestion; mostly a food, not a strong distinct remedy
method: Chopped fresh into food, or occasionally steeped into a mild tea.
note: Old folk belief held that the stronger an herb tasted, the more healing power it carried, and pungent chives benefited from that reasoning — Roman writers claimed chives were fed to wrestlers and racehorses for strength. But next to onion or garlic, chives were always the mild, everyday kitchen herb rather than a serious home remedy, and it would be overstating things to claim otherwise.

name: Rutabaga
people: Scandinavian (especially Swedish and Norwegian) and Finnish immigrant farm families
use: Just a food — no distinct remedy history found
method: A hardy root vegetable, stored through winter in root cellars and cooked into soups, mashes, and stews.
note: Rutabaga is a genuinely Scandinavian crop — the name comes from the Swedish rotabagge, “thick root” — and it became a staple for the roughly three million Scandinavian and Finnish immigrants who settled Minnesota, Wisconsin, and the Upper Midwest between the 1820s and 1920s, because it thrived in that same cold, short-season climate. It was reliable pantry food, not medicine, and it's more honest to say so than to invent a remedy for it.

name: Tomato
people: General American public, via an Ohio physician's commercial promotion
use: Marketed in the 1830s as a cure for indigestion, headache, and even cholera
method: Sold as “tomato pills” or “compound extract of tomato” — commercial patent-medicine tablets ordinary households bought and took like any other pill, rather than a plant prepared at home.
note: Ohio physician John Cook Bennett publicly promoted tomatoes as a wonder medicine starting in 1834, and rival brands (“Tomato Pills Cure Your Ills” was one slogan) fought over the market for the rest of the decade. By 1840, critics discovered many of these pills contained no actual tomato at all — a reminder that plenty of “genuine” 19th-century home medicine was really just marketing. Bennett himself later ran a diploma mill selling fake medical degrees, which says something about his credibility.

name: Eggplant
people: American households broadly, largely via Mediterranean and Middle Eastern immigrant cooking
use: Just a food — no remedy history found
note: Eggplant arrived in American kitchens later and more slowly than most of its nightshade relatives, like tomato and pepper, and was viewed with some of the same suspicion for a long time. I found no genuine historical home-remedy tradition attached to it in America; it was, and is, simply a vegetable.

name: Butternut Squash
people: Native peoples originally, and general American farm households afterward
use: Seeds used as a home remedy to expel intestinal worms
method: Squash and pumpkin seeds were dried, then eaten plain, ground into a paste, or steeped, as a dewormer for children and adults alike — a folk remedy with a real, documented effect from compounds in the seed.
note: This remedy has a genuinely traceable path: Native peoples across the Americas used squash and pumpkin seed this way first, American physicians adopted it as standard practice by the early 1800s, and the U.S. Pharmacopoeia officially listed pumpkin seed as a recognized anthelmintic from 1863 all the way to 1936. One honest wrinkle: “butternut squash” as a named variety didn't exist yet in that era — it was bred and named in 1944 by Charles Leggett, a Massachusetts farmer, so a 19th-century household would just have called this a squash, not a butternut.

name: Winter Squash
people: Native peoples originally, and general American farm households afterward
use: Seeds eaten to expel intestinal worms
method: As with other winter squash, the seeds were dried and eaten, or ground and steeped, to expel intestinal worms — a folk remedy well-regarded enough to earn a spot in the official U.S. Pharmacopoeia from 1863 to 1936. The squash itself was stored whole in a cool cellar and helped keep a household fed well into winter.
note: One well-documented squash story from this same species: seedsman James J.H. Gregory of Marblehead, Massachusetts traced an unusually good squash back through a chain of local growers to a Mrs. Elizabeth Hubbard, who'd praised it as the best she'd ever eaten. Gregory introduced it commercially in 1854 and named it the Hubbard squash in her honor — it's still sold under that name today.

name: Cucumber
people: English and other European colonists, and their American descendants
use: A cooling wash for sunburn and heat-inflamed skin or eyes
method: Slices were laid directly on the skin, or the juice pressed out and dabbed on with a cloth.
note: This comes out of the old humoral system of medicine colonists brought from England — herbalists like Culpeper classified cucumber as “cold and moist,” the right remedy for anything hot and inflamed, whether sunburned skin or tired eyes. It's the same logic behind the modern spa cliche of cucumber slices on the eyes, just with a few centuries and a different vocabulary in between.

name: Muskmelon
use: Just a food — no remedy history found
note: An early, once-common melon, ancestor of the modern cantaloupe, that colonial and 19th-century Americans grew and ate fresh in season. I didn't find a genuine, documented home-remedy use for it distinct from being a food — some other “cooling” fruits and vegetables of the period picked up a minor medicinal reputation, but I don't have solid evidence muskmelon was specifically one of them.

name: Apricot
use: Dried fruit eaten as a gentle, general laxative
method: Dried apricots were stewed or eaten out of hand for their mild laxative effect.
note: This is really a general property of dried stone fruit rather than something special to apricots — prunes (dried plums) were always the much more famous and specifically documented example of this same home remedy. Apricot rode along on that general reputation rather than having a strong distinct tradition of its own, which is the honest version of this entry.

name: Lime
people: American sailors on long ocean voyages, following the same practice as the British navy
use: A preventive against scurvy on long sea voyages
method: Juice was preserved with sugar, and sometimes rum, into a “shrub” that was rationed out on long voyages after fresh food ran out.
note: This story is really a British Royal Navy one first — “limey” started as an American jab at British sailors for their citrus ration — and there's a real irony buried in it: lime juice actually has less vitamin C than lemon juice, so when the Royal Navy switched from lemons to cheaper West Indian limes in the 1860s, scurvy crept back in on some longer voyages. American whaling and merchant ships carried citrus for the same reason, but lemons and limes were used fairly interchangeably rather than lime being singled out as the more effective one.

name: Bitter Orange
people: American Eclectic physicians, and Creole apothecaries in New Orleans
use: A digestive bitter and tonic
method: The dried peel was steeped or tinctured into a bitter tonic taken before meals to stimulate digestion, and also used as a flavoring to make other, harsher medicines more palatable.
note: New Orleans had its own real tradition of bitters-making by Creole apothecaries in the 19th century, and citrus peel — orange included — was a common building block of those bitters, made as much for the stomach as for the bar.
caution: Bitter orange's stimulant compound, synephrine, has drawn real modern concern at concentrated or supplement-strength doses, particularly for people with heart conditions.

name: Grapefruit
people: General American public, following its introduction from the Caribbean
use: Just a food — no historical remedy tradition found for this period
note: Grapefruit is a true New World fruit — an accidental 18th-century hybrid of sweet orange and pomelo first recorded in Barbados, named in Jamaica in 1814, and planted in Florida in the early 1800s before becoming a real commercial crop there by the century's end. Its later reputation as a diet or health food is a 20th-century development, well outside this app's historical window, so I'm not reaching for a remedy use that doesn't belong to this era.
caution: Grapefruit is well known today for interfering with how the body processes many common medications — a real concern, though obviously not one anyone understood historically.

name: Almond
people: European colonists broadly, and later American health reformers
use: Almond milk as an easily digested food for the sick, and almond oil for chapped skin
method: Almonds were blanched, ground fine, and steeped in water to make “almond milk,” a dairy substitute given to invalids, infants, and anyone with a delicate stomach. The pressed oil was rubbed into chapped hands, lips, and dry skin.
note: Almond milk for the sick is a genuinely old practice, well documented in Europe back to the Middle Ages, that colonists simply carried across the Atlantic and kept using into the 19th century. It got a specifically American second life through the Seventh-day Adventist health reform movement, which promoted nuts and nut milks as replacements for meat and dairy from the mid-1800s onward.

name: Sesame
people: Gullah Geechee people of the South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry
use: Valued as food and for good luck, not documented as a remedy
note: Benne — the Gullah word for sesame, from the Wolof and Bambara languages of West Africa — arrived in the Carolina Lowcountry with enslaved Africans in the early 1700s. It was treated as a “goodwill” plant that carried good luck, and benne wafers are still sometimes called America's original fortune cookie. That's a real and rich food story, though — not a documented medicine, so no remedy use is invented here.

name: Millet
use: No remedy tradition found — grown chiefly as animal feed, not human medicine
note: Millet shows up in early American farm records mostly as feed grain for poultry and livestock rather than something households ate or treated themselves. It never became a food staple here the way corn or wheat did, and no genuine home-remedy tradition is attached to it — noted honestly rather than invented.

name: Sorghum
use: No remedy tradition found — valued chiefly as an affordable homemade sweetener
note: Sorghum cane became the Appalachian household's answer to store-bought cane sugar, especially after the Civil War disrupted supply. Families grew it, then gathered each fall for communal “stir-offs” to press and cook the juice down into syrup, a tradition documented well into the 20th century. That's a real and important food story — but it's a sweetener, not a documented medicine.

name: Cacao
use: Restorative drink for the sick, weak, and convalescent
method: Roasted, ground cacao was mixed into a hot drink — sometimes made from just the roasted shells, for a lighter version that was easier on a weak stomach — and given to invalids as a nourishing, easily digested tonic rather than a mere treat.
note: Chocolate's medicinal reputation traveled with it from the Spanish Americas into English colonial life: Martha Washington reportedly steeped cacao shells into a thin chocolate drink for the sick, and Benjamin Franklin was among its outspoken 18th-century champions. Apothecary shops sold chocolate alongside their other remedies, not only as a treat.

name: Vanilla
people: 19th-century American physicians, drawing on a reputation vanilla carried from Mesoamerica and Europe
use: Nerve stimulant for hysteria, nervous complaints, and low fevers
method: The cured pod was infused into a tincture or syrup — Dr. John King's 1859 American Dispensatory recommended it this way — and it was also used to make harsher medicines easier to take.
note: Vanilla was first cultivated by the Totonac people of Mexico's Gulf coast, and the Aztec used it to flavor cacao drinks. By the mid-1800s it had a real, if now-forgotten, place in American medicine: praised in dispensatories of the day as a stimulant thought to invigorate the nerves — a claim no one would make today.

name: Cinnamon
people: English colonists and their descendants, via the international spice trade
use: Warming digestive remedy for upset stomach, gas, and chill
method: The bark, or ground cinnamon, was steeped into a warming tea, stirred into possets and caudles (warm spiced drinks made for the sick), or simply chewed.
note: True Ceylon cinnamon was the costlier of the two “cinnamons” reaching colonial ports. Most households actually reached for cassia (see Cassia Cinnamon) as their everyday kitchen-and-medicine-chest spice, saving true cinnamon for when it could be afforded.

name: Cassia Cinnamon
people: American households broadly — colonial, immigrant, and pioneer alike
use: Warming digestive remedy for upset stomach, gas, and colds
method: Ground bark was stirred into hot water, milk, or spirits and drunk to warm and settle the stomach, or added to poultices and warming plasters for chest colds.
note: This, not true Ceylon cinnamon, was what most early Americans actually meant when they said “cinnamon” — it was cheaper and more available through trade with China and the East Indies. That's still true today: most cinnamon sold in American grocery stores is cassia.

name: Mace
people: English colonists, via the international spice trade
use: Digestive aid, added to drinks and food for the sick
method: The dried, lacy aril was grated or crushed and stirred into warm milk, wine, or possets given to invalids and the frail, both to settle the stomach and to make other medicines more palatable.
note: Mace is the red, net-like covering wrapped around the nutmeg seed — the same tree produces both spices. Nutmeg and mace were once so valuable that in 1667 the Dutch gave up their claim to Manhattan partly to keep sole control of Run, a tiny nutmeg-producing island in present-day Indonesia.
caution: In large doses — more often a concern with its sibling nutmeg — it can cause nausea, a racing heart, and hallucinations, which is reason enough both were used sparingly.

name: Cardamom
people: English colonists and their descendants, via the international spice trade
use: Digestive aid for gas and stomach upset
method: The seeds were crushed and steeped into tea, chewed whole, or added to other bitter medicines to make them easier to take.
note: Cardamom traveled the same maritime spice routes — through ports like Salem, Massachusetts — that carried pepper, cinnamon, and other Old World spices into early American kitchens and medicine chests.

name: Allspice
people: English colonists and their descendants, via Caribbean trade
use: Digestive aid and a warming rub for sore muscles
method: Dried berries were steeped into tea for gas and stomach upset, or ground and added to warming liniments and poultices rubbed on aching muscles.
note: Allspice grows only in the Caribbean and Central America and reached American ports along the same shipping lanes that carried rum and sugar. English colonists gave it its name because its flavor seemed to combine cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg all at once.

name: Gypsum
use: No remedy tradition — used as a soil fertilizer, not a medicine
note: Ground gypsum, known as “land plaster,” was spread on fields as fertilizer, a practice Pennsylvania German farmers pioneered. As the well-known story goes, Benjamin Franklin once spelled out a message like “This land has been plastered” in gypsum across a field, so neighboring farmers could see for themselves how much greener the treated grass grew. That's real agricultural history, not medicine — no remedy use is invented here.

name: Musk
people: American physicians and apothecaries, following British and European medical practice
use: Antispasmodic for fainting spells, hysteria, and convulsions
method: Musk grains were formed into a small bolus (a pill-like dose) and given for fainting fits, heart palpitations, whooping cough, and infant convulsions — documented as late as 1898 in King's American Dispensatory, a standard American medical reference of the era.
note: True musk came from the musk deer of Central and South Asia and was genuinely imported into early America — an expensive, exotic item stocked by apothecaries, not something a household could gather or make itself.

name: Yogurt
people: Southern and Appalachian households (as clabbered milk); more broadly, American households swept up in a health fad by the early 1900s
use: Digestive aid, and, by the early 1900s, a supposed longevity tonic
method: Milk was left to sour and thicken naturally into “clabber,” eaten plain or lightly sweetened, and considered gentler on the stomach than sweet milk — especially for the sick, the very young, or the elderly.
note: In 1907–08, Russian scientist Élie Metchnikoff — who'd go on to win the Nobel Prize — proposed that Bulgarian peasants' long lives came from the fermented milk they ate, and the idea set off a genuine American health craze: newspapers touted it, and mail-order companies sold “Bulgarian bacillus” starter cultures to households eager to try it themselves.

name: Cobweb
people: Appalachian households, and American folk medicine broadly
use: Stopping bleeding from cuts and scrapes
method: A handful of cobweb was pressed directly onto a fresh cut to help it clot, sometimes with soot, flour, or ash mixed in.
note: This was one of the most common remedies in American households generally, not just Appalachia — and it wasn't pure superstition. Spider silk really does have mild antibacterial properties and a mesh fine enough to help blood clot, which may be part of why the practice stuck around so long.
caution: Not a sterile dressing by modern standards — a real infection risk for anything beyond a minor scrape.

name: Agar
people: Japanese immigrant communities in Hawaii and California
use: No remedy tradition found — used as a food-thickening ingredient, not a medicine
note: Agar (kanten) is a Japanese product, developed in Japan and brought to Hawaii and California by Japanese immigrants from the 1880s on, mainly to make traditional sweets and jellies. That's a real piece of Japanese American foodways, but no distinct home-remedy use for it is documented — noted honestly rather than invented.

name: Carrageenan Seaweed
use: Coughs, colds, and chest complaints; nourishment for the sick
method: The seaweed (Irish moss) was boiled in milk until it released its natural gelatin, then strained and sweetened into a soft, pudding-like drink — a soothing food for sore throats and for building up someone weak or recovering from illness.
note: In 1847, Irish immigrant Daniel Ward recognized carrageen moss growing off Scituate, Massachusetts, from back home, and began harvesting it — sparking an industry that drew so many fellow Irish immigrants fleeing the Famine that Scituate is still sometimes called the most Irish town in America. Mossers raked it from small boats by hand, a trade that lasted there for generations.

name: Koji
people: Japanese immigrant communities in Hawaii and California
use: No remedy tradition found — a fermentation starter for miso, soy sauce, and sake, not a medicine
note: Japanese immigrants brought koji-based fermentation with them beginning in the 1880s, mainly to Hawaii's plantation communities and later California, to make the miso and soy sauce that were part of daily cooking. That's a genuine piece of immigrant foodways, but not a documented home remedy — noted honestly rather than invented.

name: Kombucha Culture
people: Uncertain — possibly German or Eastern European immigrant households, but not confidently documented
use: Unclear — no confirmed American folk-remedy history in this period
note: Kombucha (“tea fungus”) was known in Russia, Ukraine, and Germany by the early 1900s, and German and Eastern European immigration to America was heavy in that era, so it's plausible some immigrant households here knew of it. But that's a guess, not a documented fact — there's no confident evidence it was actually made or used as a remedy in early American households, and its real boom in the U.S. didn't arrive until the 1990s. Left honestly uncertain here rather than dressed up as confirmed history.

name: Sourdough Starter
people: Gold Rush prospectors of the Klondike and Alaska, and American pioneer households more broadly
use: No remedy tradition found — a leavening culture for bread, not a medicine
note: Sourdough starters were how households leavened bread without store-bought yeast, and prospectors depended on theirs so completely during the Klondike Gold Rush (starting 1897) that “sourdough” became slang for a grizzled old-timer — some reportedly kept their starter close to their body overnight so it wouldn't freeze. A genuine and colorful piece of American history, but a food story, not a medical one.

name: Sesame Oil
people: Gullah Geechee people of the South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry
use: No remedy tradition found — pressed from benne (sesame) seeds mainly for cooking
note: Benne oil, pressed from the same sesame seeds enslaved Africans brought to the Carolina Lowcountry in the early 1700s, was primarily a cooking oil in Gullah Geechee foodways. No distinct home-remedy use for the oil itself is documented here — noted honestly rather than invented.

name: Almond Oil
people: English colonists and their descendants, via apothecary practice
use: Softening chapped skin and easing earache
method: Warmed oil was rubbed onto dry or chapped skin, or a few drops were dropped into an aching ear — a gentler, costlier alternative to the more common “sweet oil” (olive oil) used the same way, and considered mild enough for infants.
note: Sweet almond oil was a standard apothecary item inherited straight from British pharmacy practice, stocked in early American drugstores for exactly this kind of everyday household use.

name: Avocado Oil
people: Indigenous and Mexican communities of Mesoamerica and the Southwest
use: No remedy use confirmed for the pressed oil specifically — the fruit and leaves had traditional uses, but oil-pressing appears to be a modern product
note: Avocado leaves and bark have a real place in traditional Mexican herbal medicine, but cold-pressed avocado oil as a discrete product is a modern one — there's no confident evidence it was something households in this era pressed and used medicinally themselves. Noted honestly rather than invented.

name: Cottonseed Oil
people: The American South generally, as a food product; enslaved and formerly enslaved communities used a different part of the plant medicinally
use: No remedy use confirmed for the seed oil itself — mainly a cooking product; a different part of the plant (the root bark) has real, documented history
note: Cottonseed oil didn't become a usable cooking product until bleaching and deodorizing methods were developed in the late 1800s — Crisco, launched in 1911, was the first shortening made from it. That's genuine oil history, but it's food, not medicine. The plant's root bark, a different part entirely, does have a real and important documented history: enslaved women in the South are recorded — including in their own oral histories — using cotton root bark in attempts to end unwanted pregnancies or delay childbearing, often at great personal risk, since slaveholders punished it when discovered. That history belongs to the root, not the seed oil, so it isn't attributed to this entry as if they were the same thing.

name: Borage Oil
people: English colonists and their descendants, via inherited herbal tradition
use: No remedy use confirmed for the pressed seed oil — fresh leaves and flowers had traditional use; oil-pressing appears to be a modern product
note: Old-world herbals held that borage flowers steeped in wine “gave courage” and lifted the spirits, a belief colonists likely carried along with borage itself, a common Old World transplant in dooryard herb gardens. But that was the fresh leaf and flower, steeped or added to drinks. Cold-pressed borage seed oil as a specific product is a modern one, with no confident evidence it was made or used this way historically — noted honestly rather than invented.

name: Spearmint Oil
people: English colonists and their descendants; commercial mint growers of western New York
use: Digestive aid for nausea, gas, and upset stomach
method: Fresh leaves were steeped into tea for the stomach, or distilled into a strong oil — originally a small-batch farmhouse process — used in drops on sugar or diluted and rubbed on the belly.
note: America became a major world source of mint oil starting in the early 1800s, centered first in Massachusetts and then Wayne County, New York — home to the W. B. Hotchkiss Company, whose mint oil won prizes at international expositions — before the industry later shifted west to Michigan and Indiana.

name: Cinnamon Oil
use: Toothache relief and a warming rub for aches
method: A few drops of the concentrated oil were dabbed onto an aching tooth or gum, or diluted into liniments rubbed on sore muscles — a stronger, more concentrated form of the same bark kept as cinnamon sticks in the kitchen.
note: Listed in 19th-century American pharmacy references as “oil of cinnamon,” this was the same remedy idea as clove oil for a toothache, just from a different spice.
caution: Strong enough to irritate or burn skin and gums if used undiluted.

name: Menthol
people: American households broadly, via long-standing mint folk remedies; popularized commercially from Greensboro, North Carolina
use: Chest congestion, colds, and headache
method: Crystalline menthol, or mint oil, was rubbed on the chest and throat for congestion, or on the temples for headache — building on a much older household habit of drinking mint tea for the same kinds of complaints.
note: In 1905, Greensboro, North Carolina pharmacist Lunsford Richardson blended menthol into petroleum jelly to create what became Vicks VapoRub — turning an old mint-based home remedy into one of the best-known store-bought ones.

name: Thymol
use: Antiseptic for skin infections, wounds, and sore mouths and throats
method: Monarda (wild bergamot, also called horsemint or bee balm) was made into poultices for skin infections and wounds, steeped as a tea for mouth and throat infections, and used as a warm-water wash for inflamed eyes.
note: Thymol, the compound now used in commercial mouthwash, was later identified as the active antiseptic ingredient in Monarda's essential oil — a case of a folk remedy's chemistry catching up to what its users already knew worked.

name: Eugenol
people: American households broadly — one of the most widespread home remedies of all
use: Toothache relief
method: A whole clove was held or chewed against the aching tooth, or a drop of clove oil was dabbed directly onto the tooth and gum.
note: Eugenol is clove oil's main active compound, and this may be the longest-lived home remedy of all — dentists still use eugenol-based cement in fillings today.

name: Capsaicin
people: Samuel Thomson and the Thomsonian (“botanic”) medicine movement he founded
use: Circulatory stimulant to “restore internal heat,” and a rub for sore muscles
method: Cayenne pepper was taken internally alongside steam baths, and used in liniments rubbed on aching joints and muscles.
note: Samuel Thomson, a self-taught New Hampshire herbalist, built an entire home-medicine system in the early 1800s around the idea that illness came from cold, and that cayenne pepper, along with steam and other botanicals, could restore the body's heat. Thomsonian medicine spread widely across New England and beyond before falling out of favor by mid-century.
caution: Capsaicin is a real skin and mucous-membrane irritant — handled carelessly, it can burn the skin or eyes.

name: Salicin
people: Native peoples across many nations of North America, and, independently, European settlers carrying an old-world remedy
use: Pain relief and fever reduction
method: Willow bark was stripped, dried, and steeped into a bitter tea, or chewed directly.
note: Willow bark's fever- and pain-relieving reputation was arrived at independently on both sides of the Atlantic. Salicin is the compound modern aspirin was chemically modeled on — acetylsalicylic acid, first sold by Bayer in 1899.

name: Methyl Salicylate
people: Native peoples of the Northeast and Appalachians; later adopted widely by settlers
use: Muscle and joint pain relief
method: Wintergreen leaves were chewed or steeped into tea, or the oil was rubbed on sore joints as a liniment.
note: Sweet birch bark produces an oil that's chemically almost identical to true wintergreen oil, and Appalachian distillers — running small “birch oil” stills in the mountains — commonly sold it as a cheaper substitute, well into the 20th century.

name: Berberine
people: Cherokee and Iroquois, among other Eastern Woodlands peoples; adopted heavily by 19th-century Eclectic physicians
use: Bitter digestive tonic, and a wash for sore or inflamed eyes
method: The root of goldenseal was dried and either powdered into a bitter tonic or boiled into a strong yellow decoction, used as a wash for eyes and skin or taken for digestive complaints.
note: Goldenseal was one of the signature herbs of 19th-century American “Eclectic” medicine — the Iroquois also used it for coughs, fevers, and liver complaints — and demand grew so intense that wild populations were already noticeably scarcer by 1905. It's still listed today under CITES, the international treaty protecting species threatened by trade.
caution: Modern herbalists generally advise against use during pregnancy.

name: Podophyllotoxin
people: Native peoples of the Eastern Woodlands
use: Strong purgative; resin used topically on warts
method: The root of mayapple was dried and powdered for use as a powerful laxative and dewormer, in small, careful doses since it's a harsh purgative, while resin extracted from the root was applied directly to warts.
note: Mayapple resin (podophyllin) stayed in real medical use for treating warts for generations afterward — the FDA didn't approve a purified version for that exact purpose until 1990, an unusually long afterlife for a plant remedy.
caution: Genuinely toxic — every part of the plant except the ripe fruit is poisonous, and overdoing the root caused severe cramping and purging historically; not a home experiment.

name: Silibinin
people: English and other European colonists, carrying an inherited Old World herbal tradition
use: Liver complaints, and to help nursing mothers' milk supply
method: Seeds were crushed, or leaves steeped, into a bitter tea.
note: The white marbling on milk thistle's leaves comes from an old Christian legend that the Virgin Mary's milk fell on the plant while she nursed — the story behind both its scientific name (marianum) and its traditional use for nursing mothers. Brought over in dooryard herb gardens, it self-seeded so readily that it's now considered a weed across much of the country.

name: Cornstarch
people: American households broadly, from the mid-1800s on
use: Soothing powder for diaper rash, chafing, and skin irritation
method: Dry cornstarch was dusted directly onto irritated or chafed skin, especially on babies, or mixed with water into a soothing paste.
note: Kingsford's Oswego Corn Starch, founded in Oswego, New York in 1848, was among the first companies to mass-produce cornstarch from corn — and by 1880 it was the largest corn refinery in the world, making this a fairly late but well-documented household staple.

name: Serviceberry & Chokecherry Purge (Blackfoot)
use: Deliberate cathartic purge
method: An infusion combined the whole serviceberry plant with the cambium — the thin, nutrient-rich inner-bark layer — of chokecherry, and was taken as a deliberate purge rather than as food or a mild tonic.
note: Chokecherry bark and cambium carry cyanogenic compounds, the same chemical family that gives freshly cut chokecherry wood a faint almond-like smell, so pairing it with serviceberry turned an everyday food berry into something considerably stronger than the mild laxative and appetite remedies recorded elsewhere for the same fruit.
caution: Historical purges like this one risk dehydration and electrolyte loss on their own, and chokecherry bark and cambium contain cyanogenic compounds that can release cyanide — this pairing is preserved as documented history, not a formula to recreate.

name: Smooth Sumac for Blisters (Cherokee)
use: Sunburn blisters and blistered skin
method: A fruit infusion was poured directly over sunburn blisters, while a separate bark decoction was used as a wash for blisters more generally.
note: The same nation is recorded using red sumac berries eaten whole to deliberately trigger vomiting — here, by contrast, the fruit (steeped this time, not eaten raw) and the bark both went toward calming blistered skin instead, two very different jobs asked of one shrub best known today for turning some of the most brilliant red of any plant in the autumn woods.

name: Smooth Sumac Blossoms for Sore Mouth (Chippewa/Ojibwe)
use: Sore mouth
method: Fresh blossoms were picked and chewed directly for a sore mouth, with no cooking or decoction involved.
note: Elsewhere in the same nation's record, sumac flowers were cooked into a compound decoction and used as a mouthwash for a teething baby; here the same blossoms did similar work in a much plainer form, chewed straight off the plant by an adult with an ordinary sore mouth.

name: Smooth Sumac Root Juice for Sore Throat (Kutenai)
use: Sore throat
method: Fresh roots were squeezed by hand to express their juice, which was swallowed directly for a sore throat rather than being simmered into a tea.
note: Kutenai is a language isolate with no demonstrated relationship to any other language in North America, and the nation's homeland straddles the Rocky Mountains on both sides of today's U.S.–Canada border — a reminder that this squeezed-root remedy comes out of a genuinely distinct cultural and linguistic tradition, not a borrowed variant of a neighboring nation's practice.
caution: Fresh-squeezed root juice is a far more concentrated dose than a simmered tea and may irritate the throat or stomach; there's no modern evidence establishing how well it works.

name: Sphagnum Moss Wound Dressing (Potawatomi)
use: Wound dressing
method: Moss was rinsed clean of debris and packed directly onto a wound as a dressing.
note: One Potawatomi elder interviewed for the record described the moss as able to almost ‘suck’ the sickness out of a wound — a vivid description that isn't far from the real mechanism, since sphagnum's dead, hollow leaf cells can hold many times their own weight in liquid, drawing moisture straight out of injured tissue.
caution: Wild, ungathered moss isn't sterile, and packing it onto an open wound today carries a real risk of infection; it's preserved here as documented history, not a modern first-aid technique.

name: Lizard's Tail Leaves
use: Inflammation
method: Creole households used the leaves on their own for inflammation, apart from the root, which was prepared separately; exactly how the leaves themselves were made ready didn't make it into the surviving record.
note: This is one of the clearest “science caught up later” stories in the batch — the old Creole anti-inflammatory use of the leaf, first set down in a 1933 record, lines up closely with a modern laboratory study that found a leaf extract strongly blocking two separate inflammatory pathways (IL-1β and COX-2) in immune cells, decades before anyone could have explained why the remedy seemed to work.
caution: Human clinical trials are lacking, and because the traditional dose and preparation were never recorded, there is no established safe amount for this specific leaf remedy.

name: American Elderberry Flowers & Stems (Louisiana Creole)
use: General folk remedy within the Creole medicinal-plant tradition
method: The flowering heads and young stems were the specific parts drawn on within the Creole medicinal tradition, though no single traditional recipe survives; a modern laboratory study tested an extract of this part on its own, separately from the plant's leaves.
note: This is the one plant in the batch where the lab signal pointed toward blood sugar rather than swelling: an extract made from the flowers and stems boosted a key insulin-signaling step (Akt phosphorylation) in insulin-resistant muscle cells grown in the lab — a different kind of modern result from the anti-inflammatory hits found elsewhere in the same research program, and a reminder that a single “traditional medicinal plant” reputation could really be covering several distinct biological effects.
caution: Raw or unprepared stems and unripe plant material can contain cyanogenic compounds; historically only properly prepared parts of elder were considered safe to take internally.

name: American Elderberry Leaves (Louisiana Creole)
use: General anti-inflammatory folk remedy
method: The leaves were the specific part drawn on for this use, apart from the plant's flowers and stems; the exact traditional preparation wasn't recorded, though a modern laboratory extract made from the leaves was later tested and found to suppress several inflammatory markers.
note: Elder turns up independently in very different immigrant and Indigenous households across the East and South — Irish immigrant families kept a close cousin of this same plant in their own dooryards for coughs and fevers — but the Louisiana Creole record and the modern lab both single out the leaf specifically, a part most other traditions treated as the least useful piece of the plant.
caution: The leaves are not equivalent to the cooked, ripe berries and can be toxic if used carelessly or in quantity; they were not prepared the same way as the berries or flowers.

name: American Beautyberry Berries (Louisiana Creole)
use: Anti-inflammatory folk remedy, prepared from the ripe berries
method: The ripe berries were the part named in the Creole record, though not the method used to prepare them; a modern laboratory extract made from the berries was later tested and found to inhibit TNF-alpha, an inflammatory signaling protein.
note: This shrub earns its keep at least three separate ways across Southeastern tradition: Choctaw and Koasati healers used the root in sweat baths and for stomachache, other Southeastern nations crushed the leaves as an insect repellent, and the Louisiana Creole record singles out the berries themselves for general anti-inflammatory use — the same unmistakable purple clusters that still make the shrub easy to spot in a fall hedgerow.

name: Sugarberry Bark (Louisiana Creole)
use: Traditional medicinal use documented among Louisiana Creole communities
method: The bark itself was both the historically used part and the one later pulled for laboratory testing — the traditional recipe itself is one of the details this record didn't carry forward.
note: Sugarberry's more northern relative, the common hackberry, was used by Haudenosaunee healers hundreds of miles away for entirely different complaints — menstrual regulation and sore throat — a reminder that closely related trees earned very different reputations in different regions. Here the modern follow-up cuts the other way, too: when researchers tested this bark's effect on insulin signaling, the changes they measured were interpreted as potentially unfavorable rather than beneficial, a useful reminder that lab testing doesn't always vindicate the old use.
caution: Modern lab testing did not support any assumption of metabolic benefit from this bark — the measured effects on insulin signaling were interpreted as potentially unfavorable, so it shouldn't be taken as a folk treatment for diabetes or blood sugar.

name: Filé Powder (Sassafras Leaves)
people: Choctaw and other Southeastern Native nations (origin), carried into Louisiana Creole and Cajun cuisine
use: Dried and ground into filé powder, a gumbo thickener and seasoning rooted in food-medicine tradition
method: Sassafras leaves were dried and pounded or ground into a fine powder — filé — a technique generally credited to Choctaw practice and carried into Louisiana Creole and Cajun kitchens, where it is stirred into gumbo off the heat to thicken and flavor the dish.
note: Filé is one of the clearest throughlines from Native Southeastern plant knowledge straight into today's Louisiana kitchens. It is also a case where two parts of the very same tree ended up with opposite reputations: the dried leaf became a beloved everyday seasoning, while the root bark's oil — chemically distinct, and once used to flavor sassafras tea and old-time root beer — was pulled from the American food supply in 1960 after safrole, its main compound, was linked to liver tumors in animal studies.
caution: Filé made from the dried leaf is the traditional culinary form and is not the same product as sassafras root or root oil; concentrated root/oil preparations contain safrole, which is no longer considered safe for food or drink, and the two should never be confused or substituted for each other.

name: Spanish Bayonet Root & Tallow Salve (Choctaw)
use: Skin complaints, treated as a topical salve
method: Roots were mashed or boiled and combined with animal grease or tallow to make a salve that was worked directly into the skin.
note: The “dagger plant” name is no exaggeration — its stiff, bayonet-tipped leaves are sharp enough to draw blood on contact, which likely made this a plant people respected before they ever put it to medicinal use. Choctaw practice combined its root with rendered animal fat into a salve, a different route to the skin than the soap-like foaming wash that Southwestern and Plains nations made from other yucca species' roots — two regions, a continent apart, independently finding medicine in the same soapy, saponin-rich genus.
caution: The root's saponins can irritate skin and tissue in raw or concentrated form; historically it was combined with grease or tallow before application rather than used on its own.

name: Coral Bean Berries (Louisiana Creole)
use: General folk remedy, part of the historic Creole medicinal-plant corpus
method: The bright red berries were the part named in the record and the one a modern laboratory study later tested, though not by way of any recipe that survived.
note: The seeds are genuinely striking — a hard, glossy scarlet that stands out against the plant's own bare gray branches long after the leaves drop — and that same visibility is likely exactly why they entered the historical medicinal record in the first place, even though they carry some of the most potent alkaloids of any plant in this batch. Archiving a dangerous historical remedy like this one is deliberate: the old use is real regardless of whether it was ever safe to try.
caution: The seeds and berries contain potent toxic alkaloids and should never be ingested; this entry is preserved as a historical record only, not a usable remedy.

name: American Black Nightshade, Green Berries & Root (Louisiana Creole)
use: Anti-inflammatory folk remedy, prepared from the unripe berries and root
method: Both the unripe green berries and the root turn up in the Creole record as the parts used; a modern study tested each separately, and it was the root extract that drew the closer laboratory attention for suppressing a key inflammatory marker, IL-1β.
note: The record is careful to specify “green” berries, and that word is doing real work: like other nightshades, the unripe fruit carries glycoalkaloids that the same berries mostly lose once they ripen fully black and soft. The reason this entry stays in the archive despite the danger is that erasing risky historical medicine erases real history — not that the remedy itself is safe to try.
caution: Unripe (green) berries and other plant parts can be toxic due to glycoalkaloids; treat this as a historical record, not a home recipe to try.

name: Yellow Birch Sap Beverage
use: Spring beverage, tapped and blended with maple sap
method: Sap was tapped from yellow birch in spring and mixed with maple sap to make a beverage.
note: Yellow birch sap runs thinner and less sweet than maple, so on its own it rarely got the trouble of boiling into syrup — cutting it into the maple harvest instead let Flambeau and Couderay families stretch a good sap run further without wasting a tree most people today walk right past.

name: Paper Birch Bark Roofing
use: Waterproof wigwam roofing and wall covering
method: Large sheets of bark were stripped from the tree and layered over a wigwam frame as a waterproof covering.
note: Birch bark owes its waterproofing to betulin, the same waxy compound that gives the bark its papery white color — and because sheets can be peeled from a living tree in early summer without killing it, a single well-managed birch could reroof a family's wigwam more than once in its lifetime.
