name: Paper Birch Bark Canoes & Scrolls
use: Canoe hulls, baskets, buckets, and ceremonial record-scrolls
method: Bark was shaped and sewn into canoes, buckets, and baskets, and separately used to record medicine-lodge ceremonial content.
note: The 'records' here almost certainly means wiigwaasabakoon, the mnemonic birch-bark scrolls used to preserve Midewiwin ceremony songs and teachings across generations — meaning the same tree that carried people across the water also carried the memory of an entire religious tradition.

name: American Beech Nuts
use: Food, eaten fresh from the tree
method: Fresh beechnuts were gathered and eaten; the harvest was usually too small to store in any quantity.
note: Beech is a classic 'mast' tree, producing a heavy nut crop only every few years rather than reliably each fall — the same unpredictable abundance that once fed vast flocks of the now-extinct passenger pigeon made beechnuts a welcome but never quite dependable addition to the table.

name: Bur Oak Acorn Food
use: Food, after leaching out bitter tannins
method: Bitter acorns were treated with a lye solution to remove tannins before being eaten.
note: Bur oak produces the largest acorn of any North American oak, wrapped in a shaggy, fringed cap that gives the tree its name — turning that generous but mouth-puckeringly bitter nut into food took real chemistry, since only a lye soak breaks down enough tannin to make it edible.

name: Red Oak Acorn Food
use: Major starchy food staple, after leaching
method: Acorns were leached with lye to remove their tannic bitterness before being prepared as food.
note: Red oak belongs to the 'red oak group,' whose acorns carry noticeably more bitter tannin than white-oak-group acorns like bur oak's — foragers today still sort by that same red-versus-white divide, because it decides how long a batch actually needs to soak before it's worth eating.

name: Black Ash Basket Splints
use: Basket-weaving splints
method: A peeled log was pounded to separate the wood along its annual growth rings, then split into splints, dyed, and woven into baskets.
note: Black ash is almost the only tree where pounding the trunk works as a harvesting technique — its growth rings are so weakly bonded that a beaten log separates into thin ribbons a full year's growth thick, a property the invasive emerald ash borer is now pushing toward extinction across the same Great Lakes basket-making region.

name: Red Ash Utility Wood
use: Snowshoes, bows, arrows, sleds, and cradleboards
method: Wood was shaped into snowshoe frames, bows and arrows, sleds, and cradleboards.
note: The same strength-with-flex that made ash a reliable choice for a snowshoe frame or a bow stave is exactly why, decades later, industrial America reached for ash to make baseball bats and axe handles — different centuries, same trusted wood.

name: Fir & Pine Resin Waterproofing Pitch
sci: Abies balsamea / Pinus resinosa / Pinus strobus
use: Waterproof sealant for canoe seams and roofing
method: Resin was collected from notched trunks, boiled, then boiled a second time with tallow or fat to make a pliable waterproof pitch.
note: Boiling raw resin a second time with rendered fat wasn't decorative — pure conifer resin turns brittle and cracks in cold weather, while the added fat keeps the pitch flexible enough to survive a Great Lakes winter without a canoe seam splitting open.

name: Cedar Purification Incense
use: Purification incense burned over sacred objects in the medicine lodge
method: Dried cedar leaves were placed on live coals, and the rising smoke was fanned over sacred objects and participants during medicine-lodge ceremonies.
note: This wasn't cedar tea for a cough — dried leaves were burned specifically to bathe sacred medicine-lodge objects in smoke, a purification aimed at objects and ceremony as much as at any bodily complaint, and one of the clearest tree-based ritual techniques on record for the Flambeau Ojibwe.
caution: Burning cedar leaves produces smoke that can irritate the lungs, and this was a specific sacred medicine-lodge practice, not a casual home incense to recreate.

name: Cedar Sweat-Bath Formula for Cough & Purification
use: Cough relief and ceremonial purification, taken as tea and inhaled as sweat-bath steam
method: Cedar leaves were combined with white pine, balsam fir, and hemlock in a sweat bath; leaves were also boiled and drunk as tea, with the rising steam itself considered to purify the blood.
note: Pillager healers didn't rely on cedar alone for this one — it was blended with white pine, balsam fir, and hemlock into a four-tree sweat-bath formula, and the steam wasn't just soothing a cough; it was understood to be actively purifying the blood, folding a physical remedy and a belief about the body into the very same breath of steam.
caution: Sweat-bath heat and smoke can stress the heart and lungs, and cedar taken internally can be toxic in concentrated amounts — this compound formula is documented history, not a recipe to reproduce.

name: Wild Plum Bark Dye Fixative
use: Dye fixative (mordant) for plant-dyed materials
method: Astringent inner bark was used as a color fixative in plant dyeing.
note: Long before anyone had a word for 'tannin,' Ojibwe dyers had worked out that wild plum's astringent inner bark would bind color fast to a fiber — the same basic tannin chemistry that, unrelated tree by unrelated tree, kept showing up wherever a plant-based dye needed to survive washing and sunlight.

name: Hawthorn Bark Hunting Lure
use: Smoked scent lure to attract deer while hunting
method: Bark was added to a smoked deer-scent mixture used to attract deer.
note: Elsewhere in this archive hawthorn shows up as a 19th-century heart tonic; here the same genus turns up in a completely different toolkit, smoked into a scent mixture meant to draw deer within range — one plant's reputation splitting entirely differently depending on whether the person reaching for it was treating a patient or setting up a hunt.

name: Cow Parsnip Root Hunting Charm
use: Root smudged in fire for spiritual protection while hunting
method: Roots were smudged in a fire to drive off a hunting spirit called Sokenau, believed to spoil a hunter's luck if it followed him.
note: The same plant shows up elsewhere in this archive as a cough-and-fever tea, but here cow parsnip root wasn't taken internally at all — it was burned as a smudge specifically to drive off a spirit blamed for ruining a hunter's luck, a reminder of how differently one plant's power could be understood from one context to the next.
caution: Cow parsnip sap is phototoxic and can cause severe skin burns in sunlight, and the smoke from smudging it can irritate the airway.

name: Water Hemlock Hunting Medicine
use: Smoked hunting medicine believed to attract buck deer
method: Root was used in a smoked hunting-medicine mixture believed to attract buck deer.
note: Water hemlock is often called the most acutely poisonous plant native to North America — a bite of raw root can kill an adult within hours — so it's notable this hunting medicine used it only as smoke rather than anything eaten or drunk, a real distinction given how unforgiving the plant is in almost any other form.
caution: Water hemlock is one of the most acutely toxic plants in North America and can be fatal even in small amounts. This is a historical record only, never a plant to handle or experiment with.

name: Reindeer Lichen Newborn Wash
use: Newborn baby wash
method: Lichen was boiled, and the resulting water was used to wash a newborn baby.
note: Reindeer lichen isn't a plant at all — it's a partnership between a fungus and an alga growing as a single organism, so slow-growing that a disturbed mat can take decades to recover, which makes its appearance in something as routine as a newborn's first wash a small use of a genuinely ancient partnership.

name: Basswood Inner Bark Cordage
use: Cordage and string fiber
method: Young bark was stripped, the outer layer removed, and the inner fiber rolled, boiled, recoiled, and soaked before being twisted into cordage.
note: Basswood's inner bark is technically called 'bast' fiber — the tree's name is a corruption of 'bast-wood' — and this multi-step process of stripping, boiling, and resoaking it before twisting cordage is essentially the same fiber-retting principle used for flax and hemp half a world away, arrived at independently.

name: Bittersweet Inner Bark Winter Soup
use: Emergency food, cooked into soup during food scarcity
method: Inner bark was separated from the vine and cooked into a thick soup when food was scarce.
note: American bittersweet already carries real toxicity risk, which makes this use striking: it wasn't a food reached for casually but a genuine hunger food, cooked into soup only when little else was on hand — a reminder that 'traditional use' sometimes meant survival calculus in a hard winter, not routine cuisine.
caution: American bittersweet contains toxic compounds; this was documented only as a last-resort famine food, not a safe ingredient to prepare today.

name: Red Elderberry Bark Purge
use: Severe constipation, taken as a last-resort purge
method: Four bark sections were measured from ulna to humerus, peeled downward, steeped or boiled, and the liquid drunk.
note: Four was considered a powerful, sacred number across many Ojibwe traditions, and it shows directly in the dosing here — four measured bark sections, no more, no less — while the direction the bark was peeled was believed to flip the very same plant from a purge into its opposite, an emetic, entirely on its own.
caution: Elderberry bark is strongly cathartic and can be genuinely dangerous taken internally. This is historical documentation only, not a remedy to try.

name: Red Elderberry Bark Emetic
use: Emetic, to induce vomiting
method: The same four measured bark sections were used, but peeled upward instead of downward, and the tea was drunk to induce vomiting.
note: Huron Smith, the ethnographer who recorded this, said as much himself — he suspected the up-versus-down peeling rule was more superstition than mechanism, since the same bark seemed chemically capable of acting as either a purge or an emetic regardless of which way it was stripped.
caution: Elderberry bark contains potent, potentially toxic compounds; deliberately inducing vomiting this way carries real risk and should not be attempted.

name: Bush Honeysuckle & Ground Pine Urinary Remedy
use: Urinary complaints
method: Root was combined with ground pine, a clubmoss, into a compound urinary medicine.
note: 'Ground pine' isn't a pine, or even a seed plant at all — it's a clubmoss, a spore-reproducing lineage that predates dinosaurs by hundreds of millions of years — and pairing that ancient plant with an ordinary flowering shrub's root into one urinary remedy shows healers combining ingredients by effect, not by any sense of botanical relatedness.
caution: Urinary symptoms can be a sign of infection or kidney disease that needs real medical evaluation, not home treatment alone.

name: Highbush Cranberry Bark Purge
use: Physic, used as a purge
method: Inner bark was prepared and taken as a physic.
note: Despite the name, highbush cranberry isn't a true cranberry at all — it's a viburnum whose tart red fruit just resembles one — and while most people who know the shrub today know it for jelly, its inner bark carried an entirely separate reputation as a purge, with nothing to do with the berries at all.
caution: This bark was used as a strong purge; self-dosing with plant purgatives carries real risk and is not something to attempt at home.

name: Highbush Cranberry Bark Tea for Cramps
use: Stomach cramps
method: Inner bark was brewed into a tea and drunk for cramping.
note: This is the same shrub sold in health-food stores today under the name 'cramp bark' — one of the rarer cases in this archive where a historical Ojibwe use and a still-current herbal product point at exactly the same plant part for exactly the same complaint.

name: Snowberry Root Postpartum Tea
use: Postpartum recovery, to help clear the afterbirth
method: Root was brewed into a tea taken to help clear the afterbirth and speed postpartum recovery.
note: Snowberry's chalky white berries carry enough saponins that many nations treated them as inedible or purely ornamental, which makes this use, specifically of the root rather than the berry, and specifically for postpartum care, a distinct and specialized piece of women's medicine rather than a general-use plant.
caution: Retained placenta after childbirth is a medical emergency; this historical remedy is not a substitute for medical care.

name: Hawthorn Fruit & Bark Women's Medicine
use: Historically used as a women's medicine (specific indication not recorded)
method: Fruit and bark were prepared into a women's medicine that, even by the early 1930s, was rarely still being made.
note: By the time this was recorded in the early 1930s, informants said this particular hawthorn medicine was already falling out of use — a small window into how much Ojibwe plant knowledge was disappearing even as it was first being written down, with the specific ailment it treated lost before anyone thought to record it.

name: Mountain Holly Berry Medicine
use: Used medicinally (specific ailment and preparation not recorded)
method: Berries were used as medicine, though the specific ailment and preparation were never recorded.
note: Even the ethnographer who recorded this admitted he could never discover what illness this berry treated or how it was prepared — and it is kept here anyway, on the theory that a fragment, 'this plant was medicine,' is still worth more than silence, even once the full recipe is already gone.

name: Giant Puffball Nosebleed Remedy
use: Nosebleed, to stop bleeding
method: Mature, powdery inner material from a ripe puffball was kept on hand and snuffed directly into the nose to stop bleeding.
note: Unlike a fresh herb that has to be gathered when needed, a ripe puffball's papery, spore-filled interior stays usable long after the mushroom itself is finished growing, meaning a piece could be kept dry and ready in an Ojibwe household for the exact moment a nosebleed needed fast attention.
caution: Inhaling puffball spore material can cause respiratory problems, especially from an over-ripe specimen; this is not a safe substitute for modern nosebleed first aid.

name: Bloodroot & Maple Sugar Sore Throat Remedy
use: Sore throat
method: Fresh root juice was squeezed onto a lump of maple sugar, which was held in the mouth until it melted.
note: Squeezing bloodroot juice onto sugar rather than swallowing it straight was itself a kind of dosing control — sanguinarine, bloodroot's main active compound, is caustic enough to damage tissue undiluted, so letting a small, sugar-slowed amount dissolve in the mouth kept the dose gradual rather than a shock all at once.
caution: Bloodroot juice is caustic and can burn or damage tissue; this is a historical record, not a home remedy to reproduce.

name: Bloodroot Ceremonial Face Paint
use: Face paint for medicine-lodge ceremony and the warpath
method: Root juice was used as a pigment to paint the face for medicine-lodge ceremonies or before going to war.
note: Cut open a bloodroot rhizome and it bleeds a startling orange-red sap almost immediately, a visual so striking it gave the plant its English name outright, and made it just as natural a choice for war and ceremony paint as for medicine.
caution: Bloodroot sap can irritate skin and eyes and should never contact mucous membranes.

name: Smooth Sumac Blossom for Sore Mouth
use: Sore mouth, relieved by chewing the blossoms
method: Fresh sumac blossoms were chewed directly for a sore mouth.
note: Where most of the recorded sumac medicine in this archive involves boiling galls, roots, or compounded flower decoctions, this one is refreshingly direct: no fire, no water, just the blossom chewed straight from the plant for a sore mouth.

name: Shining Willow Bark Kinnikinnick
use: Ceremonial and social smoking-mixture ingredient (kinnikinnick)
method: Bark was peeled, toasted over a fire, and reduced to flakes to be added to a kinnikinnick smoking mixture.
note: Kinnikinnick, an Algonquian word that means roughly 'what is mixed,' refers to a whole tradition of smoking blends built from barks and leaves rather than tobacco alone, and toasted willow bark like this was one of the ingredients that gave those mixtures their character.
caution: Smoke of any kind, plant-based or tobacco, carries real respiratory harm; this is documented cultural history, not a habit to take up.

name: Balsam Fir for Sore Eyes
use: Sore eyes, applied directly
method: Fresh liquid balsam was collected from a bark blister and applied directly to sore eyes.
note: Balsam fir stores its resin in raised blisters dotting smooth young bark, rather than oozing more generally the way most pines and spruces do, which made it unusually easy to collect a clean, fresh dose — though putting any tree resin straight into the eye, rather than onto skin or a wound, is a striking and genuinely risky use compared to how balsam shows up elsewhere in this archive.
caution: Putting nonsterile tree resin directly in the eye risks real injury and infection; this historical use should never be attempted.

name: Balsam Fir Leaf Reviver Wash
use: Reviver, used in combined medicinal washes
method: Leaves were used as a reviver and combined into medicinal washes.
note: 'Reviver' shows up again and again across Ojibwe conifer medicine in this collection — jack pine, black spruce, and white pine all carried the same basic role — suggesting aromatic evergreen foliage was treated as its own recognized category of restorative, used the way a startling scent or a splash of cold water might be used today.

name: White Spruce Needle Inhalant
use: Inhalant and fumigator for respiratory complaints
method: Needles were used, like tamarack, as a nokwesikun: an inhalant or fumigator.
note: Nokwesikun was a specific, named category in Ojibwe medicine: an aromatic plant burned or steamed specifically to be inhaled. The fact that white spruce, tamarack, jack pine, and white pine were all separately recorded serving this same role suggests it was less about any one tree's unique chemistry and more about a whole practiced method of treating the airway with aromatic smoke.
caution: Smoke or steam inhalation can irritate the lungs or cause burns; this traditional inhalant practice carries real respiratory risk.

name: Black Spruce Bark Medicine (Method Unrecorded)
use: Used medicinally (specific method not recorded)
method: Bark was identified as a medicinal material, though the exact internal preparation was not detailed in the surviving record.
note: Black spruce reportedly carried separate Ojibwe names depending on whether the bark or the leaves were meant as medicine — the language itself drew a line between the tree's two medicinal identities, even though the specific ailment the bark treated didn't survive into the written record.

name: Black Spruce Leaf Reviver
use: Reviver
method: Leaves were used as a reviver.
note: This is the other half of black spruce's split medicinal identity: where the bark's specific use was lost to history, the leaf reviver use survived intact, showing how unevenly this kind of knowledge got preserved even within the description of a single tree.

name: Jack Pine Leaf Inhalant & Reviver
use: Reviver and inhalant
method: Leaves were used as a nokwesikun inhalant.
note: The original notes on this one point out that jack pine was used as medicine here even though no corresponding remedy could be found in the settler medical tradition of the recorder's own era — a small sign that Ojibwe medicine wasn't simply a folk parallel to Euro-American medicine, but its own system, with categories that didn't always have a ready translation.

name: White Pine Bark Ceremonial Medicine
use: General bark medicine
method: Bark was gathered with a ceremonial song addressed to Grandmother Earth, with tobacco placed on the ground as an offering before harvesting.
note: The harvest itself was the medicine here as much as anything applied afterward — bark wasn't just cut, it was requested, with a song and a tobacco offering left on the ground first, a protocol that treated the tree as a participant being asked for something, not simply a resource being taken.
caution: The internal dose used historically isn't well documented, and this practice carries specific cultural and ceremonial significance beyond its medicinal use.

name: White Pine Cone & Bark Pitch
use: Topical pitch and resin medicine
method: Cones were boiled for their resin, and young trunk bark separately yielded medicinal pitch as well.
note: Most pitch remedies in this collection come from resin blisters on the trunk, which makes the cones worth noting here: pine cones are themselves coated in protective resin to guard the seeds inside as they mature, and Flambeau healers evidently knew that boiling the cones, not just the bark, yielded medicine too.
caution: Topical pine resin can cause skin sensitization in some people, and it was not meant to be taken internally.

name: White Pine Needle Powder Inhalant
use: Reviver and inhalant, used as a powder
method: Dried needles were powdered and used as an inhalant and reviver.
note: Unlike the better-known white pine needle tea, this preparation never touched water at all — dried needles were ground to a powder and used as an inhalant, putting white pine alongside tamarack, jack pine, and spruce in the nokwesikun tradition of aromatic powders and smokes rather than teas.
caution: Inhaling powdered plant material can irritate the lungs, especially with repeated use.

name: Red Pine as White Pine Substitute
use: Substitute medicine for white pine, used the same way
method: Red (Norway) pine was used in every particular the same way as white pine, substituted whenever white pine medicine was needed.
note: Recording a formal, sanctioned substitute species is its own kind of evidence: it means Ojibwe herbalists were working from principles about what a tree does, not just fixed single-species recipes, and could reach for whichever of the two pines actually stood nearby when the medicine was needed.
caution: Historical sources note this substitute wasn't necessarily assumed to be identical in strength to white pine; treating them as interchangeable in potency isn't well supported.

name: Cedar Headache Tea
use: Headache remedy, taken as tea
method: Cedar leaves were brewed into a tea and drunk for headache.
note: Cedar's reputation in Ojibwe medicine usually runs toward fevers, colds, and ceremony, so it's worth noticing this tea was recorded for something as ordinary as a headache — evidence cedar functioned as a genuine everyday household remedy, not only a ceremonial plant reserved for bigger occasions.
caution: Cedar leaf tea contains thujone, which is neurotoxic in concentrated amounts; historical infusions were mild and occasional, not a concentrated dose.

name: Tamarack Leaf Inhalant & Fumigator
use: Inhalant and fumigator for respiratory complaints
method: Dried leaves were used as a nokwesikun inhalant and fumigator.
note: Because tamarack drops every needle each autumn, gathering its leaves for this inhalant, unlike the evergreen spruce, pine, and cedar needles used the very same way, meant working within a real seasonal window rather than being able to harvest whenever the need arose.
caution: Smoke or steam from this preparation can irritate the airway or cause burns if handled carelessly.

name: Red Oak Bark for Heart Trouble
use: Heart trouble
method: Bark was used medicinally as a treatment for heart trouble.
note: A nearly identical use of red oak bark for heart trouble is independently recorded among the Cherokee, hundreds of miles to the south. Whether that reflects two nations separately noticing the same astringent bark, knowledge passed along long-distance trade and kinship networks, or simple coincidence isn't something the record can settle, but the overlap itself is striking.
caution: Heart symptoms can signal a serious underlying condition and need real medical evaluation; this historical remedy is not a substitute for that.

name: Red Oak Bark for Bronchial Complaints
use: Bronchial complaints
method: Bark was used medicinally to treat bronchial complaints.
note: The same bark shows up treating two entirely different organ systems in this record, heart trouble in one use and bronchial complaints in this one, which points toward red oak bark carrying a broad, general reputation as a strengthening astringent medicine rather than any single, narrowly targeted cure.
caution: Persistent breathing problems need real medical evaluation; this historical bark remedy is not a treatment to rely on.

name: Paper Birch Root Bark & Maple Sugar Syrup
use: Stomach cramps, soothed with a bark-and-sugar syrup
method: Root bark was cooked together with maple sugar into a soothing syrup for stomach cramps.
note: Cooking bitter root bark down together with maple sugar wasn't just about taste. It turned a plain decoction into something closer to a true syrup, thick enough to coat and sweet enough to actually get a cramping stomach, quite possibly a child's, to take the medicine at all.

name: Balsam Poplar Bud Salve for Wounds
use: Cuts, wounds, and bruises, treated with a bud salve
method: Buds were cooked in lard or bear fat, and the cooled salve was applied to cuts, wounds, and bruises.
note: Balsam poplar buds carry a thick, resinous coating that protects the tender leaf curled inside through winter, and rendering that same coating into fat is essentially the principle behind 'balm of Gilead' salve, a poplar-bud preparation that outlasted this specific recipe and is still sold as an herbal salve today.
caution: A fat-based salve applied to an open wound carries a real contamination risk, and some people are sensitive to the salicylate compounds in poplar buds.

name: Balsam Poplar Bud Salve for Congestion
use: Cold, catarrh, and bronchitis congestion, salve rubbed inside the nostrils
method: Bud salve was rubbed inside the nostrils so its balsamic odor could reach the respiratory passages directly.
note: Rubbing an aromatic salve just inside the nostrils for chest congestion is functionally the same idea behind a modern menthol vapor rub: a scented, medicinal-smelling ointment placed close to the airway on the theory that its aroma alone eases breathing, using the very same balsam poplar buds that, prepared as a salve elsewhere, went straight onto cuts and bruises instead.
caution: Putting a nonsterile, fatty salve inside the nostrils carries a real risk of irritation or aspiration and is not a safe practice to copy.

name: Prickly Ash Bark for Quinsy & Sore Throat
use: Quinsy and sore throat
method: Bark, obtained by trading or traveling farther south where the tree grew, was used medicinally for throat complaints.
note: Quinsy, a severe throat abscess that could become genuinely dangerous before antibiotics existed, was serious enough that healers reportedly traveled south to obtain prickly ash bark specifically for it, since the tree didn't grow locally — a real logistical investment for a single ingredient, and a sign of how much the bark was trusted.
caution: A severe throat infection like quinsy can become dangerous and needs real medical care; the bark itself can also irritate the mouth and digestive tract.

name: Prickly Ash Berry Tea for Sore Throat
use: Sore throat, taken as a hot tea
method: Berries were brewed into a hot tea and drunk for sore throat.
note: Prickly ash's other common name, 'toothache tree,' comes from the genuinely numbing, tingling sensation its bark and berries produce on contact with tissue — the same effect that likely made a hot berry tea feel like it was doing something real for a sore, raw throat, whatever was actually causing the soreness.

name: Prickly Ash Berry Tea Chest Spray
use: Bronchitis congestion, sprayed on the chest
method: Hot berry tea was used as a spray applied to the chest to cool and relieve congestion.
note: Interestingly, this same tingling bark that felt warming as a throat tea was applied externally here and specifically described as cooling relief when sprayed on the chest — a reminder that 'hot' and 'cold' in old medical language often described the intended therapeutic effect, not the plant's actual temperature or a consistent physical sensation.
